body:
I have reservations. The proposed method is a worthy ergonomic addition to Rust's standard libraries, but the consequences are substantial. In brief:
1. The proposed method conflicts with an `Itertools` method of the same name.
2. The proposed `IteratorExt` trait opens a pandora's box of future conflicts.
author: jswrenn

body:
```suggestion
pub trait IteratorAlloc: Iterator {
```
I'd caution against calling this trait `IteratorExt`. The name isn't wrong—this *is* an extension trait of `Iterator` for contexts where `alloc` is available—but it's not the *only* reasonable extension trait of `Iterator` that could exist: what about an extension trait for `Iterator` that's usable in contexts where `std` is also available?

I'm *really* worried about the floodgates of future itertools breakage that this trait opens up. It's bad enough that the Itertools [readme](https://github.com/rust-itertools/itertools/blob/cae2ab2331d0fc365a7094f27f22b73ca731192a/README.rst#how-to-contribute) has to beg people not to contribute methods that could reside on `Iterator`, but at least we can welcome methods that involve allocation:
> However, if your feature involves heap allocation, such as storing elements in a Vec<T>, then it can't be accepted into libcore, and you should propose it for itertools directly instead.

An `IteratorExt` trait in `alloc` blows this advice up. If such a trait is introduced, I'm not sure there's *any* situation in which we can accept useful PRs without risking future conflict with the standard libraries. Itertools is less and less an ergonomic multitool than it is a ticking timebomb that will break your builds if you have the audacity to `rustup`. [**Can we *please* fix this problem?**](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2845)

author: Mark-Simulacrum

body:
Yeah, I've thought about that, but decided against. The problem with `stringify!` is that it erases whitesapce. While you still can use that for whitespace-insensitive comparison, producing a readable diff becomes hard.

It *is* possible to get whitespace back by reading-out the source of the file in case that you are going to produce an error anyway (which I actually didn't consider before).

Hm, yeah, I guess I still lean towards using just strings -- this is much simpler implementation wise, and I am not convinced that highlighting&completion are that much important -- the snippet in `expect` is inserted automatically, you rarely have to edit it by hand.

I'll be more worried about syntax highlighting in the input, which is genuinely valid rust-code. In rust-analyzer, we have a hack for that, but we need some form of stable custom attribute to generalize it (I guess we can use a no-op proc-macro, but that feels like an overkill for a syntax highlighting).

body:
So, I'm the current maintainer of Itertools. I'm *thrilled* to see this PR! `Intersperse` is widely useful, and very deserving of being a method on `Iterator`. My very first PR to Itertools was actually optimizing `Intersperse::fold`, because `chain`s of `Intersperse`ed tokens are widespread in the internals of the standard proc macro libraries.

> I personally suspect that it might not be a good idea to land this given the itertools conflict

I really wouldn't want Itertools to get in the way of a good addition. As an Itertools _user_, the fixes for these sorts of conflicts are pretty simple: you just used the fully-qualified method call syntax, or limit the scope of your import of `Itertools` so that your call to libcore's `intersperse` is unaffected. (For the uninitiated, the introduction of `Iterator::flatten` caused the same issues. I don't think it posed much more than a minor inconvenience.)

It's only as an Itertools _maintainer_ that these sorts of conflicts cause me a real headache. I really don't like that our README has to *discourage* contributions to minimize these sorts of issues, and I don't like not merging PRs that seem *so* useful that I can foresee them making their way into `Iterator`.

On that note, our upcoming 0.10.0 release is going to include [`intersperse_with`](https://github.com/rust-itertools/itertools/pull/381), a generalized form of `intersperse`. If `Iterator` is going to gain `intersperse`, it doesn't seem out of the question that it might want `intersperse_with` too. Should I cut it from the release to avoid a potential future conflict?

> in the future at least: itertools could have #[cfg(not(rust_has_intersperse))] on its extension trait method, set in build.rs via something like https://docs.rs/autocfg/1.0.1/autocfg/

This seems promising(!!!), but maybe a little unpleasant for contributors. Any new, non-allocating method added to `Itertools` poses a potential future conflict with `Itertools`. We'd need to test for *every* such method name in our `build.rs`. [I'd much prefer a permanent solution to this problem.](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2845)

body:
I believe this is an additional symbol. So that if you set this attribute on a function named `toto`, the compiler will generate the following assembly:
```text
toto:
__acle_se_toto:
    INSTRUCTIONS
```
and the `toto` symbol will be set as weak. That way the linker can create the veneer like so:
```text
toto:
    SG
    B.W __acle_se_toto
```
and the symbol `toto` and its address is passed to NS.

This is explained section 3.4.4 in [here](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ecm0359818/latest/).

I don't think it modifies the mangling. However, as you can see in the examples in this PR, I believe you would always use the `no_mangle` and `extern "C"` ABI on the entry functions as they go through FFI.

 ^~~

I believe LLVM should emit a similar error but I am not sure why it is not. I will investigate.

author: pickfire

body:
> But what's the point of a const function then?

It makes code like this compile:
```rust
const FOO: i32 = my_const_fn(13);
```
That code is rejected unless `my_const_fn` is a `const fn`.

That is the *only* effect `const` has on `fn`. And AFAIK we never say anything else anywhere in the docs, so I do not comprehend where all these extra assumptions come from that you have been making. I'd really like to know as I'd like to avoid people making such false assumptions. :)

>  I always thought that const means all of these happens in compile time and none of it goes to runtime except those called in non-const places.

Code in const "places" (usually called const contexts) *must* run at compiletime. So this statement is true but I don't think it means what you think it means. In particular, `format` is impossible to use in const contexts:
```rust
const FOO: String = format!("abc"); // does not compile
```
Since `format!` can only be used in non-const-contexts, that means it never happens at compiletime. Or rather, it is never guaranteed to happen at compiletime -- optimizations can do whatever they want, but there's no guarantee they ever happen.

body:
Thanks a lot for the PR. Sorry for my late review. 

The reasoning for adding this method makes sense and I'm on board merging it unstably. However, I strongly agree that the name still has to change. As @danielhenrymantilla said [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75911#issuecomment-694851468), it's confusing that "unwrap" and "drop" in the name don't refer to the same thing. I think `into_inner` is a pretty good name. Whether we rename/deprecate `try_unwrap` is another question.

Regarding the implementation: I checked it briefly and couldn't find any problems. However, this is code using relaxed atomics and I don't feel comfortable approving this kind of addition. I don't have experience with it and generally, it's a hard topic and the standard library was always very conservative with these kinds of changes. However, here, this is mostly just a copy of existing code and it seems to make sense to me. (And yes, I might or might not have spent the last 4 hours trying to understand `Arc::drop`.) So before merging this, I will probably ping the team to have a few more eyes on this.

Lastly, I left a few inline comments.

body:
I think you meant if `aligned_alloc` and `malloc` have the same requirements. I don't think they have the same requirement.

from manpages:
> The obsolete function memalign() allocates size bytes and returns a  pointer  to  the  allocated
    memory.  The memory address will be a multiple of alignment, which must be a power of two.

> The  function  aligned_alloc()  is the same as memalign(), except for the added restriction that
    size should be a multiple of alignment.

About the safety for `unsafe impl`, do you have a suggestion of what should I add? As most functions rely on the caller of safety.
author: Amjad50

body:
I am saying that the current safety comments are incorrect -- we cannot arbitrarily place requirements on our caller. The only "special" knowledge implementors of GlobalAlloc::alloc have is that [the passed Layout is non zero sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#safety-1).

In this case, calling `libc::malloc` should be entirely safe, AFAICT -- there are no preconditions that I can see in the man page. The safety comment on the malloc call should say something to that effect.

With regards to aligned_alloc, the "size should be a multiple of alignment" condition does not seem to be checked in this function, and I cannot find any reason that we can assume that is true. Do you have evidence otherwise? If not, we should likely file an issue and leave a FIXME here.

As to the `unsafe impl`, there should be a comment noting that each function in the trait has been checked to meet the requirements listed in the [safety section of the trait docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#safety). Obviously, we should make sure to actually do so :)
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body:
Ok, so `malloc` call is safe because it's guaranteed that non zero layout size will be passed.

Like you said there is no check here for layout `size` being a multiple of `alignment`, but is there  any check from the caller? If not, then maybe as you said we should file an issue for it.
author: Amjad50

body:
> Ok, so malloc call is safe because it's guaranteed that non zero layout size will be passed.

This does not seem to be a precondition of malloc, AFAICT. malloc call is just always safe.

We cannot assume that there is a check in the caller in unsafe code, unless the method documents such a precondition. GlobalAlloc::alloc does not. Filing an issue would be good.

>In what case can these casts cause unexpected behaviour? In this case the constant is definitely in the u64 range.<

(That specific "as" doesn't cause unexpected behaviour. But being willing to use "as" everywhere is like being against the presence of unsafe{} statement in Rust language on the base of the code inside a specific usage of unsafe{} in a program being evidently safe. Even if a specific usage of "as" is safe, it's a sharp tool, and it may lead to problems in other cases, so better to minimize its usage in a codebase. I can call this language blindness: what a language puts in front is visible and taken care of, what a language doesn't care about the programmer too doesn't care regardless the troubles it could cause. But eventually the unsafety of using "as" will come out in Rust culture. The recently introduced Rustc suggestions to use try_into are a step forward).

body:
Regarding the ipv4 in ipv6 concern by @KodrAus:

Using `to_ipv4` causes Rust to consider both ipv4-mapped and ipv4-compatible addresses, i.e. `::ffff:127.0.0.1` and `::127.0.0.1`. This is inconsistent with other languages:

| language | ipv4-mapped | ipv4-compatible | demo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Go | ✔️ | ❌  | https://play.golang.org/p/dqDfRtz0AGW |
| C# | ✔️ (since .NET 5)| ❌  | https://dotnetfiddle.net/hhYXgK |
| Java | ✔️ | ❌  | https://ideone.com/2U0peb |

IPv4-Compatible IPv6 address have also been officially deprecated for a long time https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75150#issuecomment-668680333, therefore I think it would be better to use `to_ipv4_mapped` everywhere.

Edit: I tried `ping ::ffff::127.0.0.1` and `ping ::127.0.0.1` on my machine, the mapped address worked and the compatible address gave `destination net unreachable`, an additional point why I think `::127.0.0.1` should not be recognized as a loopback address in Rust: to avoid user confusion.

body:
Two comments regarding the [IANA IPv6 special purpose address registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/iana-ipv6-special-registry/iana-ipv6-special-registry.xhtml):

Technically all IPv4-mapped addresses are designated as not globally reachable. However, the entire point of those addresses is to represent IPv4 addresses. So while e.g. `::ffff:1.1.1.1` is technically not globally reachable, most? applications will treat it as `1.1.1.1`, which is globally reachable. What should Rust do here? 

Also, this implementation ignores some other addresses in the registry designated as not globally reachable, such as IPv6 benchmarking addresses: `2001:2::/48`.
author: CDirkx

body:
> Technically all IPv4-mapped addresses are designated as not globally reachable. However, the entire point of those addresses is to represent IPv4 addresses. So while e.g. `::ffff:1.1.1.1` is technically not globally reachable, most? applications will treat it as `1.1.1.1`, which is globally reachable. What should Rust do here?

I really don't know one way or the other which option would be "more correct." My gut feeling is that it makes sense to kick the can down the road, and ignore IPv4-mapped addresses in this context, the reason being that if someone is trying to make their IP globally routable they likely won't want it to be IPv4-mapped.

> Also, this implementation ignores some other addresses in the registry designated as not globally reachable, such as IPv6 benchmarking addresses: `2001:2::/48`.

What do you think should be done to address this?

body:
It does sound like there's sort of a lot of potential here but the current `Hash/Hasher` API doesn't readily allow specializing like we want to.

I was looking at the Hasher API, and it feels like it might be worth adding something like a `write_hash` or similar, where the Hasher can expect the incoming value to already be "hashed" or at least nicely distributed across the range. To start we could just take a u64 since that's what `Hasher::finish()` returns, though e.g. for Fingerprint we really want u128. Maybe `fn write_hash(impl Into<u128>)` makes sense, not sure.

I am leaning towards saying that we should just merge this PR as-is: it seems like a clear, if small, win, and while there may be more hidden through careful hash-skipping it's probably better to evaluate each in a standalone manner, particularly given the relative complexity of the Unhasher design. We can consider other improvements, like the one I suggested in the previous paragraph, later.

body:
Yes, just double-checked that this ICEs without the changes in this PR.

I was kind of leaning on reviewers to be able to tell me if there's a better way of doing this. :) The important thing is that the span of interest is the same in all ways except end line/col in both compilations (i.e. file name, start line/col, and length). I'm not sure that's possible to do with the other testing methods, but that's mostly on account of being new. :)

Edit: as for what would cause it to ICE, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/74890#issuecomment-685898704 has the full analysis, but I'll summarize here. In the second compilation, `hir_owner(foo)` is considered green because the hash of the function's span doesn't account for the end line and column. This causes the serialized `optimized_mir(foo)` query result to be reused. The problem is that _that_ query result contains a span which it derived from the old function's span--in particular, it contains a span which started on the same line at which the old function ended. But the old function's span started on a line number which is beyond the end of the new file. When we deserialize the span in the `optimized_mir(foo)` result, we get line number which is out of bounds of the file in the new compilation session. We index the file's lines vector and ICE.

It's also possible for the query result to get reused without an ICE (the function span changed in end line/col only, but the old span's line number is still in bounds of the new file), but I'm not sure how it plays out and what the full ramifications are.

body:
> I think it's intended this way.

rustc not checking crate level attributes is very much a bug causing #64734 and #69365 for example. I would like to see a proper fix for this.

> What do you mean? As far as I can tell, it checks the crates' attributes once and that's it. Did I miss something?

You can see from where `check_mod_attrs` is called that it is called once per module in the crate: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/da897dfb6daa268a965d2d73620316ba56020a19/compiler/rustc_interface/src/passes.rs#L812-L818 and https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/445f34bb144c5b163163d8243e9845c644d3662d/src/librustdoc/core.rs#L514-L517

That means errors are emitted multiple times. This can be seen be compiling a crate with this PR applied like:

```rust
#![feature(doc_alias)]
#![doc(alias = "hello")]
mod foo {}
```

When `-Zdeduplicate-diagnostics=no` is passed to rustc or rustdoc the output is:

```
error: `#![doc(alias = "...")]` isn't allowed as a crate level attribute
 --> foo.rs:2:8
  |
2 | #![doc(alias = "hello")]
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

error: `#![doc(alias = "...")]` isn't allowed as a crate level attribute
 --> foo.rs:2:8
  |
2 | #![doc(alias = "hello")]
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

error: aborting due to 2 previous errors
```

Adding more modules causes the error to be repeated even more.

> In which case would we want to have a doc alias on the crate module itself?

I have no idea, but I also don't know why you would want doc aliases on any module. I'm fine with disallowing it because we can always allow it in the future if someone has a use case.

The leaked reference from `Box::leak` can not be `'static` in that case: it must not outlive `'x`. This is not an issue here, as `str` doesn't contain any references/lifetimes. body:
For `read` itself to be well-defined (not cause UB), it is sufficient to consider validity. The same is true for `assume_init`. For the latter we added a remark, which we should likely reference (but probably not copy to avoid duplication) from the other `assume_init` methods: it is dangerous to use this to create something that is "valid" but does not satisfy all library invariant, but if you are really careful in what you do with this data (i.e., you never call any library method, you jsut move the data around), you are fine.

This is very different from `drop`, which *calls library-controlled code on the data*, namely `T`'s drop implementation. That's why the extra library invariants are much more important for `drop` than for any other method.

Does this make sense? It's hard to explain these things without having solid established terminology, so if I should add some examples or so, let me know.

body:
> I wonder if it's worth just having C and Cunwind instead. I guess that's less good in most other ways. **[..]**

I thought about this as well! It would certainly make the changes specific to this file much easier :slightly_smiling_face: The primary reason I found that to be an unsatisfactory route forward was that RFC 2945 also includes [other `unwind` ABI strings](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2945-c-unwind-abi.md#other-unwind-abi-strings).

`stdcall-unwind`, `system-unwind`, and `thiscall-unwind` are specified currently, but the RFC also states that "_More unwind variants of existing ABI strings may be introduced, with the same semantics, without an additional RFC._"

Adding more `FooUnwind` variants would certainly be _possible_, but it felt like it would make the process of introducing these new unwinding variants much more prone to error. It would require manual auditing of our `match` statements, and the number of variants could become tough to manage.

The `debug_assert!` is an excellent idea, I will add an additional commit with this logic. I certainly bumped my head against an error that this assertion would have prevented while working on this PR! :angel:

In other words, I think we should have a test for the fastly use case, where we invoke a C function that invokes a Rust function which panics, and we test that this panic propagates up the stack. I'm not sure how easy/hard it will be to write such a test though, including C code might be a pain. At minimum we could have a test for panics propagating through Rust functions with C-unwind ABI (and perhaps the same but where those functions are in an auxiliary crate).

(Cross crate tests can be created by using the `// aux-build:` comments in tests; I didn't find any docs on this, but you can maybe grep around to see how it's done. You basically write `// aux-build: foo.rs` and then add a file `auxiliary/foo.rs`. You can then import the crate `foo`.)

body:
> It will be overridden if the more specific ones are set right? 

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/76625#discussion_r487408735

There are three main use cases I want to support (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76619):
1. people compiling from source, who don't care about all these fine subtleties and just want `--stage 2` for everything. They will be setting `stage = 2` in `config.toml`
2. new contributors, who will use the defaults: different stages for each command
3. frequent contributors (like me), who have strong opinions on what the defaults should be: different stages for each command, but with _different defaults_: `doc_stage = 1`.

Removing `stage` doesn't allow use case 1. Setting a default for `stage` makes it take precedence over the defaults for `doc_stage`, disallowing use case 3.

Yeah, for example call destinations must not alias any call arguments (maybe this only applies to copied arguments, as you mentioned). I ran into this when writing the destination propagation pass.

Unfortunately these invariants haven't really been consciously designed or documented from what I know, but the MIR validator does try to enforce them (or what I think is a reasonably approximation of them).

It seems that this pass is still correct though – aliasing restrictions generally only apply when one of the places is being mutated, and when that happens we invalidate all affected locals.

body:
There is also implicit assumption about when the move invalidates the local. As far as I can see this pass could make a following transformation:

```
_2 = _1
_3 = f(move _1, move _2);
```

```
_2 = _1
_3 = f(move _1, _1);
```

EDIT: Either way it it looks OK, just for far more subtle reasons.

But generally speaking the aliasing concerns do apply to the inputs alone in the move case. For example, running this optimization and then just before codegen turning copy operands into move operands results in the same miscompilation that affected copy propagation.

body:
The concerns of #62429 are mostly separate from the concerns of `fold` specialization. The overlap is just that using `fold` or `for_each` often introduces a generic closure.

The point of #62429 is that closures inherit *all* of the generic type parameters of the surrounding scope. In your example that would be `B`, `F`, and `Self` -- but the closure doesn't really need the whole iterator type, just `Self::Item`. So you can end up generating the same closure for `<B, F, vec::IntoIter<i32>>`, `<B, F, Cloned<hash_set::Iter<'_, i32>>>`, `<B, F, Map<Chain<Range<i32>, Once<i32>>, map-closure{...}>>`, etc., when our closure could be just `<B, F, Item = i32>`. This is a compile-time concern for excessive monomorphizations, and can also make it exceed type-length limits. There has been some compiler work to trim unused parameters, but it still doesn't know how to reduce that `Self` to `Self::Item`. So the trick in #62429 is to use a "closure factory" function with tighter control over the generic parameters.

The `fold` specialization is more about runtime performance, which is why it changes your benchmarks. For example, `Chain::next()` has to check its state every time it is called, whether to pull an item from its first or second iterator, whereas `Chain::fold()` can just fold all of the first iterator and then all of the second. The default `for_each` is just a `fold` with an empty `()` accumulator, which is why it also benefits here.

body:
I experimented with different implementation approaches:

1. Statistics definitions are in the context together with their values.
2. Statistics definitions are in MIR passes, their values are stored in the context.
3. Statistics definitions and values are stored together with MIR passes.

I strongly prefer variants that put statistics definitions together with MIR passes that uses them. In that approach, adding and removing counters is trivial, additionally any unused counters are detected as such during compilation.

Values can be stored in the context if we want to support multiple rustc sessions in a single process, although it requires passing context to all those places where counters are used. But is there any real use-case? Why would you use rustc with debug-assertions and MIR optimizations counters inside the RLS?
author: tmiasko

body: That would give a wrong impression that some form of synchronization is required here. Atomicity of RMW operations is sufficient for correctness.
author: tmiasko

body:
I agree with @bjorn3. We've tried pretty hard to move these sorts of things into `Session` and `TyCtxt` to allow running multiple sessions in the same process (both for RLS and eventually for one rustc process compiling multiple crates simultaneously). 

Since this is essentially unstable, diagnostic data and doesn't effect the compilation artifacts, it may be worth bending that rule because, as you point out, having the counters defined in their MIR passes is quite nice. I don't personally feel comfortable approving that since this is a cross-cutting concern for the compiler as a whole and there may be others on the compiler team that have strong opinions about breaking that rule.

I wouldn't otherwise weigh in, but since I am the assigned reviewer: my preference would be to keep poll_fn.

I think the *"idiom to use `from` and `into` when you create a value from another one"* is overstated. What does this mean? Functions with 1 argument (or 2, like ptr+len?) which return non-`()` and do not perform I/O? There are plenty of counterexamples with a clearer name, e.g. [iter::repeat](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/fn.repeat.html) I don't think would be clearer as iter::from / from_val / from_repeat / from_repeated_val / into_repeating / into_repeater / ...

`future::poll_fn` makes a future which polls a fn (poll as a verb) or you give it the implementation for its Future's poll fn (poll as a noun), so there are two sensible ways to internalize what this does that both draw exactly the correct distinction from other ways of treating a fn as a future.

> shouldn't this entire code just be self.inner.truncate(0) then? Also then len argument to this function... is it equal to self.inner.len()? If not why?

The len argument is not equal to self.inner.len(). Thus it's not equivalent to truncate. The elements up to `count` are initialized, the ones beyond until self.inner.len() aren't. Calling truncate would drop uninitialized data. ~But this reminds me, writing this felt a bit off and now I get where the problem was: it needs to be `Vec<MaybeUnint<T>>` instead of `Vec<T>`.~ Edit: disregard that, it's not a `Vec<MaybeUninit<T>>` but a plain old `Vec<T>` as each item at indices < len() is initialized. The length is just only updated once, instead of at each push call. This means the `set_len` call this thread is attached to is redundant.

body:
The concern as I understand it is that you have a crate tree that looks like:

```
      A
      | \
      |  B
      | / 
      C  
```

Where `A` has some function `fn foo<T>() { .. }` which `B` and `C` both instantiate for some type (ie, `B` and `C` both use `A::foo<u8>()`). Because we want to share the same instantiation of `A::foo<u8>()` within the crate `B`'s codegen units, it will not be a `LocalCopy` or marked private, then the symbol will be exported as part of `B` (although with visibility `Hidden`). Of course, the same logic applies to `C` and so now there will be two symbols in different crates with the same. 

This is where `may_conflict: true` comes in. When this is set, the mangled name for this instantiation includes information about the instantiating crate which means the symbols are no longer the same and thus linking will succeed. 

See also 

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3c45bff23dfbb13d9d28afe5dba57c028ba156da/compiler/rustc_symbol_mangling/src/lib.rs#L220-L233

> ### Disambiguating Function Calls
>
> Rust treats all function calls as sugar for a more explicit, fully-qualified syntax. Upon compilation, Rust will desugar all function calls into the explicit form. Rust may sometimes require you to qualify function calls with trait, depending on the ambiguity of a call in light of in-scope items.
>
> > Note: In the past, the Rust community used the terms "Unambiguous Function Call Syntax", "Universal Function Call Syntax", or "UFCS", in documentation, issues, RFCs, and other community writings. body: Function pointer equality is not well defined, since we give functions to LLVM as `unnamed_addr` which means their address is claimed to not be significant to the execution of the program. See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/54685. This expression can evaluate to unequal even if lookup failed, and can evaluate to equal even if lookup succeeded. Is there a different way to implement is_available, or is there some reason to believe this wouldn't hit bizarre behavior?
author: dtolnay

body:
Oh, interesting. Thanks.

If I understand correctly, `unnamed_addr` allows for merging functions. Meaning that `f1 == f2` might give true for different functions, but not that `f1 == f1` might give false for the same function. So false positives, but not false negatives. That would be fine here. The functions loaded from `GetProcAddress` are definitely not merged with `fallback` (since they come from external `dll`), and that's the only one that matters. If multiple `fallback` functions happen to have the same address for example, that's fine.

So the question here is whether 'the address is not significant' means 'not significant but at least constant', or that it may assume`f != f`.

Disabling `unnamed_addr` on `fallback` would also work, but it seems there's no way to do that in Rust.
author: m-ou-se

body:
Ah, @eddyb tells me *rustc itself* might *duplicate* functions too. So, in this snippet it could mean that `fallback as usize` (which is short for `fallback as fn() as usize`) might result in a copy of `fallback`. Using a `static FALLBACK: fn(..) = fallback;` and using that static instead should prevent that. The assumption that that works is already made in `core`:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/9cba260df0f1c67ea3690035cd5611a7465a1560/library/core/src/fmt/mod.rs#L246-L267

See also https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/54685#issuecomment-425864863

I'll update the PR to do the same.

body:
@tmandry @wesleywiser - I don't think this is practical at the current time. There are very few special cases now. (There used to be more, but I was able to remove most of them.) The special cases that are left are (for the most part) necessary right now.

I think the only way to avoid this in the long term would require removing the spans from `StorageLive` and `StorageDead` (which I doubt is feasible). But that's just moving the special case handling outside of the InstrumentCoverage pass.

From a coverage perspective, these statements are problematic because their spans refer to the variable declarations, which are quite often in a completely different area in the source from where they actually need to come alive or die.

(Control Flow vs. Data Flow)

As for the other "special cases", I could remove `Coverage` and `Nop`. They are just included for completeness, but should not crop up here anyway.

The `ForGuardBinding` special case is definitely something I would like to remove, but there's already a FIXME for that. That's there because there is a bug somewhere else in the MIR code (I guess) producing an invalid Span.

author: tmiasko

body:
> Without seeing this discussion, I would presume that Process owns the pidfd and will close it on drop.

If we do that, then I think we should add a way to prevent this behavior (other then calling `mem::forget` on the `Child`). Otherwise, users who just need the pidfd will be forced to potentially leak memory (if `Child` ever heap allocates internally), or keep a `Child` around when it's not actually needed.

> The pidfd should be closed when clone3 succeeds but exec fails, since a user has no ability to do so on their own, right?

The pidfd only exists in the parent process. Once `clone3` succeeds, the pidfd is perfectly useable, regardless of what happens in the child process from that point on.

body:
> If we do that, then I think we should add a way to prevent this behavior (other then calling mem::forget on the Child). 

To keep things RAII we should introduce a new wrapper type akin to other fd-wrapping IO types such as `File`, `TcpStream` and so on. E.g. `struct ProcessDescriptor(RawFd)` which could implement `Drop`.

Then `Child` could have
* `take_pidfd(&mut self) -> ProcessDescriptor` 
* `pidfd(&self) -> &ProcessDescriptor`

`ProcessDescriptor` then could implement `IntoRawFd` and `AsRawFd`

body:
The storage names are rather internal, and `--default-setting` sets them directly.  That's good for flexibility but it is rather too raw.

Indeed, as you can see from the implementation, `--default-theme` doesn't just set the `theme` setting.  Because of the way the "use system theme" option and the light/dark themes operate, since #77809, it is necessary to change the default for "use system theme" to "false" for the `--default-theme` option to work.

Indeed, I think this fact about #77809 shows that my pre-#77809 approach of having a raw `--default-setting` option, and a cooked `--default-theme` option, was correct.  Before #77809, `--default-theme` just set the `theme` setting.  Now it does more.

Notice that the stability caveats for the two options are rather different.  Another aspect of this is that it might easily make sense to stabilise the `--default-theme` option soon, after we've had some experience with it.  Stabilising the raw `--default-setting` option would involve thinking about what additional promises that would imply (maybe none that we care about? but I'm not sure and it's certainly harder to think about)
author: ijackson

body:
Yes.  That is inevitable and deliberate.  As you can see from the usage message we do not make any promises about the particular behaviour of `--default-setting`.  The available settings and their semantics and not documented and not stable.

Whereas the semantics of `--default-theme` are well-defined, and are implemented by setting the two internal settings.

I do think it is worth keeping `--default-setting` even despite these caveats because in practice the storage settings are visible to users via their browser and of course if they look at the JS.

The difference between `--default-setting` and `--default-theme` is like the difference between firefox's `about:config` and `about:preferences`.

Basically my few comments apply to all of the changes. I don't see the benefit in documentation of the form:

```rust
/// Adds one to the `u8` called `a` and returns it
fn add_one(a: u8) -> u8 { a + 1 }
```

Documentation should describe the things that the code doesn't/can't tell us, such as nuances or warnings or usage guidance. 

On the other hand, putting implementation details into the documentation is dangerous because a decision has to be made about if those details are things we want to commit to forever. See [the blurb in `std::io`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/index.html#platform-specific-behavior) as an example about guarding against that.

The problem with that reasoning is that people aren't _using_ it as if it's unstable. `module@` does not seem particularly niche to me and neither does `function@`. One design that was floated in our Libs meeting was to define `Backtrace::capture` and co in `std`, so there would be no way (yet) to capture a `Backtrace` in `core`, even though we could refer to one there. That could remove the need for figuring out hooks right now. Supposedly adding impl blocks in `std` to types defined in `core` is something we can already do. An alternative option could be a free `backtrace::capture` function.

So this would look something like `RawWaker::new` where it accepts a `*mut dyn RawBacktrace`.
author: KodrAus

body: I am in favor of this idea. As added bonus it would probably (unstably) allow arbitrary backtraces to be constructed for for example language level backtraces in interpreters or jit engines. Or allow mixing of language level and native frames.

So `WithOptConstParam` is used if we ever call `type_of` for the mir body. 

As we call `type_of` in some annoyingly annoying places, we have to somehow get the `DefId` of the relevant const param there.

body:
The invariant of `WithOptConstParam` is that if `self.const_param_did.is_some()`, then `self.const_param_did == tcx.opt_const_param_of(self.did)`. To prevent cycle errors `self.const_param_did` should also be `Some` if it is used during `typeck`, `did` is a const argument and we want to know `tcx.type_of(did)`, which we then replace with `tcx.type_of(def.def_id_for_type_of())`.

You should never have to call `try_upgrade` except at the start of a query taking `ty::WithOptConstParam` so that we only evaluate it once.

It is okay to use `unknown` if we are either done with typeck or `tcx.opt_const_param_of(self.did)` would/did return `None`.

Looks like it might be worth it to add a section to the rustc-dev-guide about `WithOptConstParam` :thinking:

We don't deduplicate automatically at the error level, we do it on a case by case basis ahead of time. For `_` E0121 errors it was a bit ad-hoc (introduced in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/69148).

I remember having to [tweak the logic a bit to have correct coverage](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pulls?q=is%3Aclosed+is%3Apr+author%3Aestebank+bad+placeholder+type+) (the `self.tcx().sess.delay_span_bug(span, "bad placeholder type");` in one of the `ty_infer` impls had triggered a couple of times due to it). I would imagine that we'll need to do something along the lines of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/70294 because two different codepaths that evaluate `static`s end up calling `placeholder_type_error`.

Edit: Oh! I see, this only happens for `const`/`static` for trait types. This is exactly the same type of duplicated problem I was seeing. I _think_ you can get away by looking at the type we're evaluating...

body:
This was me moving things for hypothetical cache friendliness (though I know the default representation doesn't guarantee anything), without going as far as using `#[repr(C)]` or `#[repr(C, align(N)]`. I didn't go that far, because I don't have the performance numbers to really justify it. I didn't gather cache hit/miss numbers either, though I suppose I could.

I was thinking that `nbuf` shouldn't follow `buf`, because then the beginning of `buf` and `nbuf` would be on different cache lines, which might pessimize performance for small total input lengths. I realize now that it probably doesn't happen that way in practice. The whole structure has to be touched in `new_with_keys` anyway, and everything is needed in `finish128`, so things are probably in cache for the entire hashing process for small inputs.

Still, the general access pattern during the core of the hashing process is `nbuf` -> `buf` -> `nbuf` -> `buf` -> ... -> `state` -> `processed`, so it's not the worst layout.

body:
Your example seems to be an infinite loop, since bb3 jumps to bb4, which then again repeatedly jumps to bb4. Did you intent this loop?

**If you meant false: bb6 in the switchInt of bb4:**

That happens here https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/77486/files#diff-cd637909adce5b1294c12644e9783b7eR19-R31.
I think bb2 and bb3 can be seen as isolated cases.

bb2 will execute the following sequence of operations:
- `_2 = const true;`
- `goto -> bb4;`
- `switchInt(_2) -> [false: bb4, otherwise: bb5];` // since _2 is true, this jumps to bb5.
The optimization will replace `goto -> bb4` with `goto -> bb5` in bb2.

bb3 will execute the following sequence of operations:
- `_2 = const false;`
- `goto -> bb4;`
- `switchInt(_2) -> [false: bb4, otherwise: bb5];` // since _2 is false, this jumps to bb4.
The optimization will replace `goto -> bb4` with `goto -> bb6` in bb2.


In both bb2 and bb3, _2 is not written to in the sequence of operations, which is why I think it is okay.

```rust
fn copy_nonoverlapping(&mut self, src: OpTy, dst: OpTy, count: OpTy) { ... }

Note that `OpTy` is `interpret::Operand` + type information; don't confuse that with `mir::Operand`. The JS code previously used the search index to fill the crate list in the sidebar, and used the (plaintext) summary for search result as the alt-text (actually the `title` attribute) on each crate in the list. But now the search result summaries are HTML. However, we can't use HTML in the alt-text since it is rendered literally to the user, i.e. if you hover over an element it will show a tooltip that looks like "This crate has a \<code\>Foo\</code\> struct". It used to look like "This crate has a \`Foo\` struct".

So the solution I went with for now is to still get the alt-text from the search index, but to first pass it through a function to convert it to plaintext. So I think the worst that can happen if this function doesn't work correctly is that the alt-text will look a little funny. Personally I think for now we should go with this approach and then in a separate PR change it so that it doesn't convert the HTML to plaintext in the JS. **P.S.** When I say "alt-text" I mean the text in the tooltip that is shown when you hover over an element.

body: > we have the same issue as in [#68699 (comment)](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/68699#issuecomment-627465641) that we don't know what was originally html and what was markdown I do not think that is correct. The example given in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/68699#issuecomment-627465641 was: ```rust /// foo `this is a code span` bar \`this isn't\` baz pub struct Foo; ``` That is stored in the search index as: ```html foo this is a code span bar `this isn't` baz ``` And then `convertHTMLToPlaintext` converts that into: ``` foo `this is a code span` bar `this isn't` baz ``` Which is *exactly* the same as the current hover text (that you get with rustdoc nightly). ----- That said, I am open to just stripping every HTML tag if we decide that would be better. I just don't think https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/68699#issuecomment-627465641 is relevant.

body:
In principle, the PR makes sense. There are two things that concern me, though:

1. Since the feature is exposed by defining a new function on an existing trait, this could be a breaking change. I know it's an obscure case, but still, the Rust Project aims to provide an objective definition of non-breaking changes.
2. This feature works on an entire command-line, rather than individual args. So this solves your current need, but it's easy to imagine a case in the future where you wanted to pass an arg string like `"foo*.c" bar*`, which would not be possible with this PR.

Perhaps a better approach would be to allow the caller to provide a verbatim `String` that provides exactly the arg that is passed to `CreateProcess`. That way, callers who know they're on Windows and know that they need control over argument parsing can provide exactly the string that they want.

@JohnTitor I just took a look at this. The problem is that `is_lowercase(𝕟)` is true but `to_uppercase(𝕟) == 𝕟`. Changing `char_has_case` to instead of asking whether the char is `lowercase ^ uppercase`, we can do `c.to_lowercase().to_string() != c.to_uppercase().to_string()`. body:
That could make sense. After all the PascalCase convention for types is good to differentiate them from bindings and functions, but when writing a struct or trait called 𝛅 you probably are encoding "business logic" with prior conventions. It doesn't make that much sense to complain about it. The problem is that then we _wouldn't lint any of these cases then_. Maybe we need _two_ lints, for different levels of checks: one for the "simple" rule check of what PascalCase is "supposed to be" and another for the more lenient but also more useful in practice check of "can this string be mechanically changed into a valid form". But that would be... likely controversial. I guess if you're doing "mathy" things, you would just have to disable the lint...

I am somewhat surprised at the behavior here because although 𝕟 doesn't have a corresponding upper-case character, 𝕞  does: 𝕄, but `to_uppercase` doesn't touch it, it ignores all math symbols and gives you the same symbol, which is why the `to_lowercase(x) != to_uppercase(x)` check would be more resilient.

author: m-ou-se

body:
That's a very good question. I believe `TrustedLen` is actually too weak here and we always need `TrustedRandomAccess`.

With `TrustedLen` we could get `(usize::MAX, None)` and then don't know anything more about the length other than it being big. So the assumption would have to be `idx < len || len == usize::MAX` and that defeats the whole purpose of this PR.

`TrustedRandomAccess` OTOH gives us the guarantee that `len < usize::MAX`. That's not specifically written in the documentation of that trait (I'll add it now), but otherwise wouldn't work for its purpose (the specialized `Zip`).
author: sdroege

body: `ExactSizeIterator` + `TrustedLen` would work equally well. The former guarantees that the length fits into an `usize`, the latter guarantees that it's actually the length.

body:
Yeah that seems problematic. I'm looking now into implemented `TrustedRandomAccess` in a few places that are `TrustedLen` but not `TrustedRandomAccess` yet. That should make the difference here smaller and also generally improve performance of those iterators so useful anyway.

I guess the main place where this can't be done (easily?) is for types like `BTreeMap` or `HashMap` that don't have an easy way of implemented `Iterator::__get_unchecked()`.
author: sdroege

body:
Considering that `TrustedLen` is unsafe + unstable + `rustc_unsafe_specialization_marker` it is more or less implied that any type that implements it is some iterator owned by the standard library. Which means there are no lifetime shenanigans that would make `ExactSizeIterator` unsafe for min_specialization.
Using that justification a `rustc_unsafe_specialization_marker` helper trait inheriting from both should be fine. Probably.

On the other hand `TrustedRandomAccess` is extending its tendrils into ever more places, so soon it should be almost equivalent in power to `TrustedLen + ExactSizeIterator`.
author: the8472

body: `TrustedRandomAccess` seems like it would always be more specific than `TrustedLen+ExactSizeIterator`. Implementing the former on things like `BTreeMap` would probably be not a good idea, while `TrustedLen+ExactSizeIterator` would be easy.

Ok, I see the issue: if you have something like

```rust
/// [reference][link] and [inline](link)
```
both `link`s should give an error, but if you don't include `cache_resolution_failure` in the cache key, then the second link will pick up the `None` and be returned.

So I have a further question now - when will you hit the cache and *not* have `cache_resolution_failure` set? That would only happen for `[inline](link)` twice in a row, right? But we explicitly choose *not* to insert it into the cache on error. I think there's an optimization here where you can make the size of the cache smaller by explicitly checking `cache_resolution_failure` on a cache hit, that way you don't need that extra bit of info; and the logic seems more clear to me too.

body:
In the current patch, if this is `[b]: ref`, the error emitted for `[reference link][b]` will point to the definition of `a`. This is because the link cache ignores the name of the reference and handles a and b as if identical. This isn't ideal, but I consider this acceptable: we don't report all errors, but if the user fixes link `a`, we will report an error for link `b`, so eventually, every error can be caught :)

We could fix this by adding the span to `ResolutionInfo` (Optionally, only for Shortcut/Reference links), but I'm not sure if the complexity is worth it. This would also make `ResolutionInfo` and `DiagnosticInfo` overlap, if only optionally.

Indeed, `rustdoc` uses the public-reachability info to decide whether or not to inline the definition of the item when it is left unspecified.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/76188b6830897a875a1289809c12b5c5d69bb7ef/src/librustdoc/visit_ast.rs#L179-L184

If `rustc` says the item is always publicly reachable, then `rustdoc` decides not to inline the definition, which is thus then missing when the private items are stripped.

I have hacked my way around this limitation with https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/77862/commits/73369151b4278ca665494d449c3e4d8e1278d5ba, but I'd welcome some feedback regarding what is deemed the best course of action, here.

  - cc @jyn514 @petrochenkov

author: tesuji

body:
I've considered an enum, and think that #77604 is a good idea, but in this instance a number feels more natural to me.

1. Enums have to be imported, which causes overhead. Most of the present enums in the spec module are on the optional `TargetOptions` structure, so only have to imported by the few targets that specify those options. @petrochenkov 's PR moves the only enum currently imported by all target files `LinkerFlavor` into `TargetOptions`.

2. Ideally one would have `PointerWidth::16` or something, but identifiers can't start width digits, so it'd be `PointerWidth::W16` or something, which isn't pleasant IMO.

3. Many places in the compiler assume the values to be integers already, some also do comparisons with other widths specified.

That being said, there are advantages of enums, main one is that one can build exhaustive matches throughout the compiler, and that it's immediately clear that only 16,32,64 bits are supported.

body:
@est31 I guess `ExactSizeIterator` isn't `unsafe` and so it's technically allowed to misbehave? I'm not sure.

Regarding the memory question:

TypedArena works in pages. When a page can't hold the requested data, a new page is created. The allocator then uses pointers in the last page. This complicates things a bit, but I don't think by a huge deal.

If an allocation panics, we can drop the memory that *we* allocated, as well as the memory that the inner operations allocated. We know about these regions, because we have them saved on our stack, or we can if currently something is missing.

If a nested tree of of `alloc_from_iter` calls fail for whatever reason, the panic will bubble up, and can be caught by each level of alloc call, basically unwinding their work.

~~The only question is, how do I bubble up the innermost panic? :)~~

Since `Iterator` isn't `UnwindSafe`, this looks like a lot more complicated than what should be done.

body:
Both write_place(expr) and propagate_through_expr(expr) will use the same live node for path expressions. Using them with the same expression is incorrect, since they will overwrite the previous content. In this case propagate_through_expr will access with READ & USED, overwriting WRITE set by write_place, which will lead to a false negative if a result of inout is in fact unused and should be warned about.

The inout case is quite unlike anything else here, but the initial version looked correct to me. A few additional positive & negative test cases should clarify the situation.

Implementation LGTM; I think I like this change, but I'd like to clarify a few things. These are the primary cases that this concerns, right?

- Alias has same name as type that it aliases - alias would be printed using the full path, but (more common) use of type wouldn't (e.g. `Result`). This seems reasonable, improves the common case and I don't *think* it'd lead to much confusion.
- Alias has the same name as an entirely unrelated type (from a different crate, for example), alias would be printed using the full path and if unrelated type were used then it would have its short path printed. Could this lead to a user using alias `Foo` without a path throughout their code, and then having type `Foo` (used in their code as `foo::Foo`) be printed without the full path in diagnostics? Wow, I had to do some archeology for this! The comment was first introduced in 1bceb98084b0e1010d123f48785a89bc7ad7e40f all the way back in 2013. `fn enforce_object_limitations` was removed in 8d8d8d4e5292c2fa4a622d981a5f85fd3d8f34d0 and replaced by `fn check_object_safety`, but the comment was never updated. Then `check_object_safety` gets removed in 843db01bd925279da0a56efde532c9e3ecf73610 and the check is moved to `report_selection_error` in src/librustc/middle/traits/error_reporting.rs. That got me far enough that I found that the error is `SupertraitSelf` and now lives in `compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/object_safety.rs`.

In short I think it would be helpful to mention `SupertraitSelf` so other people can find this in the future.
```suggestion

```

body:
This one is hard to get rid of because it's shared between `DocContext` and `clean::Crate`. `clean::Crate` only seems to use it as a bridge between `DocContext` and `Cache`

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/9b471a3f5fe57e5c6e08acf665f2094422415a3d/src/librustdoc/clean/types.rs#L58-L60

`Cache` then `take`s the data

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/src/librustdoc/formats/cache.rs#L164

I think we'll need bigger architectural changes, like passing the field directly to `Cache`, in order to get rid of the intermediary. Doing that should make the code clearer and reduce the potential for sneaky bugs like giving the field to `Cache` via `Crate` and then trying to use the `DocContext` version later and finding nothing in it.

body:
This breakdown helps, thanks. I don't want to prematurely optimize but it's nice to have a mental model for thinking about later if it is a problem.

If it were O(n log n) the number of dominators per node would have to be O(log n) which doesn't seem obviously right to me.

(The simplest counterexample – a long function with no branching – would be one long BCB, which highlights the benefits of simplifying the graph into BCBs. But I suspect one could possibly extend that idea to construct a graph whose dominators grew as a linear factor of the length of the function.)

Maybe it's easiest to leave that as a separate parameter?

Yeah that description does not seem to have much to do with what the PR does (but our [terminology](https://github.com/rust-lang/const-eval/blob/master/promotion.md) is likely somewhat confusing^^).

A short summary could be something like: promotion of references to `'static` lifetime inside `const fn` now follows the same rules as inside `fn`; in particular, `&foo()` will not be promoted to `'static` lifetime any more inside `const fn`.

This is a bugfix, we should never have done this to begin with (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/75586). It is part of an ongoing effort to fix promotion, and then to restrict it a bit further to make it less painful throughout the compiler (see https://github.com/rust-lang/const-eval/issues/53).

body:
I was thinking it might be nice to say _why_ this is such a big deal.

````suggestion
- [You can now link to items in `rustdoc` using the intra-doc link
  syntax.][74430] Before, you would have to know exactly how rustdoc generated its URLs:
  
  ```rust
/// [`Send`] is in the standard library.
  
/// [`Send`]: ../std/marker/trait.Send.html
  
  Now, you can now write:
  ```rust
  /// [`Send`] is in the standard library.
  ```
  to automatically generate a link to `Send`'s documentation. Rustdoc will give a warning if the link fails to resolve, which means in most cases you no longer need an external tool to ensure your documentation has no broken links.

See ["Linking to items by name"][intradoc-links] for more information.
````

(most cases -> see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/77199, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/77200, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75855, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/77971)

In particular, the coherence code accepts distinct impls (as eddyb demonstrated) for some such cases.

> Right, I understand. I guess inserting into a slice of genuine values is a bad idea, because there is no way for a slice to know how to expand its footprint.

Exactly. However, making those functions return a slice of `MaybeUninit` is probably the best solution (assuming this is not too hard on other callers). Then the slice no longer claims to be fully initialized. (However this means the function needs to be made `unsafe` as it relies on the caller not doing weird stuff like putting a `MaybeUninit::uninit` into one of the existing slice elements.)

> I do use Miri from rustup, but sometimes and right now it doesn't swallow the code in the Rust master branch. Until a day or two later, rustup finds an update and all is right again. I managed to build Miri in the past, but never figured out how to apply that in a x.py build.

Since you just need the standard library from an x.py build, something like this should work:
* Clone [this branch](https://github.com/RalfJung/miri/tree/track-raw)
* check rust-version file, and use that commit as your basis for the rustc PR
* in Miri, install the right rustc: `./rustup-toolchain`
* in Miri, `XARGO_RUST_SRC=/path/to/rustc/library ./miri run tests/run-pass/btreemap.rs -Zmiri-track-raw-pointers`

If you get weird build failures in the standard library in the last step, your rustc checkout does not match the rustc that Miri was built against -- it has to be exactly what `rust-version` says (or "close enough" without any incompatible changes). Actually, it doesn't seem useful to change `key_at` after all. To copy a slice from one node to another, miri-track-raw-pointers wants the source pointer to point something it can read entirely, not just the first element. Which is sensible and easy to do, but it leaves `key_at` only useful to read a key.

The next problem, to which I don't see a way out at the moment, is `as_internal_mut()`:

```
302 |         unsafe { &mut *(self.node.as_ptr() as *mut InternalNode<K, V>) }
    |                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ trying to reborrow for Unique at alloc22839+0x140, but parent tag <58889> does not have an appropriate item in the borrow stack
    |
```

We disguise a `*mut InternalNode` as a `*mut LeafNode` to squeeze it into `BoxedNode`, and there's no way around that. Now how do we unpack such a party pooper and convince Miri that this is an InternalNode?

-Zmiri-track-pointer-tag tracks the tag to the creator, `BoxedNode::from_internal`:
```
BoxedNode { ptr: Unique::from(&mut Box::leak(node).data) }
```

It does not help to make the reference raw:
```
BoxedNode { ptr: unsafe { Unique::new_unchecked(&raw mut Box::leak(node).data) } }
```

body:
One class of methods that has been very clear to me from the start, is those on a plain `self` like `first_edge`, `left_kv`: they simply return the same ownership, borrowship, or whatever you call it.

Next to the easy ones are those on a plain `self` called `into_X` (where I think the unwritten rule is that X is a part of the original, not a neighbour). Some of them return an `'a`  lifetime, which stems from the `NodeRef`'s `marker::Immut<'a>`/`ValMut<'a>`/`Mut<'a>`. It didn't understand what that implied for a long time, but they didn't look daunting either, thanks to the plain `self`.

I now understand why there is both `into_key_at` and `key_at`: because the former profits from the lifetime incorporated into `marker::Immut<'a>`/`ValMut<'a>`/`Mut<'a>`, and the latter is defined and used for all 3 of those, and the only way to do that is to define it over some `BorrowType` without lifetime. Therefore you can write the latter using the former, but not the other way around. `into_key_at` is easy enough and more sophisticated.

Therefore I turned all the new/changed function into the `into_X` class, and I like it.

I'm leaning towards keeping them separate, since mode changes (as currently designed) are trivial and doesn't touch the buffer, but modifying the buffer size is not.

> but we only mutate the vector after the inner iterator finishes.

The [UnsafeCell](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/cell/struct.UnsafeCell.html) docs say:

> A &mut T must always be unique.

And:

> There is *no* legal way to obtain aliasing &mut, not even with UnsafeCell<T>.

If you used `Cell` instead of `UnsafeCell` you'd get an unwrap error when the second level of `alloc_from_iter` tries to get a mutable reference. You could either call `as_ptr` instead, and work with `* mut`, or limit the lifetime of the `&mut` so that it doesn't stick around when the for loop's next function is called. It's a solvable problem, not the end of this PR, unless I'm missing something.

body:
The idea is that– suppose the buffer size is 10. If we have an incoming write of [12, ...], it makes sense to just write it directly and skip the buffer. On the other hand, if we have an incoming write of [2,2,2,2,2,2, ...], we don't want to issue 6 small writes (since we know the wrapped writer is `!is_write_vectored()`), we want to buffer as much as possible together.

Suppose now that the incoming write is [2,2,2,20]. When we reach the `20`, we have a decision to make– do we leave it for a future write, when it can be forwarded directly, or do we buffer as much as possible? I chose to buffer as much as possible, because the follow-up write will be 16, which can still be forwarded directly. It can't result in any *more* writes than we've already seen.

Essentially, once we've *started* to buffer something, we can no longer make attempts to *forward* anything (because we have to report `Ok(n)`). So it's just a decision of "when do we stop buffering stuff", and I think for `write_vectored` the best answer is "when the buffer is full".

body: In what ended up being a very long and surprisingly enjoyable refactor, `BufWriter` now takes advantage of vectored writes when it makes sense to do so! The key new method is `flush_buf_vectored`, which is the same as `flush_buf` but will also attempt to send *new* data via a vectored write during the flush. Critically, it only continues writing while there is still unflushed data in the buffer; once the buffer is empty (even if none of the *new* data has been sent) it will return immediately. I'm certainly assuming that no one is *going out of their way* to use vectored writes if it isn't imminently convenient to do so, and in particular they probably aren't dynamically doing their own "buffering" of IoSlice objects to eventually forward. For instance, `write_fmt` isn't going to be creating a buffer of IoSlice for writing the constitutent parts. I'm instead assuming that people are using vectored writes in cases where they happen to already have a fixed set of buffers available; for instance, an HTTP protocol might use it to forward HTTP headers, or a variant of `println` might use it to append a newline to the base content.

This reflects my own usage of `write_vectored` in `BufWriter`; I only call it in cases where I conveniently have a fixed set of buffers I'm interested in writing.

The quoted documentation from @m-ou-se supports this "always return true" behavior: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/78551#issuecomment-719483925

Surrounding in parentheses should not disable destructuring (but should trigger the unnecessary parenthesisation lint), which matches how patterns work. (That is, this implementation should be tweaked to ignore parentheses.)

I think this "shielding" is a bug in the current implementation. From the RFC:

> We also allow arbitrary parenthesisation, as with patterns, although unnecessary parentheses will trigger the unused_parens lint.
author: varkor

body:
I agree with @varkor. The "shielding behavior" of parentheses is a bug and I'll fix it. 

> (Yes, there's a symmetry with `(..)` in patterns, but I'm not sure supporting that in patterns was a good idea in the first place.)

Well, for better or for worse, patterns work that way now. I think it would add more inconsistency to disallow `(..)` in destructuring assignments now. The RFC doesn't make an exception for it, so I don't think we should just depart from what the RFC says.

> This case has no practical value, but has to be specifically implemented.

Implementation complexity shouldn't be a reason for inconsistent behavior. I don't see a super convincing use case for `(..)` in patterns either. A somewhat convincing use case would be usage in a macro `m!(x1, x2, x3)` generating `(x1, x2, x3, ..) = foo()` , which would otherwise have to special case the empty sequence `(..)`. A lot of constructs in Rust don't have a use case (just have a look at https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/src/test/ui/weird-exprs.rs), but they are allowed *for consistency*.

body:
I always wondered the same question. Funamentally an IPv4 address is a 32-bit integer, and an IPv6 is a 128-bit integer. For IPv4 especially, these integers don't have hardcoded semantics regarding their position, as ever since the custom netmask days you could arbitrarily split it into a network/host component, e.g. 1.2.3.4/27. So splitting into octets of 8 bits is arbitrary and only useful for presentation, which should be done with Display or some other trait, rather than the core representation. Additionally, this split might make low-level operations (such as computing ip+netmask map either slower, or require more complex code, than just doing bitwise addition of two 32-bit integers.

IPv6 may be more complex in case different parts have more fixed semantics, but even then it's different than 16 octets of 8 bits.
author: egilburg

body:
I'd welcome benchmarks showing which representation is more efficient performance wise. Most of the methods on `Ipv4Addr` work on octets though. Even the constructor happens to take the four octets separately, and not a single 32 bit integer. As a result most of the implementation was shorter and cleaner when represented as `[u8; 4]`.

If we were to represent it as a `u32` I have no doubt there would be a long debate about whether or not it should be stored as host byte order or network byte order. If going for a "ideal Rust layout" I'd definitely argue for host byte order though.

I don't have a super strong opinion on `[u8; 4]` vs `u32`. But this at least makes the code a bit simpler, and the byte order becomes more apparent.

The option to get clippy out of the way is to sprinkle `#[allow(clippy::or_fun_call)]` in the few places where this is deemed overly detrimental. 
Problem I have with that is now we have to do `#[allow(...)]` in a bunch of files to silence the 3,000 or so warnings clippy has. Some lints do not say how to disable them, and so we have to change clippy to help cleanup this repository. 
Additionally, some of these lints are useful, but if we freely `allow` them, we will never learn which ones are. Only through trying to apply the changes will the community learn which lints to heed, which give false positives, and which are to be ignored always.
author: Nicholas-Baron

body: I personally also feel that some of these changes slightly worsen readability without having a benefit apart from silencing clippy. I do agree with https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/78814#issuecomment-723257685 here and would prefer to explicitly uplift lints we deem useful, or even keep them in clippy and add them to CI if they are really relevant but do not quite fit into rustc, for example `invalid_regex`.
author: lcnr

body:
> The option to get clippy out of the way is to sprinkle #[allow(clippy::or_fun_call)] in the few places where this is deemed overly detrimental.

That is assuming the *goal* is to reduce clippy lints. But the lints are only a means to an end, especially when they are inaccurate heuristics. The actual goal of the lint in question is to improve performance. If there are many cases when it doesn't it should only be used as a tool to search for optimization candidates, not as a guide how to rewrite all code.

So then the question should be "which subset of cases are most useful?". Any file containing any other case would be silenced with an `#[allow(clippy::or_fun_call)]`.

I think we can keep the resolution-based check in a slightly different form for diagnostics.

If `self.resolver.get_partial_res(id)` returns `Some(partial_res)` and `partial_res.unresolved_segments() == 0` and `!matches!(partial_res.base_res(), Res::Def(DefKind::Ctor(_, CtorKind::Fn), _) | Res::SelfCtor(..))`

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/87a0997ef9c0bfad0ba362741afa601d8fb285b8/compiler/rustc_resolve/src/late.rs#L301-L303

then we are sure that it's not a tuple struct and can treat it as a regular assignment, otherwise defer to type checking.

This will need a comment telling that it's for diagnostics and a link to `PathSource::is_expected` telling to keep the logic in sync with that function.

I believe the issue is here:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/ffe52882ed79be67344dd6085559e308241e7f60/compiler/rustc_parse/src/parser/diagnostics.rs#L1823
`expr_is_valid_const_arg` returns false for an identifier like `N`, because we usually simply parse identifiers as type arguments instead, and then resolve them to const arguments later. (The comment at the top of `handle_unambiguous_unbraced_const_arg` is misleading and should probably be changed: it doesn't just handle an error code, it is also for parsing valid const arguments that are not surrounded in braces.) I think if you add the identifier case to `expr_is_valid_const_arg`, this might work as expected. I'm not quite sure off the top of my head why this is the only place we're hitting this issue, though, or why there's not an ambiguity issue with type arguments.

We can do this as a follow up, though.

"available expression analysis" is often the term I see used in compiler theory, which refers to an analysis that can answer if an expression can be reused at a point since it is not modified along the way from its definition.

as `emscripten_futex_wait` is taking a double i think we should better use `as_secs_f64` here?

```suggestion
    let timeout_ms = timeout.map_or(crate::f64::INFINITY, |d| d.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0);
```

although [Atomics.wait](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-atomics.wait) → [SuspendAgent](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-suspendagent) suggests that the *timeout* is always a non-negative integer (but at the same time accepting +∞<sub>𝔽</sub>), it is not clear that the actual implementation *can* accept fractional milliseconds. For instance [V8](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/f1ae68351f19069346e623badf42be0e4385633b/src/execution/futex-emulation.cc#L321-L324) seems to accept waiting for 0.5ms as it just converts to nanoseconds without rounding.

author: tmandry

body:
> @jyn514 Yeah, my point was largely that if you `panic!` on next instead of implementing `FusedIterator`, the `Some`, `None`, `Some` allowance on `Iterator` becomes fairly broken, in these cases it _should_ implement `FusedIterator` which does preclude `panic!`.

As I see it there are three major allowed `Iterator` and `Stream` implementations/requirements:

 1. A `FusedIterator` (and probably `FusedStream` in the future, though [`futures::stream::FusedStream`](https://docs.rs/futures/0.3.8/futures/stream/trait.FusedStream.html) works off a different system where it pre-checks whether it should be polled at all) which guarantees any amount of `Some` followed by an infinite number of `None`.
 2. A "resumeable" iterator which guarantees a mix of `Some` and `None`, and documents under what conditions it switches between them.
 3. A "single-use" iterator which guarantees any amount of `Some`, followed by a single `None`, and then doesn't guarantee its behaviour afterwards.

Distinguishing between the second and third variants is only a matter of documentation, and the majority of the time all that's needed is the third variant, resuming an iterator seems to be a very uncommon thing, especially in a context where you have a generic `I: Iterator` since you don't know the exact conditions under which it switches.

> Part of @taiki-e's point was that generators panic if you resume them after they return. So adapting from generator to Stream would have to involve storing another bit of information (whether it has returned) if panics aren't allowed.

And this will be relevant for iterators in the future when we have generator-backed `Iterator` implementations.

> If the allocator has an API to query the number of allocs, I think the compiler is not allowed to bypass this, as calling alloc has a side effect (e.g. incrementing a counter in the allocator).

At least for the global allocator, that would be a massive optimization regression compared to `malloc`. To my knowledge, LLVM will assume that `malloc` calls can be removed when the result is not needed -- even if you end up supplying your own `malloc`.

I assumed the goal was to make the pluggable global allocator in Rust work the same way, which is what lead to this PR. If we are okay with losing this optimization potential, we can go back to the drawing board -- but that will have [severe effects for allocator support during CTFE](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/79045#issuecomment-727233857).

body:
Note that Rust allocation calls currently go through `__rust_alloc`, which is not handled specially by LLVM (`malloc` is a "magic name"). But if we ever *do* want to treat them specially, we need to carefully document this.

Or rather, this is the extent of the current special treatment:
```
; Function Attrs: nounwind nonlazybind uwtable
declare noalias i8* @__rust_alloc(i64, i64) unnamed_addr #0
```
Notable are `nounwind` and `noalias` -- so this must not unwind, and the returned pointer must be "fresh", i.e., not alias any other pointer that the calling context might use. If that is not already the case, this should also be documented.

Is it currently possible to disable this optimisation using some compiler option/preprocessor define?

The ability to do (de)allocation counts and sizes is widely used in products such as game engines. Especially if you're working in codebases that are not 100% safe (e.g. a Rust to C/C++ interface), it'd be important for Rust to still reliably support that behaviour - even if it'd only be supported in and if-cfg.
author: Wodann

body:
> Is it currently possible to disable this optimisation using some compiler option/preprocessor define?

That is a good question to which I do not know the answer. LLVM would have to expose this as an option.

> The ability to do (de)allocation counts and sizes is widely used in products such as game engines. Especially if you're working in codebases that are not 100% safe (e.g. a Rust to C/C++ interface), it'd be important for Rust to still reliably support that behaviour - even if it'd only be supported in and if-cfg.

Note that Rust with this PR supports this at least as well as C and C++ -- at least clang will perform the kind of optimizations this is about.

Also, allocation counts are still *supported*. What this PR enables is, basically, allocation counts being different between debug and release builds. Usually compilers have to ensure optimizations do not change program behavior; if the program prints the number of allocations to stdout, that means no allocation may be optimized away! So if we want to optimize allocations, we need a clause like this somewhere.

body:
> is removing this heap allocation (and ptr.is_null() becoming a constant false) considered changing program behavior?

I wish I knew the answer.^^ In practice, LLVM *will* optimize away even such huge allocations that can never succeed. So the LLVM devs consider this to not be changing program behavior.

However, I know of no formal model that would actually explain this, and it might even be inconsistent. Somehow the formal model needs to say that the allocation can succeed even if it is too big to fit into the finite memory, and then proceed in a consistent way even if the program sanity-checks the integer addresses that it got (since those checks can be optimized away if their result is unused) and so on.

I consider this to be one of the hardest unanswered questions in formal semantics for low-level languages: to either show that this makes sense, or to show that the optimization is broken and leads to miscompilations.

body:
This is actually correct.

The condition `countdown < 5` executed 10 times (10 loop iterations).

It evaluated to `true` 4 times, and executed the `might_abort()` call.

It skipped the body of the `might_abort()` call 6 times (hidden `else`).

I wanted to capture the coverage of the non-true condition. Say the condition was `countdown < 50`, which is always `true`. In that case, we wouldn't have a test for what happens if `might_abort()` is not called.

So counting the "hidden else" is important.

I can clarify this, but I should probably clarify it in a different test that's more focused on `if` blocks inside loops, and keep this test focused on testing the `Abort` terminator.

One side-note... The Span for the "hidden else" starts as a 0-length span right after the right brace, if I'm not mistaken. But code region counts versus line counts are confusing for 0-length regions, so I always expend them by 1 character, preferably to the right (in the typical case, after the brace) UNLESS it's at the end of the line, in which case I have to expand it to the left (which is the right brace). 

You can't see it because there are no more code regions on that line, and the code block ends at the semicolon after the `might_abort()` call.

If there was no semicolon (say, if might_abort() returned a value), then there would be multiple code regions on that line, and you would see the one character highlighted. I'm not sure that would help clarify things anymore than in it's existing state though.
