body:
@tmandry @wesleywiser - I'm a little unsure how to proceed here.

I'll try my best to summarize my understanding and what I think I want to do but don't know how:

1. Given a `Crate`, `rustc_mir::monomorphize::collector` finds the "root" `DefId`s (via the `RootCollector`, a HIR `ItemLikeVisitor`), and traverses them to generate a set of `MonoItem`s. This is where the async closures (`Generator`s) are getting dropped if they are not going to be called. (From debug logs, `i::{closure#0}()` and `f::{closure#0}()` are both logged, because they are going to be called, but the other async functions' closures are not mentioned at all. There is no "path" from the roots (only `main()` in this case) to those closures.

2. It seems to me I can make another `ItemLikeVisitor`, find all of the `hir::ItemKindFn`s, get their `DefId`s, and look them up in the set of `MonoItem`s. If a `DefId` is not found among the `MonoItem`s, then it will not be codegen'ed, and therefore won't have coverage.

3. At that point, I want to add at least one `Zero` counter with span (code region) for the span of the closure/generator, for each missing `DefId`, to the `rustc_codegen_ssa::coverageinfo::map::FunctionCoverage` (the collection of counters and coderegions built up during the codegen phase, and eventually written out as the "Coverage Map". I would do this with `FunctionCoverage::add_counter(self, counter, region)`.

Here's where I get confused...

The `FunctionCoverage` is stored in a hash map in `CrateCoverageContext`, and that object is constructed as a field in `CodegenCx`, but `CodegenCx` appears to be constructed for a *specific `CodegenUnit`*

IIUC, codegen of a given crate can be partitioned across multiple `CodegenUnit`s, and each `CodegenUnit` will have only a subset of the crate's `MonoItem`s; so if that's true:

1. Given a `DefId` in some `Crate`, even if the `DefId` is not be found among the `MonoItem`s of one `CodegenUnit`, the `DefId` might still be found among the `MonoItem`s of one of the other`CodegenUnit`s for that `Crate`. If so, that prevents me being able to check for missing `DefIds` when I'm starting to codegen the Coverage Map, because the Coverage Map finalization happens within the `CodegenCx` of only one `CodegenUnit`.

2. But if I search for a `DefId` among all `MonoItem`s of all `CodegenUnit`s, and don't find it, how do I know which `CodegenCx` to use, to add the missing Counter and code region for that function?

What's even more baffling to me is, it looks to me like a CoverageMap is codegenned for each `CodegenCx`, and assuming there are more than one, then the code appears to be set up to generate multiple coverage maps. I don't really get how that would work (or why it appears to work now), but I assume it does work since evidence suggests as much.

So I guess I just don't understand something, and hopefully the solution (to adding counters and code regions for functions/closures that are missing from the MonoItems is easier than it appears.

body:
> By the way, is SPIR-V able to handle more exotic types such as `i128`?

For a general background: theoretically yes, integers are declared using an arbitrary bit width (like llvm), and the spec doesn't disallow (or even mention) 128 bit integers. Practically no, though, considering that there are extensions to enable support for 8 bit, 16 bit, and 64 bit integers, which implies no support for 128 bit considering there's no extension for it (the SPIR-V world is full of weird unsaid implications like this).

However, I think in this case, 128 bit integers will either be disallowed outside `asm!` and so cannot leak into `asm!` and cause problems, or, they're represented as a pair of `u64` or whatever, and so still won't cause `asm!` problems with unrepresentable types.

> Not exactly: this is still limited to primitive types and SIMD vectors.

Yeah, we'd like to allow any type here, not sure if that's easiest to do in this PR or a follow-up (or if it's even possible to allow any type). It's certainly a little weird having an IR in `asm!`, arbitrary types are just... regular SSA IDs that look exactly like primitive types.

> Sorry if I'm misunderstanding here, but spec_extend(and extend in general) and to_vec are sufficiently different in that extend has to reason about prior spare capacity

When coming from a `FromIterator` implementation then it should know that length is 0 and eliminate most branches. `Vec::new().reserve(x)` and `Vec::with_capacity(x)` should have more or less the same performance.

>  I for some reason thought the other specialization was for collect() not extend, in which case it'd also not have any prior capacity to deal with

Uh, that usually is the case. `SpecFromIter` is for `collect()`. It just that some of the specializations sometimes happen to do `Vec::new().extend(iter)` (well `SpecExtend::spec_extend`) in some cases where collect and extend would do almost the same thing modulo a few branches the optimizer can eliminate. That way an extend specialization without duplicating it for the collect case.

Maybe now that the generic allocator support has landed I should move some of this stuff to a separate module and provide a better overview.

> I can definitely expand the bound from Copy to Clone (as that's the bound on to_vec), not sure what perf impact that will have tho.

Sorry. I realize how useless my previous post was.

I'm in full agreement that this should be caught. What I was trying to ask is whether what you encountered was a const eval post-monomorphization error. If it is *not* that, then I'm very confused.

We should have a proper check, and I think the only way to do that is to do it via well-formedness checks, though I'm not sure if we need a new one. Basically we need to add that additional wf-check only from within const contexts.

body:
> Why on earth does rustfmt reports them though? It's not its job?

Generally speaking rustfmt doesn't suppress parser errors so that it doesn't silently fail and exit without giving users any inclination as to why it was unable to format. Since rustfmt works directly with the AST we're reliant on the parsing calls to succeed so that we have something valid/safe to reformat. However, in cases like this where invalid syntax doesn't impact formatting one way or the other, it really isn't necessary to emit and we can suppress/skip emission; user's will be informed whenever they actually run rustc.

`MutexGuard` doesn't have any methods right now, because it implements Deref. If the `T` already has an `.unlock()`, this will make it harder to call that `.unlock()` through this MutexGuard. Any existing code calling such an `.unlock()` would change meaning with this change.

Other types like `Box` solve this by not taking `self` in their methods (e.g. [`Box::into_raw`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.into_raw)), and must be called with the more verbose `Box::into_raw(mybox)` syntax.

But I think `MutexGuard::unlock(guard);` wouldn't be a big improvement over `drop(guard);`. :(

What do you think?

This also seems pretty odd to me - it means that if `ignore_order` isn't set, this might not even compare the right set of objects!

I think a good way to resolve all the concerns both I and @camelid have mentioned is to unconditionally print *all* the objects, then show a *diff* between that and all the expected objects. That means:
- The order won't matter (assuming you print them sorted)
- All objects that don't match will be shown

body:
I took a look at the llvm-ir again (the one I suggested) which basically boils down to this pseudo-like code:

```
zip(rhs: u8*, lhs: u8*, ret: u8*):
    iter = stackalloc(128)
    dst = stackalloc(128)

    memcpy(iter, lhs, 64)
    memcpy(iter + 128, rhs, 64)

    fill `iter` with `dst` in "zipped form"

    memcpy(ret, iter)
```

Theoretically, all three memcpys could be eliminated by copying the items directly from `rhs` and `lhs` into `ret` (at llvm-ir level). But it looks like this is an issue with LLVM's GVN not detecting this pattern.

I think this violates the transitivity requirement of `sort_by`.

Given `a = Positive; b = None; c = Negative` then

* a == b
* b == c
* a != c

The change is not to require unique access (to the tree), we admit that the caller has it and needs to have it. We don't get you a slice of edges, but a slice of containers of edges. The actual use case is to unify the various methods that access `MaybeUninit`s in another PR.

body:
> it still seems unnecessary, as this PR doesn't introduce any cases where key_area is being used with the unique access being provided here

The compiler doesn't notice, but I think the uniqueness is being used and required. You cannot sensibly copy a `MaybeUninit<K>` if there might be someone else copying it too, because the key would be duplicated. The callers of `key_area` move ownership, so they need uniqueness, even though the `ptr::copy` doing the hard work for them doesn't care about the uniqueness of the source .

> Can we include the next step of this refactor (but avoid the other changes)?

body:
Yes, you're right. The substs for the associated type include the substs for the parent item. However, the problem for this line is that the trait ref is *not* for the associated type, it's for the parent trait (`trait_ref.def_id`). So instead of `[FreshTy(0), 'a, T]` we have `[FreshTy(0), 'a, T, 'b]`.

Now, this doesn't exactly end up being a problem, since we don't use the trait ref defid between here and `from_ref_and_name`, and this is actually the form that `from_ref_and_name` expects. However, `from_ref_and_name` was probably created pre-GATs, where the substs for an associated type will always equal the substs of the parent trait ref. And it's a bit scary and confusing that this trait ref gets created like this.

If you just use the associated item `DefId`, then this is completely fine, since the substs we have match the substs we expect. But, you would have to change the `from_ref_and_name` call below, since that expected the `def_id` to be the parent trait DefId, not the associated item's. (And this is actually a bit nicer because we already have the associated item's `DefId` and don't have to look it up, which happens in `from_ref_and_name`.

body:
I did mean that... and i must apologize... I completely mixed up a bunch of things.

`const_ptr.rs` and `mut_ptr.rs` are `*const T` and `*mut T` respectively. They have nothing to do with const eval, except that some of their functions are `const fn`.

`align_offset` was a big topic around CTFE some time ago, but we only ever ended up landing it in miri: https://github.com/rust-lang/miri/blob/510e62c9ea5c9da6c7b29ba89568456e035f70c6/src/shims/mod.rs#L36

So... before you can do this PR, we'd need to move the `align_offset` logic from miri to rustc and thus CTFE. This is not as easy as with other low level intrinsics, because `align_offset` is a `lang_item` which contains the runtime code, but different code from the function body will be run in the CTFE/miri case. While miri has this working already, and it would be simple to use the same trick as the one linked above, it would still not compile, because our checks would see non-const code in the `const fn align_offset`. So we would need to create a new system which makes a function `const` from the outside, but not `const` on the inside. I'm not sure about the extend of the work necessary to do that, but it's probably as simple as not const-checking the function body of lang items.

body:
We've reached a point in the design where I think we need to invoke @rust-lang/wg-const-eval and see what they think of it.

> Is there some code to add before the return to tell the compiler that everything is fine or is the instant return what tells it that all is fine?

No, because *it is already working*! You did everything right, you can notice this because `FOO` actually is getting evaluated now, when before it errored before evaluation. The error you are seeing is an actual evaluation error with a backtrace and everything. We have a second safety net for catching calls to non-const fn during evaluation, and we don't want to change this. What we do want is to catch the call to `call_con_const_fn_unleashed` and not even evaluate its body, but run special code within the const evaluator.

Initially I thought we'd have to make such functions a lang item *in addition* to `unleash_the_miri_inside_of_you_here`, but I think I have an alternative idea that could work: we change the attribute to also take a string argument, so we have `unleash_the_miri_inside_of_you_here(guaranteed_eq)` and then fetch that attribute in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3d9ada686fb42bd036b3a4916526f413f1d5d1f8/compiler/rustc_mir/src/const_eval/machine.rs#L213 and if it's one of a list of things that we know (match on the symbol, you'll have to register the symbol in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/e4297ba39ce07a0b0000841b50154ea53783a024/compiler/rustc_span/src/symbol.rs#L123 ), we do the special logic, and otherwise we go back and continue with the current https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3d9ada686fb42bd036b3a4916526f413f1d5d1f8/compiler/rustc_mir/src/const_eval/machine.rs#L217 (which we'll be able to replace with your new scheme, too, which is great imo).
author: oli-obk
usbalbin

body:
> Wait, so we are not just catching the call to `non_const_fn`, but the entire call to `call_non_const_fn_unleashed`?

Yes. Otherwise we'd need *another* system to catch calls to `non_const_fn`, and this way we can just catch the `call_non_const_fn_unleashed`. If you need some preprocessing, you can do that ahead of time in a regular const fn that calls `call_non_const_fn_unleashed`.

> So then the `const_eval_select` thing would not work?

I think you would write it as

```rust
#[unleash_the_miri_inside_of_you_here(const_eval_select)]
fn const_eval_select<ARG, F, G, RET>(arg: ARG, called_in_const: F, called_at_rt: G) -> RET {
    called_at_rt(arg)
}
```

and then the CTFE engine has to process that function and can't just keep evaluating on.

But you are right, we could also do this without catching, if we made `this_is_run_in_const_eval` a `unleash_the_miri_inside_of_you_here` and caught only that and returned `true` from CTFE but the function is declare as

```rust
#[unleash_the_miri_inside_of_you_here]
fn this_is_run_in_const_eval() -> bool {
    false
}
```

I guess we could do it this way, but it will require some care because we have never done function calls via generics in const eval before, I'm not sure what problems you would encounter. We should carefully try out all of these different use cases in individual PRs that make it easy to look at all effects of just the single change

I think I would prefer not to add this. Whether or not it's also given a name under std::primitive, it remains valuable to make `!` work as a type because it already partially does in stable Rust, such as in `let _: fn() -> ! = std::process::abort;`. As for whether to expose `never` as a synonym for it, to me it's not a strong enough motivation if it's a symbol that appears for other purposes in the grammar, or if googling is hard. These are factors that are taking into account by the language design team as a tradeoff against many other things. Other languages land at a different balance of keywords vs punctuation (ALGOL with `begin` `end` instead of `{` `}`; `comment` instead of `//`) but there is still value in syntax for the sufficiently special things.

I'll close the PR but mention @nikomatsakis, the never type stabilization lead according to https://github.com/rust-lang/lang-team/issues/60, in case they see value in reopening and putting this through lang team fcp.

body:
I think I'll go ahead and close this, since this API addition doesn't strike me as the most appropriate solution to either of those use cases.

> An example use case would be to print an arrow pointing to the exact location of parsing failure as mentioned in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/22639#issuecomment-737079729 where this feature was requested.

For parsing, ordinarily you need some variation of a lexer to decide what part of the input you are suppose to parse as a number in the first place. Consider input like `{"id":987654321,"username":"ethanboxx"}`. Some piece of logic needs to determine that the substring `987654321` is the correct thing to pass to u32::from_str, which it does by scanning ahead valid digits. Having from_str report an invalid digit position is only useful if you are planning to pass an entire suffix of the input to from_str i.e. `987654321,"username":"ethanboxx"}`, then collect the invalid digit position, and run from_str a second time up to that position. This seems more confusing than just lexing the valid digits yourself up front.

The standard library already exposes the concept of "valid digit" by way of:

- `u8::is_ascii_digit` / `char::is_ascii_digit` (for base 10)
- `u8::is_ascii_hexdigit` / `char::is_ascii_hexdigit` (for base 16)
- `char::is_digit` (for arbitrary radix)

> Another example could be writing a parser that ignores invalid characters.

Again I don't think an invalid digit position reported by from_str is really appropriate here. It sounds like you are planning to take an input containing a mix of valid and invalid digits, and run from_str on it in a loop, removing one invalid digit at a time. That seems needlessly complicated and confusing compared to filtering for valid digits up front (using the above set of methods) and running from_str a single time on only valid digits.

Ack that this is less compact, but I refactored to use the nested match because it reduces duplication and imo makes this code easier to grok, albeit longer. We no longer have to put `name` in multiple arms of the match, like we had previously:

```rust
match s.split_once('=') {
  Some(("dylib", name)) => (),
  Some(("framework", name)) => (),
  ...

body:
Apologies, I intended to update the non-deprecated sleep() function instead of this one! 

I'll add another commit to move it, and add more detail regarding the platform-specific behaviour (if it is deemed necessary).

e.g. on unix systems we check for a zero duration and _return immediately_ without calling the underlying libc `nanosleep()` function ([std/sys/unix/thread.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/55794e43960ad3647e78ea5b0cb5ad0c5c0596a8/library/std/src/sys/unix/thread.rs#L157)), whereas on the Windows platform the underlying win32 `Sleep()` function is always called ([std/src/sys/windows/thread.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/ac48e62db85e6db4bbe026490381ab205f4a614d/library/std/src/sys/windows/thread.rs#L88)) and it's behaviour can be to either _relinquish the time-slice_ or _return immediately_ see: [https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/synchapi/nf-synchapi-sleep](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/synchapi/nf-synchapi-sleep)

I do think this edge-case needs the extra clarification given the difference in the underlying behaviour between platforms. Perhaps we could instead standardise the behaviour to always check for a zero duration and return immediately before calling the underlying OS sleep function for all platforms?

body:
That is not quite true. `io::copy` uses a `DEFAULT_BUF_SIZE`-sized buffer internally. `BufWriter::new`  also sets its capacity to `DEFAULT_BUF_SIZE`, which means if you toss a `BufWriter` into `io::copy` then for every single iteration of the copy loop it will try to write exactly as much as needed to fill that buffer, i.e. doubles the `memcpy` traffic.

That said, this can be solved with specialization and #78641 does just that.

body:
But doesn't this encourage inlining slightly? It adds the `inlinehint` attribute to the LLVM IR anyway.

And if there's a question of whether or not we want to encourage inlining, I think we really do, as the point of the optimization is to inline writes to the internal buffer in hot code. I only separated it out into a function for code reuse. The `#[inline]` is just saying "please don't undo the optimization I'm trying to do". :)

Of course, we could trust the compiler to make the right decision based on context. There are probably cases where `write` and `write_all` are called in cold code where the client doesn't want this function to be inlined. But I'm hesitant to optimize for that case at the risk of undoing the intended optimization. Also, in those cases, I think they actually wouldn't want `write` or `write_all` to be inlined, and would need to do something like wrap them in a function marked `#[inline(never)]` anyway.

body:
While excessive or cyclic symbolic links are the most common scenario in which this will arise, there are other drivers and subsystems which can return `ELOOP`. For instance, if you attempt to execute a binary on Linux that's using `binfmt_misc`, and that ends up recursing (because the interpreter needs interpreting) too many times, you get `ELOOP`. Or if you use epoll and try to put the epoll fd inside itself. Or if your network routing has a cycle. In general, Linux tends to use `ELOOP` for any case of "I'm refusing to follow a cycle this deeply inside the kernel", not just for symlinks.

I think, at a minimum, it'd be helpful to include a catch-all in the documentation for this: "or a similar kind of unexpected cycle or excessively deep recursion occurred".

I'm also wondering if it'd be appropriate to leave "SymbolicLink" out of this name, and just call it "Loop". I don't want to make this less descriptive, but I think this is one case where it'd be actively *confusing* to assume this is always about symlinks.

body:
I have updated the description to include this (and will push that shortly).

I don't think the name should be changed.  Because of the way Unix reuses errno values, it is often going to be the case that there will be use cases which don't fit the primary summary.  These are typically less common (and less user facing) than the older or more primary meaing.

I think trying to capture all these uses of every errno value would result in distressingly vague names for `ErrorKind`.  Sometimes, even, the uses are quite incoherent.  (Consider `EAGAIN` from `fork` vs `read`.)

I think it is better to capture this information in the extended description.  Also we agreed to add to the documentation information about which errno values map to which `ErrorKind`s.  That will help too.

In the case of `ELOOP`, I think it is important to retain a good experience for an end user who uses some Rust program which finds a symbolic link loop, and print a message and an abbrevation that is meaningful to them.  And it is important that Rust programmers who are writing generic file-handling code can easily find the symbolic link loop error code.

Conversely `ELOOP` from `epoll_ctl` will generally be experienced by an event loop, and be fatal.  It's also, I guess, really quite rare.

body:
I actually prefer it this way and I think the overall impact will be negligible.

Yes, functionally, we have the option of inserting the statement anywhere in the BCB, but it is standard practice to `insert()` into the `statements` vec in MIR processing when order is critical. 

As I was trying to say in my reply here (though maybe not clearly):

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/80045#issuecomment-745786169

I believe inserting the coverage statement between the last statement and the terminator is going to break up some sequences in unexpected ways. 

It wouldn't be a problem if I could insert the coverage statement **after** the terminator (which is impossible without a new BB, and that's much worse).

But the `Terminator` is really just a special case of a `Statement`, and the sequence from one statement to another is sometimes important, analytically at least. (Possibly even important at runtime, for context switching reasons, in fact.)

To drive the point: Think about a typical instruction sequence like, Load followed by Add (adding to the value that was just loaded). Most people would expect these to come in uninterrupted sequence, so injecting code to increment a global counter between the two, even if possible, would not be right.

I would rather not insert Coverage statements between a Statement and it's following Terminator, and it's not just about this one issue.

body: Currently the RDRAND backend will be only used on SGX, UEFI, and Hermit targets. Libc's `backtrace` function does a naive walk of frame pointers. Rustc and LLVM are normally compiled with frame pointers omitted, meaning that only DWARF based unwinding is reliable.

In addition it is not safe to call it from asynchronous signals like SIGSEGV.

> [...] AS-Unsafe init heap dlopen plugin lock [...]

body:
While in the long term we'll probably want some sort of `build.pgo = true` in `config.toml`, I think there is a quick improvement we can make to have the PGO setup be more reusable:

```dockerfile
ENV PGO_HOST x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

ENV SCRIPT /tmp/pgo.sh python2.7 ../x.py dist --host $HOSTS --target $HOSTS \
        --include-default-paths \
        src/tools/build-manifest
```

`pgo.sh` would then compile the compiler for `PGO_HOST`, run the sample compilations with it and invoke:

```sh
$@ --rust-profile-use=/tmp/rustc-pgo.profdata
```

With a setup like this we could move `pgo.sh` outside of the docker directory and almost effortlessly apply it to other platforms (when we get CI time budget for that).

I do not know if it is possible in general to optimize this function. There are different formulas to calculate padding etc., each optimized for different cases. body:
The issue is that `struct S;` desugars to something like
```rust
struct S {}
fn S() -> S { ... }
```
except with compiler magic so you don't need the parentheses. If you look at the debugging @LeSeulArtichaut found, it contains
```
kind: Use(Path { span: src/test/rustdoc-ui/check-doc-attrs.rs:8:9: 8:17 (#0), res: Def(Struct, DefId(0:5 ~ check_doc_attrs[8787]::bar::Bar))
kind: Use(Path { span: src/test/rustdoc-ui/check-doc-attrs.rs:8:9: 8:17 (#0), res: Def(Ctor(Struct, Const), DefId(0:6 ~ check_doc_attrs[8787]::bar::Bar::{constructor#0}))
```
So I think the fix is to ignore attributes on Ctor items, because they can never occur without also occurring on the struct itself.

body:
For this the steps are:

1. Extract this code into a function: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/e48eb37b9470a26748c916f7153569906f3c67bf/compiler/rustc_mir_build/src/build/matches/mod.rs#L1678-L1702
2. Create another file in this folder (compiler/rustc_mir_build/src/build/expr) that lowers an expression into a switch on whether that expression is true. For most expressions it would return look like the first 6 lines of the `ExprKind::If` branch here, and would then return the then and else blocks (it's probably worth creating a new struct so that it's clear which way around they are).
3. For `ExprKind::Scope` the function would unwrap the expression and recur in the same way this function does.
4. For `ExprKind::Let` it would use the function from step 1.
5. Use the function from step 3 here and in `ExprKind::If`. See `ExprKind::LogicalOp` here for how to assign `true` and `false` to the destination.

body: This is not "the same safety requirements as `align_of_val_raw`", though. `align_of_val_raw` quite deliberately only talks slices, trait objects, and `extern` types -- for all other unsiezd tails, "it is not allowed to call this function".
author: RalfJung

body:
This is super awkward to specify cleanly without copying over the entire docs from `align_of_val_raw`. When I made this adjustment, I figured that "comes from an unsize coercion" would be a tighter bound than `align_of_val_raw` spells out, since the only types of unsize coercion are for slices and trait objects. "Comes from unsize coercion" is in fact a simpler spelling of the requirement for trait objects (valid vptr). For slices, it's exactly equivalent iff it's impossible to name a fixed-size array type that has a layout close to the size of `isize::MAX` (such that `RcInner<T>` is too big). I think that the error "values of the type `rc::RcBox<[u128; N]>` are too big for the current architecture" is enough for that, though I do think relying on said error for soundness is suboptimal.

(Also, we could potentially relax `align_of_val_raw` to limit the magnitude of alignment (which it probably should anyway) rather than size.)
author: CAD97

body:
The reason I don't like "comes from an unsize coercion" is that it is open-ended -- it is true for the unsizing coercions that currently exist, but that  set might change in the future. The `align_of_val_raw` docs are quite deliberately stated in a way that is *not* open-ended in this way.

That's also why "comes from an unsize coercion" is *not* tighter than the bound on `align_of_val_raw`.

body:
I was using `pointer` since `Cow` calls itself a “smart pointer” and `Rc` and `Arc` describe themselves as “reference-counting pointer[s]”. Furthermore, `Cow` already provides shared access, so the word “shared” is not really differentiating `Rc`/`Arc` from `Cow`. The thing that reference-counting provides is shared ownership, so “access” might not be the best word either; furthermore I don’t think there should be any further explanation of what reference-counting pointers are/do on a page about the `Cow` enum; the main point of this new paragraph is the fact that `Rc::make_mut` and `Arc::make_mut` are mentioned (and linked) at all.

But if you’re unhappy with my phrasing, feel free to give some more explanation on why you’d prefer a different phrasing 😉; the current one is not set in stone. E.g. one could discuss dropping the word “pointers” entirely or using a singular form.

I don't think I'm a fan of this change (adding the `min_mir_opt_level` constants). The `mir-opt-level` values are organized around the effects they have on code and compiler performance not so much about what specific optimizations are applied (that's why when the inliner is more stable/performant it might be enabled at `mir-opt-level=1`). 

However, I do see why you made this change and I think a simpler thing to do might just be to add an explicit check for `-Zinstrument-coverage` to `Inliner.rs` and if that flag is enabled, skip the inliner at any `mir-opt-level`.

body:
Sorry, I should have expanded on my position a bit more. 

I think the reason I don't like this approach is that I think it makes `rustc_session` far too knowledgeable about which MIR optimizations are run and even what parts of those optimizations are run. This seems strange to me because the option `rustc_session` is responsible for configuring is intentionally vague about what optimizations are run exactly. For instance:

- `-Zmir-opt-level=0` => don't run any MIR transformations that aren't required to do codegen
- `-Zmir-opt-level=1` => run any MIR optimizations as long as they don't hurt debugging or compilation time 
- `-Zmir-opt-level=2` => run any MIR optimizations as long as they don't hurt compilation time "too much"
- `-Zmir-opt-level=3` => run any MIR optimizations without regard to debugability or compilation time cost

Since the flags aren't specified as running any particular optimizations, it seems weird to me that `rustc_session` needs to know what optimizations are available to be run. Especially since some optimizations are tuned to be more or less aggressive depending on the optimization level requested.

I guess another way to look at it is that the details of MIR optimizations are currently encapsulated in `rustc_mir::transform` and I think that's a good thing. I would prefer that we don't expose what optimizations are available or configured to run outside of `rustc_mir`. 

> I was hoping to avoid scattering coverage-specific exceptions in unrelated parts of the codebase. (If the code changes, it's easy to miss little unrelated piece of logic like this.)

I think this is generally a good goal but a lot of the MIR optimizations are already fairly context sensitive as to what the build flags are and what kind of MIR `Body` they are operating on. Adding the check for `-Zinstrument-coverage` to the Inliner doesn't seem like a big deal in this case. 

Of course, the option would be to fix the Inliner so that we can inline things even when code coverage is enabled. If you think there's a way to make that work, I would be willing to work on implementing that. 🙂
author: wesleywiser

body:
Done.

I get that my proposal is a bigger change than just fixing the ICE (and the debate is more philosophical than practical at this point), so I defer to your judgement here.

> Of course, the option would be to fix the Inliner so that we can inline things even when code coverage is enabled. If you think there's a way to make that work, I would be willing to work on implementing that

I doubt it's worth doing. I don't see a benefit in optimizing code while also injecting coverage counters. There might be exceptions, but generally it seems like solving all of the problems this can introduce, while also making sure the coverage results are still accurate, is a lot of hoops to jump through, and unnecessary if we accept the limitation that coverage is a feature meant to be used in non-production environments.

That's just my opinion though.

body:
Let's get the easy ones out of the way first:

 * The comment tries to hint at the current problem: we get a `Borrowed` string that contains the destination of a reference-style link, and a range that points at the link usage itself.

 * I'm not sure about `Inlined`, but it seems like it's a small string optimization for the `Boxed` variant. It exists to avoid allocating on `clone` if the boxed string is short enough.


As far as I can see, Pulldown provides a `Borrowed` if the string directly comes from the source. If any transformation is necessary (e.g. [unescaping](https://github.com/raphlinus/pulldown-cmark/blob/d4bf0872b14f68c1afedee918710fb401e3e6e9a/src/scanners.rs#L960) used when [scanning ref defs](https://github.com/raphlinus/pulldown-cmark/blob/d4bf0872b14f68c1afedee918710fb401e3e6e9a/src/parse.rs#L1408) or such), Pulldown builds and hands out a `Boxed` string.

The issue is not that `Borrowed` strings can have an incorrect span, it's that for those, we can actually restore the span we need. For any other variant, it's reasonable (I think) to assume that the string contained in the variant is some sort of derivative of the original source, and can not be located by either pointer arithmetic or string search. (Just as I write this, if I'm correct this makes `rfind`-ing on the `Boxed` variant kinda pointless, because the string will not be an exact match anyway. Otherwise, Pulldown would have handed out a `Borrowed`).

Hope this makes sense.

```suggestion
impl<T: Error + ?Sized> Error for Arc<T> {
```

[unlike Box](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75180#issuecomment-670292054) we should be able to add the `?Sized` bound.
author: kennytm

body: That would prevent a `From` impl for `E: Error` in the future, we okay with that? Seems like an inconsistency that would probably bother a lot of people... (not sure this is a good reason to not do it)
author: yaahc

body: I'm not sure there would be many `?Sized` errors in practice. Could this bound be relaxed (with `?Sized`) at a later date and still be backwards-compatible?
author: richard-uk1

body: I mean, it might be that it does no harm if we assume a future specialization feature would allow `From` impl for `E: Error` in the future.
author: richard-uk1

body:
we couldn't put a `?Sized` on in the future backwards compatibly. This is a problem with `Box` right now. This causes overlap for the impls `From<T> for T` and `From<E: Error> for Arc<dyn Error + ...>`. It would become ambiguous when converting `Arc<dyn Error>` into an `Arc<dyn Error>` whether or not you should do a unit conversion or wrap the Arc in another Arc.

As for specialization, I'm not as sure but as far as I know it won't help here. I've looked this up before and my understanding is that this would require rustc to implement [the lattice rule](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/1210-impl-specialization.md#the-lattice-rule), but afaik there are no plans to implement this. That said, I've never had this confirmed by @rust-lang/wg-traits, so this might be on the roadmap even if it's not in the RFC, or I could be misunderstanding the RFC.
author: yaahc

body: This stuff is extremely nuanced, thankyou for taking the time to work though it all.
author: richard-uk1

body: I think ideally we'd want the `?Sized` bound on there. The fact that `Box<dyn Error>`, which is a very common pattern, doesn't implement `Error` is something we regret. So I think aligning this impl to [the one for `&'a E: Error + ?Sized`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75180/files) is better than aligning it to `Box<E: Error>`.

body:
I expected the `data_offset` safety comment to change because that's where the bug previously was -- "the pointer must have appropriate pointer metadata" assumes all unsized types work with wide pointers and their metadata.

So I'd make this as tight as we can, like your "tighter" but without the first part:
```
/// The pointer must be to an actual allocation of a previously valid instance
/// of T, but the T is allowed to have been dropped.
```
`Weak` cannot be implemented as-is with less than this.

> My understanding of the T-lang consensus is that the looser(?) description here -- a valid pointer to a previously-valid-but-potentially-dropped value -- is probably the maxiumum requirement we will end up with for size/align_of_val_raw

Is that so? To say one implies the other puts a constraint on custom DSTs, namely that dropping them may not invalidate the ability to determine size + alignment.
author: RalfJung

body:
Unfortunately, the two other options we<sup>[1]</sup> could think of that don't put this requirement onto custom DSTs are just as bad, if not worse:

- All `Arc`/`Rc` carry an extra two usize around in the heap allocation. (T-libs' domain rather than T-lang, but T-lang is -1 on requiring this; people already complain about carrying around an unused weak count.)
  - NB: this could probably actually go in the stack part of `Weak`, I'm now realizing (just acquire it at `downgrade` time), but is that really better? It would save `Rc` from paying the cost, but also make `Weak` huge (comparatively).
- Backpedal and require allocators to support `dealloc` without being provided the layout at dealloc time.

The common thin DSTs wouldn't be impacted by this requirement, as regular pointer metadata is required to be `Copy`, so "move the metadata into the alloc" trivially doesn't fail the "access after drop" requirement.

I can think of a scheme with dynamically constructed and refcounted vtables, but also at that point it feels like you would be beyond where you really expect to be using general purpose smart pointers. (And if you just guarantee that all allocs of that monster of a type are at least three usize big, you can do a `union { (Some(Arc<DynVtable>), T), (None, Layout) }` to support getting the layout after drop.)

Said requirement is stricter from the currently-most-active custom DST RFC for size (which takes `&self`), but actually weaker for align (which takes `Pointee::Metadata`).

---

[1]: to be clear, I was part of this T-lang meeting as a guest to present the implications of `Rc`/`Weak` on custom DSTs, but am not a member of T-lang

<details><summary>ASM</summary>

example::as_ptr_1:

        cmovne  rax, rcx

example::from_ptr_1:
        mov     rdx, rsi
        lea     rcx, [rdi - 16]

example::as_ptr_2:

        ret

example::from_ptr_2:

body:
Here are some scenarios to test. 

First, we want to test that every kind of borrow errors. Here are the ones I can think of:

* `let ref x = expr: T` should error
* `(expr:T).as_ref()` should error (invoking `AsRef::as_ref` from the standard library, which does auto-ref)
* `&(expr:T)` should error

Next, for each kind of borrow, we want to try both a regular coercion and a coercion that is part of some larger replace. I would say cover these three scenarios:

* `&(expr:T).f` should error
* `&(expr:T)[3]` should error
* `&*(expr:T)`

It's probably enough to cover those three scenarios for *one* kind of borrow, and then test that the other kind of borrows each handle `(expr:T).f` or one of the more complex cases, but ideal would be to test all for all.

body:
This one requires a much more thorough response. The short answer is that no it's not a regression, though you're not the first person to raise the question and I can certainly understand why.

For the longer answer, there's two core parts.

First, there was [an issue in rustfmt](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt/issues/4512) where in cases with multi pats and at least one `_` rustfmt was entirely unable to process the arg and thus wasn't applying any formatting at all against the mac call expr and just leaving the original formatting in place; rustfmt was just keeping whatever was here before as-is, not successfully applying the formatting rules.

An easy way to see this in practice is by running the older versions (I guess `x.py fmt` from master will work) with a wildly misformatted version of this, and you'll see that wild formatting remains untouched:

```rust
        matches!(self.annotation_type,AnnotationType::Multiline(_)
| AnnotationType::MultilineStart(_)                      | AnnotationType::MultilineLine(_)
              | AnnotationType::MultilineEnd(_)
        )
``` 

On the rustfmt side we've been particularly benefiting from the recent parser/tokens/etc. work that folks like yourself and Aaron have been working on, and now that we've pulled those rustc changes into rustfmt it's finally able to actually format these `matches!` calls producing the formatting seen here.

The second part relates to how we have to attempt to format macro call args in rustfmt. Obviously we're working with the calls in the AST pre-expansion, so when we encounter a maccall expression, we'll use the token streams to instantiate a parser and attempt to parse the args individually so that we can then apply the corresponding formatting rules when possible (e.g. an expr or type).

In the case of `matches!`, the tokens for that second arg actually ends up getting successfully parsed as a standard binop expression, and so rustfmt applies the corresponding [formatting rules for binops](https://github.com/rust-dev-tools/fmt-rfcs/blob/master/guide/expressions.md#binary-operations) which is why it gets indented this way.

Eventually I'd like to introduce some new special case process for `matches!` mac calls since we'll know definitively that second arg isn't actually a binop expr, and then be able to apply more pattern-like formatting rules instead.

Unfortunately though, for the foreseeable future rustfmt is going to continue to be formatting `matches` like any other mac call even though the emitted formatting is less than desireable

body:
It should be `open-source` because it is describing the project.

When used as an adjective before a noun, use "open-source" (with a hyphen) to prevent confusion. For example, in the sentence "I enjoy using open-source software." the word "open-source" describes a type of software.

When used as a noun, use "open source" (with no hyphen). For example, in the sentence "My software is open source." the use of "open source" is not an attributive adjective and does not require a hyphen.

[Merriaiam Webster definition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/open-sourcel)

One more thing - looks like we are never resetting `capturing` to false.
So if we enabled it once when collecting tokens for a module:
```rust
#[my_attr]
mod m { ... }
```
we will proceed to collecting tokens for e.g. every single expression in that module.
In the original token collection PR that caused prohibitive performance regressions, why don't they happen now?

Why is `capturing` necessary at all?

author: petrochenkov

body:
`capturing` is initialized to `false` when a `Parser` is created, and gets reset to its original value below.
The performance regressions are fixed by bailing out if we already have tokens, without creating a `LazyTokenStream`.

Without `capturing`, we run into problems when capturing a nontetminal that has attributes. For example,
`my_mac!(#[allow(dead_code)] 25)` will cause us to capture a `TokenStream` that includes `#[allow(dead_code)]`. The expression parsing code will skip collecting tokens, since we only have butin attributes being applied. The outer `collect_tokens` call will then apy it's `TokenStream` to the expression, which includes the attributes.

We could also fix that by unconditionally collecting tokens when we see any attributes. However, I need the `capturing` flag for the rest of the token-based attribute handling PR, so my next PR would just re-add this flag.

body:
My somewhat limited understanding of the `min_specialization` rules is that you're here promising that any specialization relying on `Clonable` will only be applied to types where `T: Clone` is not dependent lifetimes (directly or indirectly)
E.g. that there's no `impl Clone for &'static Foo` involved. That can only be guaranteed if you could also manually enumerate all T, i.e. they're not types supplied by external crates.

It would also mean that it's unsafe to use `TypedArena` for such types and users of it would have to uphold that in the future.
author: the8472

body: I'm not quite sure if this is the case, but I don't know the feature well enough. I was going by the example of `FusedIterator` and `TrustedLen`, both of which are implemented for e.g. `std::slice::Iterator<'a, T: 'a>` and I believe both are specialization marker traits.
author: bugadani

body:
The thing is that `FusedIterator` or `TrustedLen` are not implemented for arbitrary `T`. They're only implemented for structs controlled by std and those `impl` are only conditional on additional bounds that themselves are other specialization traits.

What's different here is that you're essentially declaring that any and all `Clone` types can act as a specialization marker for specializations relying on `Clonable`. This would only be valid when you have some way of reasoning about the set of `T`. And since `T` is what goes into `TypedArena` it means you've ensured that all uses of `TypedArena` are compatible with the min specialization rules. This kind of far-reaching obligation is why there's the word `unsafe` in that annotation.

But again, my understanding of `min_specialization` is quite limited, so I may be wrong here.
author: the8472

body: This doesn't seem to rely on anything specific to `Cloned`. It just relies on the length. Wouldn't specializing on `TrustedLen` be sufficient here, considering that's already a specialization trait?
author: the8472

body: No, it wouldn't compile unfortunately, or at least I couldn't get it to. Cloned needs Clone on T.

body:
Also, just specializing on anything TrustedLen is unsound, see #77945 for that. In short, Map is TrustedLen and can allocate on the same arena, which makes handling a panic safely an impossible nightmare of dropping uninitialized memory.

I went through the uses of alloc_from_iter and I found that most of those are Map and FlatMap, but some places allocate from Cloned<slice::Iter> so hence the PR.

body: I meant `impl<I: TrustedLen> IterExt for I`. That'll give you the length.

All right, makes sense. I wish I had another way to specialize for `Cloned<slice::Iter>` :( Whatever else I tried, I got a conflicting implementation error....

But even then, perf may get back completely negative or neutral as well.

That's baloney. `descend` is required during the destruction of the tree (not just to start off at the leaf nodes) and is inherently unsafe when a part of the edge array contains stale pointers and `descend` cannot know what part that is. The only way to avoid that is to define a separate unsafe `descend` (wrapper) function for the Dying type, but then you cannot access that in the generic navigation functions being used. I think the only way is to write the whole destructive iterator code with parallel unsafe functions. It doesn't look like hugely more code than the part that already is parallel (the part defined by `def_next_kv_uncheched_dealloc`), but not worth the trouble.

body:
Thanks @hanmertens. I am not familiar with the BinaryHeap implementation but I am prepared to accept this on the basis of the into_sorted_vec benchmark. I confirmed that the behavior is logically identical to before in both places.

- **If `end >= 2`** then `child < end - 1` is equivalent to `child <= end - 2` is equivalent to `child <= end.saturating_sub(2)`.

- **If `end == 1`** then `child < end - 1` is false while `child <= end.saturating_sub(2)` is equivalent to `child == 0`. However it's a loop invariant that `child == 2 * hole.pos() + 1 > 0` so `child != 0` and `child <= end.saturating_sub(2)` is also false.

- **If `end == 0`** then contradiction because it's a precondition of the function that `0 <= pos < end`, and `end` is not mutated.

We are not ignoring it, we return `false`, it means the item `#[cfg(version("garbage"))] ITEM` will be removed.
Returning `true` would also not be an ignore, any value returned from a boolean predicate can do something (e.g. `#[cfg(not(version("garbage")))] ITEM` will be removed if we return `true`).

Also hard-coded warnings should not be used, perhaps the `UNUSED_ATTRIBUTES` lint can be used here if really necessary.

I'd suggest to keep this an error to avoid these questions.
If versioning scheme changes one day, it will likely be planned ahead, so we'll get a long enough range of releases using the old versioning, but supporting the new versioning in `cfg(version)`.

If you wouldn't have a newline at the end of the file, you would get the output

$ cat .editorconfig
...
indent_size = 2$

I'm quite confused here. If with "external impls" you mean the `K: Ord` implementation, sure we can call it, we have to call it, we just had the find functions call it profusely. But we can't blindly trust it to implement a total order ~~, and even if it does, it may not correspond to the `Q: Ord` implementation that we used to check the range bounds~~.

The comparison is done with integers because those are what we end up with, what we need to identify positions in the data structure. For me, the question is: why do we compare and panic at all? Because if we didn't, and if the `Ord` implementations are invalid ~~or inconsistent~~, or until #81138 if the `range` implementation was adversarial, we could easily and silently return a result that would lead callers to loop beyond the end of the tree, which they do unsafely with `unwrap_unchecked`, because they rely on a promise delivered here but documented nowhere.

I thought "SAFETY:" was for documenting why calling something marked unsafe is in fact safe, and here it's kind of the opposite.

So I would add API documentation about the promise here and elsewhere (not sure if I could or should squeeze that into this PR), and change this comment to something like:

    We've called an external `Ord` implementation and can't trust it implements a total order

body:
> We can call it, but the result can't be used for a safety check.

Again, I don't understand why you write that. We have called it, we needed to call it, it's the purpose of the function we're discussing. Yes, the user impl could return anything, but that doesn't make it useless. We need to know what it says in case it's not trying to pull our leg.

> Otherwise, the integers shouldn't be necessary IIUC.

The purpose of this function is to translate a pair of bounds (let's say a pair of keys) to (a node and) a pair of integers, edge indices, indices into various arrays. To translate from the problem domain to the solution domain, in terms of the btree data structure.

> I debated putting it here. However, it does document that the panic allows using unsafe code later with user impls involved.

In my view, the fact that later code is calling unsafe code under some assumption about the result is not an unsafety problem in this function and not the only reason to have the panic. Even if there was no unsafe code outside, without ~~a panic~~ countermeasures, the outside code could erroneously access key-value pairs outside the range. Well, that's up for debate, because if your `Ord` stinks, there is no inside and outside a range. In any case, I think this function should define (which I tried in #83147) and honour its contract, and then callers can exploit those guarantees with any unsafe shenanigans they like.

> > We've called an external `Ord` implementation and can't trust it implements a total order
> 
> This would be okay with me, but it should say something about the panic providing safety.

Actually, come to think of it, that's not even true. AFAIK the panic used to provide safety (to code outside the function) in the old code, but no longer after #81094. The line below the main panic (`if lower_edge_idx < upper_edge_idx {`) is what provides adherence to the contract / external safety. If we'd leave out all the panics from this function, the whole btree code would be just as safe, it would merely return results as weird as the `Ord` implementation, instead of barking at users.

All the panics in this function are only there to fulfill an additional service this function delivers, diagnosing user error.

body:
My own justification attempts to follow the invariant I sketched [here](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/unsoundness-in-pin/11311/113). First of all, it seems like `Pin` might actually be `Unpin`. This might sound surprising, but really what `Unpin` means is that the "pinned" and "not-pinned" typestates of a type are the same, and `Pin` is *always* referring to pinned data, so whether it is in one or the other typestate makes no difference. Thus we can turn `Pin<&'a mut Pin

>` into `&'a mut Pin

` via `get_mut`. Now we just call `as_mut` and we are done.

Of course if you're using laptop/desktop PC `u128_mulhi` works very fast and thus this branch may be needless. However integer multiplication is still expensive operation on some modern processors. For example, on the Intel Knights Landing micro architecture (which is widely used for supercomputers and high-performance workstations), `MUL` instruction needs >7 cycles for generating result. Also it has only 1 specific port for multiplication.

https://agner.org/optimize/

In addition, As you can see in assembler output, this conditional branch generates only 2 instructions, and second call to this function always fallback to fast path because `u128::MAX / 10^19 < 2^83`. That means, if fast path exists, then these 2 calls results in 44 instructions in total, 58 otherwise.

fn foo(x: &impl FnMut()) {

body:
`[u8; N - 1]:` is not used to say anything relevant about `[u8; N - 1]`, it's only meant as a way to express that `N - 1` will evaluate successfully. We don't yet have any explicit syntax for this but instead just pretty much walk over the function signature and the where clauses and add all found constants.

`ConstEvaluatable` are completely separate from other predicates. `T: Ord` ends up as a `PrediateKind::Trait` so we won't ever look at it in `is_const_evaluatable`.

There also isn't a requirement on a where clause. You can use the where clauses to add additional requirements.
These have to be proven by the caller and are assumed by the function itself to hold.

Aha, I see the distinction you're trying to make now.

That seems like a recipe for a pretty poor experience with a very non-obvious cliff at which things may start failing in non-obvious ways. For instance, user with passing familiarity with Rust's `asm!` labels being local could write something like this:

#[inline] // not always
pub fn peach() {

body:
Yes, the probabilities mentioned here assume a hash function with the same collision probability as random values. As far as I can tell SipHash 2-4, which we use at the moment, is pretty good at providing that. But if there was some kind of glitch in the hash function (e.g. certain inputs lead to much worse collision probability) then that could be a cause increased instances of DefPathHash collisions.

I'll add more documentation regarding this.

body:
`to_smaller_hash()` is a bit more expensive because it multiplies one of the values. This multiplication leads to different values depending on the order of the two components (something that we want in a stable hashing context). `Unhasher` on the other hand is just used for hash table, so it's fine if `Fingerprint(x,y)` and `Fingerprint(y,x)` result in the same hash value. 

Let me add a comment about that.

body:
`Ordering::Relaxed` should suffice here (and below in `set_always_abort`). We're not using this flag to synchronize any other data. Any 'happens-before' relationship that might be necessary should already be provided by whatever caused that need. E.g. thread spawning, changing some global allocator property, etc:

If a thread does something like `always_abort(); some_global = 1` and another thread runs code that would somehow be unsound if `some_global == 1` is observed while it doesn't yet see the always-abort flag, that's a problem with the memory ordering on the store+load of `some_global`, and is not solved by an acquire+release ordering on the always-abort flag.

(Specifically, in `always_abort(); thread::spawn(|| ..);`, the always-abort flag is definitely directly visible inside that thread, because spawning a thread synchronizes and guarantees that everything that happened before also already happened from the perspective the new thread as well.)

The other way around, it should never be a problem if `some_global = 1; always_abort();` is executed by one thread and another thread observes the always-abort flag already set while still seeing `some_global != 1`. It might mean that it aborts instead of unrolls when it wasn't strictly necessary yet.

body:
Ok, this PR adds technical debt and this whole function needs to be refactored to use a table of heuristics with priorities and flags indicating whether they support combining or not.
I'm not going to ask you to do this work, but let's try to reduce the technical debt in this PR at least.

body:
Well, I see your point of view: `alias` is used at the moment for providing search results, and since it is case-insensitive and the search already returns Rust results, then having `NULL` or `HashMap` does not make sense.

However, if you think about it from the point of view what we are doing here (the feature itself) and what it could be used for, you can easily come up with more things to do with it, and it makes sense to keep it as a mapping of other languages identifiers/features to Rust, rather than just search terms/keywords that happen to be in other languages. In which case it seems it is useful to keep track why it is an alias (i.e. the language, or the "reason" the alias is there). It is also good for documentation purposes and to keep track of them.

For instance, you could automatically generate an index of Python, or C, or Java features that are mapped to Rust for newcomers from each language, you could show the aliases in the documentation somehow (probably opt-in), you could show a small "capsule tag" with the "C" or "Python" text when searching for a term if it matched due to an alias (unless there is a Rust one exactly), etc.

So it all depends on what we are trying to do: if we are really going to keep a mapping of many functions/types from other languages/standards to Rust, then I definitely think we should add the extra metadata so that this is documented, easier to use for tooling, useful for extra features, etc.

Let me put this in an issue so that we can reference it and discuss it there.

I'm not sure I follow. Could you rephrase your position? It reads to me like

* We get there with const evaluatable bounds when emitting errors
* these errors should be silent when encountered during selection

* trait selection should silence this errors

author: jackh726

body:
> We get there with const evaluatable bounds when emitting errors,

it is an implementation error for const evaluatable bounds to reach this `bug!` and we still don't know all the places where this happens. Often when reaching this `bug!` compilation would fail anyways so a `delay_span_bug` would not trigger in these cases. That would mean that we would only get ICE here once they get triggered by const evaluatable bounds during selection (which then succeeds using a different candidate). This happens a lot less often though, so it would take us longer to find all of these cases. Does this make more sense this way?

body:
Two ideas for this method:
- Could it require `I: TrustedLen`?  If this was exposed publicly that would be a bad idea, but for an internal implementation detail (where we're allowed to use that trait and can easily remove the bound if it proves a bad idea) I think it'd be interesting.  A scan over all the callers says it'd be fine (array::IntoIter, Map, and Zip all keep it), and it might be a good sanity check against passing something like a `Filter` to this accidentally, where we probably can't be confident in the correctness.
- Regardless of the previous, I suggest this have a `debug_assert!(N <= iter.size_hint().1.unwrap_or(usize::MAX));` at the beginning.  It'll only run on the debug builder, but that'll still be a nice error to get if I make a future PR getting this wrong at some point.  (And if we do add `I: TrustedLen`, it could also `debug_assert!(N <= iter.size_hint().0);`.)

diff --git a/src/ci/scripts/should-skip-this.sh b/src/ci/scripts/should-skip-this.sh

body: If future code somehow happens to populate `scope_for_path` for the "happy path", then we could get ourselves in a situation where the following error is never emitted and _no other_ errors are emitted, particularly in some potential future recovery code-path. If that happens, we want to make sure a binary will _never_ be created. `delay_span_bug` is triggered if _no_ error is found yet we get to codegen. Think of it as our last-ditch fail-safe against invalid codegen caused by bugs elsewhere.

body:
If we added `id` to `TestDesc`, the responsibility for generating it and ensuring its uniqueness would fall to the compiler (I’m not sure if this macro even *can* generate a unique ID):

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3e826bb11228508fbe749e594038d6727208aa94/compiler/rustc_builtin_macros/src/test.rs#L227-L297

as well as librustdoc:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3e826bb11228508fbe749e594038d6727208aa94/src/librustdoc/doctest.rs#L831-L842

and all the [tests for libtest itself](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/3e826bb11228508fbe749e594038d6727208aa94/library/test/src/tests.rs). Even if this is somehow possible, it wouldn’t reduce churn.

Another alternative would be to try using the *address* of the `TestDesc` as a unique identifier—but then instead of moving or cloning `TestDesc` we’d have to pass it by reference, which also at best wouldn’t reduce churn.

Writing to the first element doesn't seem to change that much compared to the current approach.

I played a bit on godbolt and I found 3 situations:
* They're optimized almost the same way. This often happen for [tiny `T`s](https://godbolt.org/z/3d7K6P), but sometimes also for [bigger ones](https://godbolt.org/z/5onM31). 
* The `unsafe` version may be optimized to 4-5x less assembly. This often happen for [bigger `T`s but small `N`](https://godbolt.org/z/3afGs7).
* The `unsafe` version is optimized to a `memmove` call and the safe version to either a lot of moves or a loop. This often happen for [bigger `T`s and bigger `N`](https://godbolt.org/z/Tx7xv3)

Thanks for the PR!

We discussed this in a recent Library API meeting and are on board with this API. Please file a tracking issue.

For the implementation though, we would prefer to see the approach from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/82413#issuecomment-784959612 using a buffer of size `2*N` or `2*N-1`, in which every element of the input iterator experiences at most 2 moves, rather than at most N moves. Thus the amortized cost of `next` will be O(1) rather than O(N).

If you prefer, we can land this as is (once there is a tracking issue) and follow up on the implementation in a separate PR; we expect stabilization would be blocked on that. Or feel free to make the implementation change right here in this PR.

body: You're not wrong, the `*` does dereference -- it's just that, when you combine it with a `&`, the net effect is kind of an "identity transform", at least at runtime. That is, `&*x` is sort of equivalent to `x` (the "address of the data that `x` points to" is kind of just "x") -- but only *sort of*, because now we've made a shared reference, and that has implications (e.g., if `x: &mut T`, it implies that `*x` is frozen while this shared reference is live).

body:
I dont think that is quite right. We are going from a MIR place -> HIR place. For all the HIR places we have in our capture set, we would stop at the multivairant enum and not capture anything on top of it. However the MIR place might be for something precise, eg: 

```rust
struct Foo(String, String)
x: Option<Foo>
let c = || match x {
Some(Foo(, y)) => // Upvar(x), [downcast(0), field(0), field(1)]
// ...
```

The ideal thing to do here would really be to look at the type before a downcast projection and see if it's a multi-variant enum and break, but that is a little hard to do here -- because we don't know the actual place since we don't know the capture index, and hence can't get the type. We can make it work by checking if we know any anscetors (in our capture set) of the partially converted place. This sort of makes the code hard to follow and somewhat cyclic in logic where to find a valid ancestor we need to convert the mir place into some hir place and to do that we need to find a valid ancestor.  
EDIT: Though this is like base case of a recursion.

On the otherhand, the field projection in HirPlace is defined as `Field(field_idx, variant_idx)` which as I understand is Downcast to `variant_idx` and then read the field with index `field_idx`. Which is cleaner to express, somewhat more precise and not an incorrect expression of what is happening here. We can then make the function that compares two places to check for the ancestor relation to handle this case properly, and since our capture rules don't really capture multivariant enums it doesn't have to do much for it.
EDIT: Not sure if this is any better to follow for a person who is not aware about these portions of the codebase

Another thing to note here is that a multivariant enum has a variant with index 0, so checking for 0 is not an "if and only if" like check.

body:
The documentation for [`CStr::from_ptr`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/struct.CStr.html#method.from_ptr) is less reassuring:

```
* There is no guarantee to the validity of ptr.
* The returned lifetime is not guaranteed to be the actual lifetime of ptr.
* There is no guarantee that the memory pointed to by ptr contains a valid nul terminator byte at the end of the string.
* It is not guaranteed that the memory pointed by ptr won't change before the CStr has been destroyed.

Note: This operation is intended to be a 0-cost cast but it is currently implemented with an up-front calculation of the length of the string. This is not guaranteed to always be the case.
```

So indeed, it looks safe now, but may not always be safe.
author: lzybkr

body: That’s the unsafe documentation of `from_ptr`. The ptr must meet those criteria in order for the call to `from_ptr` to be safe. So, users of CStr can assume that the internal pointer does meet those criteria. If it doesn’t, it’s a big somewhere else (a caller of `from_ptr` messed up).

body: You're introducing undefined behavior here. `i8::abs` returns an `i8` which can't represent `abs(i8::MIN)`. In debug builds that will panic and in release builds it will overflow to `i8::MIN`. Since `i8::MIN < 10`, you end up with `vec == [b'-', 176]`, but that's not valid UTF-8.

body:
The code up here does the right thing but the comment needs improvements.
1. This comment suggests that `n` is now positive. That's not true because `(!-128i8).wrapping_add(1) == -128`. Only the below cast to `u8` converts that -128 to +128. It would probably a good idea to add a comment to that cast, too.
2. You're not adding 1 to its two's complement. You're computing its two's complement by adding 1 to its bitwise negation.
3. Typo: `-128u8.abs()` -> `-128i8.abs()`

body: That optimization is no longer correct - we need to handle things like `#[cfg_attr] $item`, which we prepend attributes to a captured `Item` or `Stmt` nonterminal. In those cases, we need to create the proper replace ranges, so that they can participate in cfg-expansion.
author: Aaron1011

body:
A replace range can be entirely contained in another replace range (partial overlap is not allowed). For example, `#[cfg_attr] struct Foo { #[cfg_attr] field: u8 }` will result in two replace ranges:

1. `#[cfg_attr] field: u8`
2. `#[cfg_attr] struct Foo { #[cfg_attr] field: u8 }`

We will process `#[cfg_attr] field: u8` first, since its start token occurs after the start token of the other replace range. Therefore, the tokens will get transformed like this:

1. `#[cfg_attr] struct Foo { #[cfg_attr] field: u8 }`
2. `#[cfg_attr] struct Foo { {{ #[cfg_attr] field: u8 }} }`
3. `{{ #[cfg_attr] struct Foo { {{ #[cfg_attr] field: u8 }} } }}`

Where `{{ }}` represents the `FlatToken::AttrTarget` that we introduce.
author: Aaron1011

Oh - I actually banned inner attributes in *all* expressions (including `for`, `async`, and accidentally plain block expressions `{}`) in commit https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/b71a50687d42ad559c6bcfbbf7952805bd6447e3. I guess I misunderstood your previous comment.

This complicates things, because in a case like `for _ in &[true] { #![macro_attr] }`, the inner attribute is actually part of the entire `for` expression. This means that we cannot bail out early when parsing a `for` expression, because we don't know if it will have inner attributes before we get to the block.

body:
I made these fields public instead of adding accessors. This is somewhat uncommon in `std`, but we do the same for `std::ops::Range`.

Accessor functions here would get somewhat messy, because taking ownership of one *or both* of the fields should be possible. The alternative is `.entry()`, `.value()`, `.into_entry()`, `.into_value()` and `.into_entry_and_value() -> (OccupiedEntry, V)`. This can get confusing, as `.entry().key()` would work, but `.entry().remove()` would need `.into_entry().remove()` instead, which would also consume the `value`.

body:
You can see an example of what I mean here:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/6f43f4c3fbc99c3a6699ed8d44608c8f086b10af/compiler/rustc_parse/src/parser/diagnostics.rs#L749-L761

You have a bounded lookahead to see that you might be in a weird known situation that will for sure emit an error. You clone the parser and try an alternative parse. If it is successful, you emit a targeted error, otherwise you "revert" the parser by overriding the parser state with your snapshot. Doing this you gain a lot of confidence in any suggestions you give because you _know_ that the alternative parse worked.

@khuey I'm a little confused as to how this impl makes it easier to work with IoSlices. As far as I can tell there are no other types that implement `Into<IoSlice<'_>>` so `Cow` would be the only std provided type that works with the API demonstrated in your test. I'm pretty sure calling it `ExitStatusError` is better.  We have lots and lots of things called `SuchAndSuchError`, many of which are units or newtypes around something else.  And the name `NonZeroExitStatus` tells us rather more about the underlying representation than ideal.  Or, I think, even, portable. > One alternative I think we should consider is implementing `Try` for `ExitStatus` rather than having an explicit conversion method into `Result`. The try v2 RFC explicitly uses [return codes as one of it's examples](https://github.com/scottmcm/rfcs/blob/do-or-do-not/text/0000-try-trait-v2.md#implementing-try-for-a-non-generic-type), so this seems like a natural application of the `Try` trait to me. cc @scottmcm

Hmm.  I'm not sure exactly how this would work.  Presumably `command.status()?` which would have type `()` ?  This feels rather magical to me.

Also I'm not sure it's a good idea to block this on stabilisation of an in-development feature.  Currently **almost all of the examples in the documentation for `Command` are seriously broken**.  Almost none of them properly check the exit status of the subprocess.  The longer we leave this the more people are unknowingly writing badly broken programs, simply by following our documentation.

I'm told that providing a more ergonomic way to handle errors is a blocker for fixing that (#81452).  If instead a more ergonomic way of checking for these errors is going to be blocked behind stabilising `Try`, maybe we should revisit #81452 - i.e., add all the currently-needed boilerplate to all the examples.
author: ijackson

body:
> does this just straight up remove the `success` method or am I reading this wrong? I would think this is a major breaking change

This is the *internal* `success` method.  The structure of this code is a bit confusing.  There is the public `ExitStatus` which is a newtype facade around an OS-specific `imp::ExitStatus`.

With those internal implementations gaining `.exit_ok()`, there is no need for a specific `imp::ExitStatus::success()` - the facade `ExitStatus::success()` is still there but is simply `.exit_ok().is_ok()`.

body:
> This relies on the assumption of which signal 15 is, _and_ that the description supplied by the C library includes "Terminated". Is this a safe assumption to make in a doctest that may run on an arbitrary non-Linux UNIX target?

Yes, I think it is a pretty safe assumption to make on an arbitrary non-Linux Unix target.

Historically, when one wanted to send a particular signal with `kill(1)` it was necessary to pass the signal number in, not an abbreviation (so `kill -15 <pid>` rather than `kill -TERM <pid>`).  Many people's finger macros do this habitually because it's shorter :-).  I think at least we can rely on `9` and `15` being `Killed` and `Terminated`.

The assumption about the string is more questionable but I think use of some other string than `Terminated` will be extremely rare.

> Do we want a test failure if this assumption doesn't hold?

Well, obviously it woudl be best to avoid that, but it is difficult to check that this function is working *at all* without making *some* assumption about the output.  In practice I expect this assumption to be true everywhere.  (I'm an old Unix hand and have extensive experience of ancient proprietary unices.)

If it is not true somewhere then we might need to make this test have multiple possible permitted outputs.  I think that is better than some more vague test case.

body:
Hm, that's a good question. Today we only pass a computed list of `target-feature`s for `-Ctarget-cpu=native` only.

For other `-Ctarget-cpu`s the `target-feature` list we pass to LLVM will only contain values from `--target` and `-Ctarget-feature` flag. The features present in the string we pass to LLVM will override those that are implied from `-Ctarget-cpu` (regardless of whether it is set implicitly through target or explicitly via CLI).

In short, there ends up being a difference in feature priority: `-Ctarget-cpu=!native` is overriden by `target-features` implied by `--target` is overriden by `-Ctarget-cpu=native` is overriden by `-Ctarget-features`.

I think we still want `-Ctarget-cpu` to override the features implied by `--target`, but that sounds difficult to handle in all cases (including the one where no `-Ctarget-cpu` flag is specified at all...)

I'll sleep on this.

body:
Still, this is incorrect: consider the case where backsliding happens and produces an underflow:
old @ 0x1_0000_0000 seconds
new @ 0x0_ffff_ffff seconds

The upper bits are going to end up wrong if we use the ones from the caller since it will return a time of 0x0_0000_0000 seconds.

The solution here is that instead of using a constant `ZERO` as the base time, you should use a `Lazy<Instant>` which initializes to `Instant::now` on first use. This will allow this code to work as long as the program doesn't run for more than 63 years.

This also means that you can avoid the `UNINITIALIZED` hack and just default `MONO` to a value of 0 which means 0 difference from the first measured base time.

body:
To reproduce perf.rlo results locally under a profiler:

```
# Install and build rustc-perf
git clone https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc-perf
cd rustc-perf
cargo build --release --bin collector --bin rustc-fake

# Install rustup-toolchain-install-master and toolchains selected for comparison:
cargo install rustup-toolchain-install-master
A=d04c3aa8656f6588c87bafafb34d51239dab98bb
B=4151086b47b5fbb6f35855d9436a5a73a476f038
rustup-toolchain-install-master "$A" "$B"

# For example, to run ctfe-stress-4 check full under cachegrind.
./target/release/collector profile_local cachegrind $(rustup which rustc --toolchain "$A") a --builds Check --include ctfe-stress-4 --runs Full
./target/release/collector profile_local cachegrind $(rustup which rustc --toolchain "$B") b --builds Check --include ctfe-stress-4 --runs Full
# Output from a profiler is stored in "results" directory.
# See collector/README.md for other profilers and recommendations about using them.
# Edit collector/src/rustc-fake.rs to customize further.

# Continuing with the example, cg_diff between those two toolchains:
cg_diff results/cgout-{a,b}-ctfe-stress-4-Check-Full > results/cgdiff-ab
cg_annotate results/cgdiff-ab

# Cachegrind diff with an extra normalization of paths and function names:
cg_diff '--mod-filename=s#/rustc/[^/]*/##' '--mod-funcname=s/llvm[.].*/llvm/' results/cgout-{a,b}-ctfe-stress-4-Check-Full > results/cgdiff-ab
cg_annotate results/cgdiff-ab
```
