body:
In addition to agreeing with the comments made so far by @jhpratt I think agree with @slightlyoutofphase that a by value impl for splitting an array in two would almost certainly be useful. We should plan for it now since if we don't add it someone else probably will soon after these methods are made available on nightly, and there seem to be some non-insignificant forward compatibility hazards here to manage.

After digging into the slice split method naming consistency issue you mentioned my first instinct was to call the by value version of the method simply `split`, but that runs into the same coercion issue that you mentioned in the top level comment, since slice already has a split method.

I'm having trouble coming up with any alternatives other than the `_ref` version suggested by @slightlyoutofphase. My current lean is that it's probably fine to have one of the split methods on `slice` include a `_ref` even though similar by reference methods on slice do not. [We have a history of prioritizing forwards compatibility over internal method naming consistency on a given type](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/82703#issuecomment-827776826).

For now I'm going to suggest updating the PR to add the by value version for array and rename the by reference versions on array and slice to end in `_ref`, since I currently expect that to be the most likely resolution. I'll also cc @rust-lang/libs-api in case anyone can think of any better naming scheme here, but if nobody replies before we've updated it and resolved all the comments I'll happily r+ the `array_split`/`array_split_ref`/`array_split_mut` version.

Edit: I just realized that we probably still cant add `array_split` because of the `[T: {N - M}]` issue so feel free to ignore that part of the above advice if it's impossible and just do the `_ref` rename.

body: The panic *handling* stragety of `std` is to unwind or abort. Printing to stderr is done as part of the panic *hook*, which executes before unwinding/aborting happens. Even if you handle a panic yourself with `catch_unwind` or `thread.join()`, the hook was already executed and already printed the panic to stderr.
author: m-ou-se

body: You don't get access to the `Box<Any>` in the hook. You can only look at the payload through [`PanicInfo::payload()`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/panic/struct.PanicInfo.html#method.payload), which gives a `&(dyn Any + Send)`. Only when catching a panic (with `catch_unwind` or `join`ing a thread) you get the Box.

Looking at this with fresh eyes (maybe we discussed this before).. This will only work if there is a covered def in each file containing an uncovered def.

body:
Not sure what exactly happens there, but both imports and tool attributes are "special" in some regards.
- Import paths are split into two parts - module (everything except for the last segment, type namespace) and the final segment resolved multiple times in all namespaces.
- Tool attributes are also split into two parts but in a different way - the first segment resolved as a tool module, and all other segments that are not even resolved (because no definitions for them exist in source code), just automatically assumed to be a tool attribute. (Perhaps the implementation is taking a shortcut here and it could be done better, at least for diagnostics.)

When you combine these two special cases together you get some unique code paths.

The difference is that once you flush there's no data buffered in the program anymore.

In general, the semantics of buffering incomplete UTF-8 seem reasonable to me. I think we'll need to talk about how this interacts with flush, though; I'm hesitant to hold on to buffered data of any kind after a flush.

Possible semantics:
1) Hold onto the incomplete character even after a flush.
2) Emit the invalid UTF-8 error when flushing an incomplete character.
3) Write a replacement character or similar.

I don't want to do (3); that seems wrong. We shouldn't hide errors.

Either (1) or (2) seems *valid*, but which one is more *useful* behavior? I suspect we want (1).

@jyn514 That's kind of right and I'm taking a new look at this PR with the same goal of reducing the amount of time spent in `reserve` calls that don't cause any capacity change.

It looks to me like most of the `Vec::reserve` calls are guarded by a capacity check (such as the one in `push`). But some aren't. This manifests in the `serde_json` benchmarks because serializers do a lot of `Write::write_all` calls which is implemented by `Vec::extend_from_slice`, which is implemented (eventually) by `append_elements`, which has an unguarded `self.reserve`. I'm assessing adding an `if self.len() + additional > self.capacity()` guard around the call in `append_elements`, and going to take a look at either guarding _all_ the `reserve` calls or sinking the check into `Vec::reserve`, and deduplicating the check around a lot of the call sites in `Vec`.

body:
Hm, sounds like you're missing background information on how modern out-of-order CPUs work internally.

Basically, each assembly instruction takes a certain amount of time to execute, measured in `cycles`, and you can only use the instruction's result when that time has passed. Let's say an integer multiplication takes 3 cycles to complete.
If the result of that multiplication is needed RIGHT NOW, the CPU has to issue the multiplication and then wait 3 cycles for the result. If the instructions get reordered a bit, the multiplication gets issued, then the CPU can spend 3 cycles doing other computations, and only then the result of that multiplication is needed.
That way you can hide the instruction's latency and get the end result faster.

body:
Thanks for contribution about the ancillary socket, but I do not think that the code is correct. As far as I understand the [RFC 2292](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2292#section-4.3.2), if the given `cmsg` in `CMSG_NXTHDR` is `NULL` then it returns the first element. `CMSG_NXTHDR(mhdr, NULL) == CMSG_FIRSTHDR(mhdr)`
```
if the value of the cmsg pointer is NULL, a pointer to the cmsghdr 
structure describing the first ancillary data object is returned.
```
So, the previous code was correct. Only the android version of `CMSG_NXTHDR` is wrong. It returned the same  pointer if it is the last element in the list (it does not have to be the first one). If you examine the android [version of `CMSG_NXTHDR`](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/bionic/+/master/libc/bionic/__cmsg_nxthdr.cpp#33), you can see that they forget to check if the length is zero. If you want you can check your code by using two or more `cmsg`s on the android platform.

Also, the previous code is also work with OpenBSD if it is behaved like the Linux version or the version describe in the RFC 2292. As long as it returns `NULL` it should be fine.

See https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/79e5814f4520f2c51b5307421db45cd82d134e76/compiler/rustc_mir/src/transform/mod.rs#L498 and https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/79e5814f4520f2c51b5307421db45cd82d134e76/compiler/rustc_mir/src/transform/mod.rs#L558

The error changes because it removes an assignment, so we hit a different error path due to a different use of the constant. The specific error messages changed in this PR are fine (see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/83177#discussion_r595942238).

But this area seems undertested, I think I've found some cases where it's wrong. I'll open another PR to add tests, that we should merge before this one.

this is what's currently broken here. We look at the final `ty::Ty` for the generic arg in `visit_ty` which can be relevant even for `GenericArg::Infer`. *I also don't know why we still walk the `hir_ty` after visiting the `ty::Ty` in there, but that's probably a more complex change if it's even possible/desirable.*

This happens after typecheck, so we can get the expected generic arg here. We probably want to put this into a separate query. Something like the following which always returns either a `GenericArg::Type` or `GenericArg::Const`:
```rust
query generic_arg_for_infer_arg(id: HirId) -> hir::GenericArg
```
I think ideally we would use this query by default and never actually implicitly ignore the ty/const in `visit_generic_arg`. This would require visitors without a `tcx` and which don't care about inference types/const to manually overwrite `visit_generic_arg`.

> So I _think_ those will only be encountered if there's a problem in the user's code.

Nope, it turns out there are definitely cases where you get a layout error but the code is fine. Specifically, it seems like any generic type will give you a `LayoutError::Unknown` because it doesn't know the size of the generic parameter. For example, [`Result<T, E>` gives an error](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=e28ff4560b78baa2427ccb922d716f6b). I think this explains why many of the types in the standard library didn't have layout info—it's because they're generic.

I'm not sure if there's anything we can do about this to be able to show the layout of generic types. Maybe we'll still add the layout section but just put "layout is unknown due to generic parameters" or something like that. What do you think?

Span arithmetic like this should not be done outside of the lexer, in the world with proc macros `span.lo()` may be entirely arbitrary and point to e.g. end of a file or start of a unicode character, so any use of `span.lo() + BytePos(1)` is a sleeping ICE.

One issue with using a structured suggestion is that we will suggest invalid code in the case of

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i++ < 5 { /* ... */ }
```

We suggest

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut i = 0;
    while i += 1 < 5 { /* ... */ }
}
```

Errors:

```
   Compiling playground v0.0.1 (/playground)
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:3:11
  |
3 |     while i += 1 < 5 { /* ... */ }
  |           ^^^^^^^^^^ expected `bool`, found `()`

error[E0277]: cannot add-assign `bool` to `{integer}`
 --> src/main.rs:3:13
```

body:
That's interesting! The advantage of that is that it will preserve the behavior of `i++` in other languages. Would we always suggest `{ i += 1; i }` or would we sometimes suggest just `i += 1`? I think it would probably be pretty hard to have conditional logic in this case, so I vote for unconditionally using `{ i += 1; i }`, unless there's a simple way to encode the logic.

Also, what should we suggest in the `++i` case? In that case, `{ i += 1; i }` is **not** the correct behavior; rather, the equivalent in Rust is `{ let temp = i; i += 1; temp }`. The problem with suggesting that is that the user may have code like:

```rust
++temp;
```

and then we would suggest

```rust
{ let temp = temp; temp += 1; temp }
```

which is incorrect.

body:
Thanks for making this!

> Also since the common case will be for these arrays to be relatively small (I would imagine 2 is the most common case), I wonder if it's even worth requiring the indices to be sorted?

While discussing this in the libs team meeting recently, we were asking ourselves the same question. We imagine this will mostly be used with small values of N (e.g. 2 or 3), in which case checking for duplicates without requiring it to be sorted would be fine. (Or maybe it could first check if it's sorted to have a fast common case, but fall back to the O(N²) check otherwise?) (And since N will be low in most cases, maybe `multiple` might be a better name than `many`. But we can leave the bikeshedding for later. ^^)

That would solve the question of what to do for unsorted indices (panic vs returning None) by making the question irrelevant.

It'd also match better with the unchecked version. Otherwise we'd have cases where the unchecked version can safely be used, (e.g. `[1, 0]`), but the checked version would panic or return None, which can be confusing.

And for that same reason, I think it'd be best to weaken the requirements on the non-mut version as much as possible too.

What do you think?

A also have a few comments on the implementation:

So, I think this (and use of mmap) may be one plausible reason for the slight performance regression. If my memory of the `ar` format serves me well, obtaining the list of members in an `ar` has to process the file effectively as if it was a ump list.  I suspect that such a read pattern may be a pathological for mmap based I/O: kernel would try loading more data (page?) into memory only for us to inspect the file name and length before we jump to the next entry(-ies), discarding the rest of the data that kernel spent time loading in.

Without digging into LLVM's ArchiveRO implementation I can imagine that more precise reads could be more effective here.

body:
The blanket implementations `unsafe impl<T: TrustedStep> TrustedLen for core::ops::Range<T>` and similar are sound. Specifically, the following invariants for `Step::steps_between` exist:

> * `steps_between(&a, &b) == Some(n)` only if `a <= b`
>    Note that `a <= b` does _not_ imply `steps_between(&a, &b) != None`;
>    this is the case when it would require more than `usize::MAX` steps to get to `b`
> * `steps_between(&a, &b) == None` if `a > b`

The first invariant is what is generally required for `TrustedLen` to be sound. The note addendum satisfies an additional `TrustedLen` invariant.

> The upper bound must only be `None` if the actual iterator length is larger than `usize::MAX`

The second invariant logically follows the first so long as the `PartialOrd` implementation is correct; regardless it is explicitly stated. If `a < b` then `(0, Some(0))` is returned by `ops::Range<A: Step>::size_hint`. As such the second invariant is upheld.

In the eager collection mode (as used by incr comp) all non-generic functions are roots. In the lazy collection mode the entry fn (`fn main(){}`), items marked with `#[rustc_std_internal_symbol]` and `is_reachable_non_generic` functions are roots.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a207871d5c22f89093085da89becbb636a45ef89/compiler/rustc_mir/src/monomorphize/collector.rs#L1106-L1120

Reachable non generics includes functions marked with `#[no_mangle]` and all functions in `reachable_set`.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/dbc37a97dcf08984163133cff85af5190af037ca/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/back/symbol_export.rs#L44-L144

The `reachable_set` includes all public items, trait implementations and all functions called by inlinable functions.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/673d0db5e393e9c64897005b470bfeb6d5aec61b/compiler/rustc_passes/src/reachable.rs#L406-L436

body:
A hypothetical implementation could query `size_hint()` of one or both iterators on every call to `next()` and short-circuit when the upper bound of either is 0. That should be safe and not require any specialization. Whether that could be considered as fusing the iterator would depend on how the non-fused one calculates its size hint.

It's intentionally kept vague to leave more flexibility for optimizations while at the same time telling the users that the underlying iterators' `next()` might not be called. Previously it only said that the 2nd iterator's might not be called, now it may call neither.
author: the8472

body:
I wouldn't call this short circuiting, the fact that the zipped iterator is finite whenever one of its constituent iterators is finite should be evident by the previous sentence already, and even if it is pointed out, it should say “the iterator returned by zip is finite”, not “zip is short-circuiting”.

The “short-circuiting” in the original documentation was, as far as I can tell, referring to how the somewhat logical condition that “If either iterator returns `None`, `next` from the zipped iterator will return `None`” will be evaluated. Taking the “either iterator returns `None`” to basically be a logical disjunction “the first iterator returns `None` *OR* the second iterator returns `None`”, _short-circuiting_ this OR-statement means that the second condition is not evaluated if the first is already true.

body:
I'm not quite happy with the current `RealFileName` variants. The name of the `Named` variant does not tell you what it is for and is potentially confusing (if there is a `Named` variant then why isn't there an `Unnamed` variant, etc...). The `Named` variant can also be either (1) the local path or (2) the stable name, depending on whether remapping was involved or not. And we actually don't always have a name that is really "stable" in the sense of being system independent -- even remapping does not guarantee that the result is stable in that sense. 

So what a `RealFileName` actually can be is:

- The local path to a file
- A remapped path containing the local path and the result of remapping
- A path from upstream crate metadata which can either be 
   - an absolute local path or 
   - a remapped path without the local part

And depending on the situation we want to use the "most stable" path (for emitting to output artefacts) or the path that actually allows you to load something from disk (parsing & error messages).

I think I would suggest the following:

- Rename `RealFileName::Named` to `RealFileName::LocalPath` -- because that's what it is, right?
- Rename ` RealFileName::Virtualized` to `RealFileName::Remapped` so that the naming does not clash with "virtual files" generated by macro expansion.
- Make `local_path` in `RealFileName::Remapped` an `Option<_>` so that we can explicitly "erase" the local portion of the remapped path during export.
- Manually implement `Encodable` for `RealFileName` and panic if we encounter a `local_path` that wasn't erased (i.e. `assert!(local_path.is_none())`).
- Maybe rename the `stable_name` method to something like `most_stable_name` and documentation that it will fall back on the local path if that's the only thing available.
- Use `RealFileName` for the `working_dir` field in `Session` to make things explicit there too.

Another approach to making `local_path` in `RealFileName::Remapped` an `Option<_>` is to introduce another variant `FileName::External`, which takes two values: the path and a boolean indicating if it has been remapped already. The boolean is needed so that already remapped paths from the metadata of another crate won't be remapped again (although those haven't been remapped will be, otherwise we can't do anything about `$HOME/.cargo/registry/...` paths everywhere). A `FileName::Real` is turned into `FileName::External` in `rustc_metadata::rmeta::encoder`.

body:
Well, the `Option<Ordering>` has such u8 values 
```
Some(Less) == 255
Some(Equal) == 0
Some(Greater) == 1
None == 2
```
so, `>=` compiles to `cmp_result as u8 < 2` which easy to optimize.

Old implementation of `<=` couldn't be optimized such easily because it was `(255 == cmp_result || 0 == cmp_result)` which LLVM failed to optimize. After my change it becomes `!((cmp_result+1) > 1)` which optimized much better.


The issue is that both `mod usize` and the primitive usize are in scope. I think this might actually be a bug even before - rustdoc should give an error if the base res is ambiguous, but it doesn't:

```
$ cat primitive-ambiguous.rs 
//! [usize::MAX]

mod usize {
  const MAX: usize = 1;
}
$ rustdoc primitive-ambiguous.rs
$
```

body:
`no_run`  by itself is useless. 
To summarize:
- if you run `rustdoc -Z unstable-options --no-run` it just build the documentation, it has the same behavior  as just `rustdoc`
- `rustdoc -Z unstable-options --no-run --test` run the doctest set. It behave as if every test had the no_run meaning they won't run. Meaning that test like 
\`\`\`
panic!()
\`\`\`
will print as ok like
\`\`\`no_run
panic!()
\`\`\`
without the `--no-run` flag

I agree that is confusing. Maybe a error should be raised if no_run is active and not `should_test`. However I think that if you run `rustdoc -Z unstable-options --no-run` your intention was probably to run the test instead of documenting your project.

I assume that in the original issue the final goal would be to be able to generate bin (with `--persist-doctests`) but without running them. 

Or maybe a another possible case would be to unify the behavior of `cargo test --no-run` (provided that down the line cargo is also modified). For instance `cargo test --all` test both regular test and doctest but `cargo test --all --no-run` skips doctest  `cargo test --doc --no-run` give an error.

Now if the explicit goal is to harmonize with regular test the output should just be empty.
Another option would for me to change the test lib such that no_run test display something like `test foo ... checked`, provided that such change is desirable (to discuss thought the RFC process ?).
Moreover test with `compile_fail` should also print something different maybe checked is also desirable.

I am new contributing for rust so I am not quite sure of what to do to solve this issue.

body:
@ibraheemdev `format!` [gets](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/fmt.rs.html#575-579) the initial capacity from `fn estimated_capacity()` on `Arguments`, which is very [simple heuristic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/fmt/mod.rs.html#352-355) that triggers when the format string **mixes string literals and placeholders** (eg. `format!("hello, {}", x)` – in such case we can assume that the final string will most likely be strictly longer than then literal part and thus if `x` is short enough, avoid reallocation).

Anyway, the current implementation will simply return 0 initial capacity for `format!("{}")` (even if the `fmt` implementation does something like `write!(f, "hello, {}", x)`) – the capacity estimation is not recursive. So, with current capacity estimation heuristics, there won't be any difference when calling `format!`.

body:
I don't understand this.

The order of entries in the top level `invocations` vector is non-significant, it's a job queue - entries can return to it if they are not ready to be resolved or expanded so the exact expansion order is unspecified in general.
So this PR changes one unpredictable order to another?

Once `#[derive(Trait1, Trait2)] ITEM` produced `ITEM`, `placeholder(Trait1)` and `placeholder(Trait2)` these three items part their ways from each other and can be expanded independently in any order (you don't need any specific order to expand them correctly).
The existing code chooses the tentative order `ITEM` -> `placeholder(Trait2)` -> `placeholder(Trait1)`, but it may change later if invocations in `ITEM` are not yet ready.
The new code chooses the tentative order `placeholder(Trait1)` -> `placeholder(Trait2)` -> `ITEM` (which may also change, but only inside `ITEM` because the two placeholders here are always ready by construction).

Am I missing anything?
author: petrochenkov

body:
My reasoning was that we should be treating `#[derive]` like a normal macro as much as possible. While the special delayed-resolution behavior of multiple `#[derive]` attributes (compared to normal attributes) means that we can't guarantee this, I think it makes sense to expand derives left-to-right when possible.

By doing so, we'll make the order of messages printed by derive macros more comprehensible in some cases. Even though the order is unspecified, I don't think we should intentionally pick an order (when everything can be resolved immediately) that's inconsistent with how users normally expect attribute macros to work.

body:
>Should this use `SourceMap::load_file` instead?

I don't think so.
Dep info is filled with `unmapped_path`s, and the `is_real_file` check is supposed to filter away things like `<macros>`, not non-existing files.
Non-existing files or env vars in depinfo are a normal thing - think about reading an optional config (we need to rebuild when it appears).

Besides that `load_file` doesn't do anything except for actually loading the file, which we certainly should not do in the tracking API.

>An additional benefit is that we can use `&Path`s rather than UTF-8 `&str`

Actually, feel free to use `Path`s in the tracking API and keep them in `sess.file_depinfo` if you can pass them through the proc macro bridge.
During writing to depinfo files they will be corrupted anyway though if they contain non-UTF-8 stuff, this is is a pre-existing issue which applies to paths in the source map as well.

>If we agree on this, there needs some mitigation on using `track_path!` or `tracked::fs::path` on a regular source file that is already tracked a source file.

Currently we don't need any such mitigations, depinfo can contain duplicate paths.

body:
This raises an interesting question: what should rustc do if there are multiple extern blocks for the same library with different verbatim modifiers?  The current implementation combines all extern blocks for the same library (identified by name, since that's all we have to go on) into a single import library.

As a concrete example, should we combine the symbols from the following two extern blocks?
```
#[link(name = "foo", kind = "raw-dylib")]
extern { ... }

#[link(name = "foo.dll", kind = "raw-dylib"), modifiers = "+verbatim")]
extern { ... }
```

body: I prefer the valid expression `-0.0 == 0.0` that was the old version of the doc, as someone can just try it out, and the meaning is very clear even without the plus sign which makes it invalid in Rust. In effect, that means that in Rust comparing `-0.0` to `0.0` yields equality. I find the ≡ symbol more confusing, as I understand it to mean "is identical to", but -0 is not *identical* to +0; and I find that symbol can have different meanings to different people.
author: tspiteri

body:
Yeah, it's true. IEEE754 does have strange and seemingly self-contradictory opinions about whether or not these two numbers are actually identical or not. But a simple equals would be fine also. Alas, Rust has overloaded that meaning with assignment. IEEE754 renders it almost exactly so, though, for the same reason of disambiguation: "Comparisons shall ignore the sign of zero (so +0 = −0)."

But mmm. I am not sure why use the variant minus sign elsewhere, then? If the desire is for the values to be copyable from the text, then having the "alternate" −0.0 impedes that.

A way of diverting people away from copying the U+2212 symbols would be to move the code we expect to actually run into a \`\`\`rust context. That way it's easily clickable and runnable and also copyable... I have trouble copying small segments from the middle of a sentence and I know many other people who do, also, because they have a shaky hand or other hand-eye coordination problems, making a mouse interaction unwieldy.
author: workingjubilee

body:
Oh, I find −0.0 = +0.0 to be good as well: since it's not code it's not assignment anyway. I see two contexts here: text where U+2212 should be used and = is fine for an equality check, and code where U+002D has to be used for minus and == for equality.

That is, I'm now preferring your commit suggestion but with = instead of ≡.

See `function_source_span()`, which does adjust the `SyntaxtContext` for all other spans.

All of the function body spans are extrapolated to their `rustc_span::source_map::original_sp`. 

They are assumed to then be in the context of the body. 

The bug, fixed by this PR, was that I assumed the body would always be in the root. Now all contexts are normalized to `root`. 

This allows me to use `Span::to()`, which, otherwise, doesn't always return the expected result, if the contexts are different (even though they are in the same source).

The end result (in tests and in many practical use cases) provide the evidence that this approach works, except for the bug fixed by this PR, which is now obvious.

body:
I think that we could make this change unnecessary with smarter inference. The requirement comes about because we return a closure which captures the lifetime `'a` (via the upvar `f`), so the return type `impl FnMut(Acc, T) -> R + 'a` needs to outlive `'a` rather than `'static`. Therefore, when we return the closure, we end up needing to prove `closure: 'a`, which leads to the requirement that the return type `R` also outlives `'a` (via the new rule introduced by this PR).

Technically, I think we could get away with requiring something weaker than `closure_ty: 'a`. Since the opaque type itself is only known to outlive `'a`, then the 'inputs' to any projection we make using it can only be known to outlive `'a`. Therefore, we can only conclude that the return type `R` outlives `'a`, and not any other region.

However, I don't know how we'd go about expressing that requirement without making some subtle and complicated code even more subtle and complicated.

body:
Revisiting this: I don't think that the argument requires `R: 'a`. We could pass in a function pointer for `fold` that looks like:

```rust
fn my_fold<'b>(acc: &'b u8, other: ()) -> &'b u8 { acc }
```

If the `'a` from the original function is `'static`, then we can **not** conclude that `R: 'a` holds.
author: Aaron1011

body:
That function should outlive `'static` purely because the `'b` lifetime is constrained by the inputs so it doesn't need to live in the self type and play a role in outlives: [playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&gist=07b54eba164940719eb62b3b0f151b6b) You're right afaict though that `impl FnMut(T) -> R + 'a` does not prove `R: 'a` since that only requires `/* CLOSURE */: 'a` to hold, you'd also need `T: 'a` to prove that `R: 'a` holds. (maybe its clearer if we write it as `where ANON_T: Fn<(Acc, B), Output = R> + 'a`?)

I think the kind of implied bounds we would want to allow this to compile "as is" is different than the rules that tell us `<T as Trait<U>>::Assoc: 'a if T: 'a, U: 'a`. The reason for proving the return type outlives `'a` when proving `Closure: 'a` is because conceptually we're wanting to avoid the builtin closure impls having unconstrained lifetimes for example:
```rust
impl<'a> Fn<()> for Closure { type Output = &'a () }
``` 
This PR solves that by conceptually having the `Output` type in the `Self` type: 
```rust
impl<'a> Fn<()> for Closure<&'a ()> { type Output = &'a () }
```
Which then means that proving `Closure: 'lifetime` also has to prove `&'a (): 'lifetime`.
(`fn` items currently have a similar workaround where `fn foo<'a>() -> &'a ()` makes `'a` early bound causing the `foo` item to not outlive `'static`.)

If we have a closure with a return type containing a generic param we have to conservatively assume there might be lifetimes in it that are unconstrained, i.e. `|| { T::default() }` called with `T=&'a ()` shouldn't lead to a `Self: 'static` closure. (From what I can tell this seems to be a lot of cases of back incompat changes in this PR?)

So I think the reason we can "prove" that the following is OK:
```rust
fn find<'a, 'b, T, B>(
            f: &'a mut impl FnMut(T) -> Option<B> + 'b,
        ) -> impl FnMut((), T) -> ControlFlow<B> + 'a {
            move |(), x| match f(x) {
                Some(x) => ControlFlow::Break(x),
                None => ControlFlow::CONTINUE,
            }
}
```
is either:
- `B` has to be part of the `Self` type of the return closure because it would have unconstrained lifetimes therefore `impl FnMut((), T) -> ControlFlow<B> + 'a` requires `B: 'a`
    - the argument `f` has the same inputs so if our returned closure had to have `B` in the self type, so would `f`
        - `f` outlives `'b` and `B` is inside `f` and `'b` outlives `'a` therefore `B: 'a`
- `B` does not have to be part of the `Self` type because all of its lifetimes are constrained by input types
    -  pre-this-PR outlives rules only taking into account the `f` upvar which we know outlives `'b` which outlives `'a`

Annoyingly you cant actually know _which_ one of those is true. The important thing is that one of the two must be true, and either case allows you to prove the closure outlives `'a`.

I determined the `__DWARF` here by poking around in the [source of ld64 itself](https://opensource.apple.com/source/ld64/ld64-609/src/ld/parsers). I came upon [this file](https://opensource.apple.com/source/ld64/ld64-609/src/ld/parsers/macho_relocatable_file.cpp.auto.html) where if you search for `__DWARF` in that file you'll see a loop in `Parser<A>::makeSections()`. The goal was to make this loop drop the section with metadata, effectively triggering a `continue` somewhere.

I actually previously looked at this souce when LLVM bitcode was merged into object files since this confirmed that on macOS the bitcode setions were dropped from the final output. Rummaging around this loop the best way that seemed to trick the linker to not include the section in the final output was a `__DWARF` section with an unknown name, so I settled on that. The `SectionKind::Debug` and `__DWARF` name were both chosen to ensure that the branch there in the loop was hit.

body:
I'm a bit late to the table here, happening to stumble upon this just after it's merged, but I must state that I find both original and updated changes here to be flawed.

Filenames and paths, which of course are sometimes provided as arguments to a program, are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8 on some platforms/filesystems. Consequently there is a possibility of arguments representing real filenames/paths genuinely being non-UTF-8 strings. Use of `args` to collect arguments that take filenames/paths would obviously result in a crash for such inputs, blocking users from potentially using real files/paths with that program.

In theory any argument (or env-var), as external input to the program, could potentially be invalid UTF-8, and simply crashing in the face of this, rather than gracefully exiting with a clear error where appropriate, is really not good behaviour.

The benefit of `args` over `args_os` is simplicity for cases where for instance your app does not take any filename/path arguments, and you don't care if invalid UTF-8 argument inputs cause a crash. It is great for beginners getting to grips with the basics of playing with argument handling.

The benefit of `args_os` over `args` is that it allows you to "correctly" handle all possible filenames/paths for such arguments, and allows you to more gracefully handle situations of otherwise unexpected invalid UTF-8 input, at the expense of the minor complication of having to handle `OsString`/`OsStr` types. It could be viewed as the better/right choice for those with more knowledge and experience.

Thus the choice is nothing to do with safety exactly, as already pointed out, but also is not really about "ensuring UTF-8 validity" either. It's about (a) simplicity - avoiding you having to check for and handle non-UTF-8 situations as above, (b) whether or not you care about properly supporting possibly non-UTF-8 filename/path arguments, (c) whether or not you care about ungraceful crashes in the face of non-UTF-8 input otherwise.

This is not what is conveyed by this modified documentation. It might be best, really, for some form of what I have just written to be placed into the documentation to properly inform those trying to make a choice.

body:
Great question. I noticed this and compared the results with other test results. As it turns out, MOST of the tests already covered these identical leading comments, so from a consistency point of view, it's actually better.

As to why (academically), I suspect it's because I now check, when adding a span to the `refined_spans` to see if the new span is mergeable with the prior span, and if so, I extend the previous span to the end of the new span. This actually saves a counter. (Probably some small improvement in binary size and maybe execution time.)

I had to do this because the macro names (like `assert_eq!`) are now added preemptively (to ensure the macro call is counted, even if the macro expansion has branching logic). For macros that _DON'T_ have branches (no intermediate BCBs) the macro still gets a second `refined_span` for the span from the left paren to the right paren, but the second span is in the same BCB as the macro name. As a result, I saw one test that generated coverage results that looked something like:

```
    println!("some message");
    ^0      ^0
```

Merging spans, when possible, fixed this problem.

body:
Strictly speaking it's an equivalent of `AllocError::CapacityOverflow`, but I think the distinction is not important, and exists in Rust only because of history of its particular implementation.

1. If the preallocation check didn't exist, the same inputs would have resulted in OOM. When the sum of necessary allocations can't fit in `usize`, we know for sure it would OOM at some point, so it can be interpreted as an "as-if" equivalence.

2. This may eventually become `io::ErrorKind::OutOfMemory`. There's no `ErrorKind` for `CapacityOverflow`, and probably shouldn't be, so there's no point introducing this distinction temporarily.

body:
I used `StaticRWLock` because it was what was done with `StaticMutex`, but I can see several advantages over `SyncOnceCell<sync::RwLock>` :
- `sync::RwLock` is boxed an some platforms, and we should avoid an allocation and an indirection if possible
- You don't pay another synchronisation algorithm on top of a `RwLock`
- `StaticRWLock` exposes a safe interface anyway, and we could easily change it to include an inner value and make it totally safe to use

`data-level` is purely used as in CSS selectors, right? I think it would be better in that case to make it a class. And while we're at it, maybe we can eliminate the level = 1 / level = 2 (formerly h3 / h4) dichotomy?

For the elements we're changing here - ones inside `<summary>` tags, it looks like there is no intentional different between h3 and h4. For instance, [on a trait page](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html) the "Required Methods" are h3. But on [a struct page](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/alloc/string/struct.String.html), the "Methods" are h4, despite playing the same role in the page.

So what I'm saying is: Let's try removing the `data-level` concept entirely. Almost all of the CSS rules that needed it already have some other useful class in the selector, like `.method` or `.type`. For the small handful of rules that select on h3 or h4 with no class, we should figure out if we can be equally selective by adding a class.

I think this is fine as is. LexError is useless in practice because the parser in proc-macro will panic instead of ever returning it, so nothing in the ecosystem relies on having a meaningful LexError. (Actually it's worse -- sometimes the parser will return `Ok` even for input strings that are invalid tokens.)

Whenever the parser is fixed to be able to reliably return LexError instead of panicking or pretending like it worked, we'll likely consider adding some internal enum into LexError to provide more info on what happened. This impl would take advantage of that at the same time.

body:
Actually, I think I may have an idea for a simpler approach. It seems like HRTB only show up in two places: (1) `fn` pointer types` and (2) trait bounds. Place (1) seems to work already, so we can focus on place (2).

Within place (2), there are two "subplaces": (a) `where` bounds and (b) `dyn Trait`s. For `where` bounds, I noticed you added a `bound_params: Vec<Lifetime>` field, but I would think that would already be covered by the existing `bounds: Vec<GenericBound>` field. Could you explain a bit why you added the new field? Apologies if I'm missing something.

For place (b), I think a `DynTrait` variant that is just a `Vec<GenericBound>` *may* be enough. However, perhaps there's something I'm forgetting, in which case we'll have to revisit that.
author: camelid

body:
I somehow expected to get questions on the code because It's *really* weird, I know :sweat_smile: 

> Also, it seems odd to me that data specific to dyn Traits is stored as part of ResolvedPath. I noticed that you said in #84814 (comment) that you were planning to add a new Type variant but decided to instead change the existing ResolvedPath field. I think your original idea would actually be a better approach, and would make the code easier to understand.

Yes I agree that this is definitely cleaner and easier to understand. I will change that!

> I feel a bit confused about this. PathSegments (Path is mostly a Vec<PathSegment>) have generic arguments in them, so why are generic arguments both there and here?

This is the "hack" that rustdoc currently uses. It uses the `Path` to display trait objects. Before this PR, the `param_names` field would indicate if this `Path` is a trait object. If the `param_names` is `Some`, then this `Path` is a trait object and it's bounds are *this* path, and all the bounds in the `param_names` (`param_names` is basically a list of [these](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_hir/hir/struct.PolyTraitRef.html#structfield.trait_ref) elements, where the first trait ref is special-cased and becomes *this* path) field. The second list in the tuple, was a list containing [these](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_hir/hir/struct.PolyTraitRef.html#structfield.bound_generic_params) elements, so it includes all lifetimes that were provided using `for<...>`.
author: Stupremee

body:
> Could you explain a bit why you added the new field?

The `bounds` part does not include the higher ranked lifetimes. If you look at the doc for the rustic [WhereBoundPredicate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_hir/hir/struct.WhereBoundPredicate.html), you'll see that there's a `bounds` field, which directly translates to the `bounds` field in the cleaned `WherePredicate`, and a `bound_generic_params`, which includes all lifetimes provided by `for<>` (as written in the documentation). The latter field was previously discarded while cleaning the predicate, so I added a field to keep the information about these lifetimes.

body:
I think we can drop the `shadow_seen.len() > 1` part, because `seen` always contains at least one element, so `shadow_seen.len() > seen.len()` implies the former condition.

We can't drop the latter condition, though, because it would lead to nonsensical errors:
```
error[E0072]: recursive type `Foo` has infinite size
 --> t1.rs:1:1
  |
1 | struct Foo { a: u32 }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^      --- recursive without indirection
  | |
  | recursive type has infinite size
```
The problem is that when `are_inner_types_recursive()` is first called, `shadow_seen` equals `seen` and `ty` (and therefore `def`) is the original type (`Foo` in my example), i.e. `shadow_seen.first() == Some(def)` is always true.

The case that we are actually interested in is mutual recursion, where we have recursed to check some field's type (and therefore `shadow_seen.len() > seen.len()`) and _then_ found the original type again, e.g. when checking `B` below, we recurse into `A` and find `B` again:
```rust
struct A<T> {
    z: T,
    x: B<T>,
}

struct B<T> {
    y: A<T>
}
```

To make my point clearer:

If by carry you mean overflow, then both should return `false`, but then it is not carry and cannot be used easily for a wider addition. So that would make this function pretty useless.

If by carry you actually mean carry, then both should return `true`. The implementation would be something like:
```rust
let (u, c) = (self as $UnsignedT).carrying_add(rhs as $UnsignedT, carry);
(u as $SelfT, c)
```

body:
I believe `widening_mul` on signed integers should return the less-significant half as unsigned instead. For example consider `i8`, and −128 × 3 (`0x80 * 0x03`). Now, when widened to `i16` (`0xff80 * 0x0003`), this gives −384 (`0xfe80`), which is then returned as (`0x80`, `0xfe`). Now, `0xfe` itself is −2, so think of this as meaning −512 because it is the higher word. The correct result is −512 + 128, so the `0x80` should be interpreted as +128 not −128, so it would be `u8`, not `i8`.

Note: I'm using unsigned for all hex values to not make it more confusing, even though technically `0xfe_i8` is an error and would be written as `-0x02_i8`.
author: tspiteri

body: Also, using unsigned for the lower half would make it possible to write something like `real_result = (i16::from(high) << 8) | i16::from(low)`, or `+` instead of `|`, both work. With signed for the lower half, `i16::from(low)` would be sign extended and would actually need to be masked with something like `(i16::from(low) & i16::from(u8::MAX))`.

body:
My understanding is that `dedup()` only removes _consecutive_ duplicates, i.e. for full deduplication, we have to sort first.

If your question is why we have to deduplicate `spans` at all: The reason is that there can be multiple lifetimes missing in the same spot, e.g.:
```rust
struct S<'a, 'b> {
    a: &'a i32,
    b: &'b i32,
}

fn foo(a: &i32, b: &i32) -> S {todo!()}
```
```
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifiers
 --> src/main.rs:6:29
  |
6 | fn foo(a: &i32, b: &i32) -> S {todo!()}
  |           ----     ----     ^ expected 2 lifetime parameters
```
Here, we want a _single_ error message, stating that _two_ lifetime parameters are missing at the indicated location. Therefore, we deduplicate the spans (so that only one error message is constructed) and count how many duplicates there were (so that we can say how many lifetime parameters are expected, e.g. 2 above).

Well, it's not necessarily `'a`; it lists the available lifetimes above and then asks you to pick one of them, `'lifetime` is just the placeholder. And yes, this is preexisting, e.g.
```rust
struct S<'a, 'b, T> {

fn foo<'a, 'b, T>(a: &'a i32, b: &'b i32, c: T) -> S<T> {todo!()}
```

on current stable (1.52.0) gives:
```
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifiers
 --> src/main.rs:7:54
  |
7 | fn foo<'a, 'b, T>(a: &'a i32, b: &'b i32, c: T) -> S<T> {todo!()}
  |                      -------     -------             ^ expected 2 lifetime parameters
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`
note: these named lifetimes are available to use
 --> src/main.rs:7:8
  |
7 | fn foo<'a, 'b, T>(a: &'a i32, b: &'b i32, c: T) -> S<T> {todo!()}
  |        ^^  ^^
help: consider using one of the available lifetimes here
  |
7 | fn foo<'a, 'b, T>(a: &'a i32, b: &'b i32, c: T) -> S<'lifetime, 'lifetime, T> {todo!()}
  |                                                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```
The only change I have made is to extend this suggestion to references (as in the snippet you have commented on above). The [current implementation](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1b30245ea1286df96d673015c4519c861e06977a/compiler/rustc_resolve/src/late/diagnostics.rs#L2046-L2058) only shows the `'lifetime` placeholder for generic arguments (i.e. if `Some("") == snippet.as_deref()`), not for references (`Some("&")`), but I thought it would be more consistent if we showed the same suggestion for both.

This match case would only get hit for non-re-exported structs' constructors which is why we would miss the cross-crate case to begin with. So for a given newtype constructor we would sometimes hit both the `DefKind::Ctor` and `DefKind::Struct` arms or only hit the `DefKind::Struct` arm. It is the latter case where we didn't have the good diagnostics.

`callback` here collects the Exports which end up processed by the method `build_reduced_graph_for_external_crate_res` above:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/2bafe96272bf22cd191c6a01741184b60063292d/compiler/rustc_metadata/src/rmeta/decoder.rs#L1084-L1095

So my PR just handles collecting `struct_constructors` for diagnostics always in the `DefKind::Struct` arm instead of relying on the `Ctor` arm which isn't always present.

body:
IIRC the twox crate isn't a particularly high performance implementation of the xxh algorithms. I don't know if it's just based on an old version of xxh or what, but there are a lot of things it does that will lead to much worse performance than the C/reference implementation. A couple examples are:

- Using heap allocation here https://github.com/shepmaster/twox-hash/blob/main/src/xxh3.rs#L855 ([compare to ref/C impl](https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/blob/be534ed8c9fa677f18f230735c114373b1ed7d34/xxhash.h#L987)), means means that the loads performed in the SIMD accel versions need to be unaligned, which has *wildly* varying latencies on SIMD. (Also, I suspect that the optimizer can't see that it's not actually resizing the buffer a bunch)
- I highly suspect the way the `With` enum internally will lead to the same thing, and branching at each iteration. (I think the body of these loops are too bug for LLVM's loop unswitching to kick in)

There are probably others, this was just a glance I did when I found the crate to be about 3x slower than the C code. I ended up using it anyway since it meant I could move that code from C++ to rust, but I was pretty disappointed. (Probably, I should have filed issues, but at the time I was very busy)

Another thing is that for small keys, XXH's api assumes you aren't using the streaming API. but the way the `core::hash` API is set up, the optimizations it does like that are much more difficult. I don't know if that's relevant here, though.

The implementation found in the interpreter I mentioned earlier quite nicely avoids special casing the pointer width.

It operates on largest supported pointer width. Based on endian encodes value using `to_le_bytes` or `to_be_bytes`, and then extracts the least significant portion of data by subslicing. body:
I checked and `to_uppercase` is not always correct: `'ß'.to_uppercase() == "SS"`, but the following fails
```rust
set_var("ß", "something");
var("SS").unwrap() // panic: Err<NotPresent>
```

I can't find anything about in official documentation, but from tests I did I suspect Windows uses simple case folding (for context see [Unicode Technical Report #21 Case Mappings Section 1.3](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr21/tr21-5.html), simple case folding is the unicode case folding algorithm, but restricted to code points that don't expand under upper/lower casing like `ß`). I also checked if any normalization or locale-dependent behavior was happening, but that doesn't appear to be the case: `é` and `é` (e + acute accent combining character) are different keys and nothing changed around `i`/`I` on the Turkish locale (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dotted_and_dotless_I).

Not sure what the best way to use case folding in std would be (if that is even what Windows is indeed using). There are crates like [unicode-rs/rust-caseless](https://github.com/unicode-rs/rust-caseless) implementing case folding, but I couldn't find any that also implements the simple variant.

Edit: Windows does not use Unicode case folding, but instead has a different uppercase implementation: see the comment below.
Edit2: It does appear to be based on reverse unicode folding, but with some unique particularities, see https://github.com/ChrisDenton/Windows-case
author: CDirkx

body:
I looked through the docs some more: 

File paths and environment variables should be compared using `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` [1]. Comparisons made using `OrdinalIgnoreCase` are behaviorally the composition of two calls: calling `ToUpperInvariant` on both string arguments, and doing a comparison using `Ordinal` [2]. A comparison using `Ordinal` is just a comparison based on the numerical value of each utf16 code unit [3]. 

So the original approach was conceptually correct, but Windows apparently handles converting to uppercase differently than rust (I haven't yet found anywhere how `ToUpperInvariant` is actually implemented 🙁). I agree with the approach to instead just use the Windows API. 

(As an aside, with the relevant Windows API added a future possibility for `std` would be to expose case insensitive functionality with a `std::os` extension trait, for example for correctly comparing paths case insensitively.)

[1] https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/best-practices-strings#choosing-a-stringcomparison-member-for-your-method-call
[2] https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/best-practices-strings#stringtoupper-and-stringtolower
[3] https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.stringcomparison?view=net-5.0#System_StringComparison_Ordinal

Unfortunately, 'OsString' means 'can represent every string that the OS accepts', not 'a string that the OS can directly use'. We can't change this unless we start a 'std 2.0' or something. body:
The `mir_callgraph_reachable` is relatively expensive. If we can avoid calling it half the time that seems like a nice win!

The unpredictable nature of the check is a disadvantage, but the condition is effectively: `caller_hash < callee_hash || !reachable(callee, caller)`, which means that it becomes unpredictable only in a presence of a cycle, since otherwise MIR would be available for inlining anyway. I think this is a reasonable trade-off to make.

BTW. Does comparing `local_hash` help? It seems to incorporate complete `DefPathHash` of a parent: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/fa72878a61f2b0a2127fe7d700724642fc79ec66/compiler/rustc_hir/src/definitions.rs#L143-L156

author: petrochenkov

body:
UEFI applications run in a single address-space, everything is identity-mapped. You might get any pointer value at runtime and access it, or jump to it. You cannot tell up front how your address-space will look like. And since the entire UEFI core is running in your address-space, you cannot even tell what kind of instructions will be invoked as part of your application.

Anyway, the biggest issue I had was that I had to select something for the code-model field, and I found it quite hard to get information on what it controls. Does this only affect immediate-values of generated instructions? Or only the hard-coded relative offsets? Does it affect program-behavior? If it only affects generated constants, why can't the compiler figure it out automatically? What happens when the value is wrongly chosen?

Given all those questions, I figured that `large` was the safest compromise. If you know LLVM (or x86 ISA) better than that, please feel free to help us out here!

I'm a bit curious why you took this approach. I think I'm probably missing some context here so additional details would be greatly appreciated! 🙂 

At least from a cursory review, it seems like the following is true:
- When `-Zinstrument-coverage=off`, we never generate MIR coverage statements to begin with and we also don't care if they were made unreachable by a MIR pass. 
- When `-Zinstrument-coverage=on`, it doesn't really matter that a pass made a coverage statement unreachable as long as keep a coverage statement in `bb0` which marks the code region as unreachable.

(I suspect the context I'm missing is why my second statement is not true for some reason.)

If both of those statements *were* true, then it seems like we don't need this enum at all, we just need to know if `-Zinstrument-coverage=on` and in that case, make sure we retain the code regions as unreachable. 

What I like about that is it simplifies the calling code so they don't have to be aware of code coverage at all, they just have to pass `tcx` down. 

Thoughts?
author: wesleywiser

body:
It's a very reasonable question.

I THINK this assumption is what you may have wrong:

> * When -Zinstrument-coverage=on, it doesn't really matter that a pass made a coverage statement unreachable as long as keep a coverage statement in bb0 which marks the code region as unreachable.

I tried a very simple implementation of this, and it didn't work. One reason requires special handling:

Some passes clone blocks, and use dead-block removal to remove the original statements. `simplify_cfg` has no was to know this, so when the coverage statements from the dead block are added to `bb0`, they are duplicate code regions. The cloned blocks still have the original _reachable_ blocks and coverage statements. Adding `unreachable` code regions to `bb0` breaks coverage reports, probably because the same code region is reported as both reachable and unreachable. So we need the `Allow` enum option for this case (allow the dead blocks' coverage statements to be dropped).

So I need to at least call `simplify_cfg` with an option to either `Allow` dropping the coverage, or to `Save` the coverage.

Here's why I added the `AssertNone` option, which is the default, if the caller uses the existing function signatures (plus `tcx`):

In my view, I did "simplify the calling code so they don't have to be aware of code coverage" for those passes that don't (today) do anything that would affect code coverage.

I simplified it by keeping the original functions `simplify_cfg()` and `remove_dead_blocks()` (only adding the `tcx` parameter).

The passes that call these functions are assumed to be "safe" to coverage.

But the problem is, the only way I found out that there were a few RARE edge cases that dead-block removal broke was during codegen. By that time, I have no idea what pass broke coverage during CFG simplification.

By adding the assertion and check, if a new edge case pops up that we can't predict, we'll have a lot more to go on.

Obviously, we could remove this assert, and assume that I've caught all possible edge cases; but since I got bit twice already, I don't feel like I can make that assumption. And a new pass, or change to a MIR pass, might break coverage in the future. This is obscure enough that I think we should check.

body:
No, so this is actually a consequence by the way `normalize_erasing_regions` works. Because it needs to call the `normalize_generic_arg_after_erasing_regions`, it folds through tys and consts in a `TypeFoldable`. Importantly, it skips binders, leaving us with trying to normalize with escaping bound vars.

Here, we just add the universes that we *would* have created had we passed through the binders.

We *could* instantiate eagerly here, but it doesn't seem really necessary to me. The rest of the code is already set up to be lazy about replacing bound vars and only when we actually have to normalize.

body:
1. Yes, those `#[link]` attributes export those symbols to libstd.so. They are added to fix https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/62088. Those symbols is needed by llvm, and empty `extern "C" {}` don't export those symbols.  It's only needed when build `rustc` with feature `llvm-libunwind` and `static-libstdcpp`
2. Building rustc with feature `llvm-libunwind` is broken again because https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/72746.  The possible way to fix this is mentioned in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76020#issuecomment-707528177

>Yes, those `#[link]` attributes export those symbols to libstd.so.

Using `#[link]` for performing an entirely unrelated task is a really inappropriate behavior from rustc, although I can't say I'm surprised at this point.
I hope this is something that can be rectified in the future.

body:
I removed this line because:
- It is redundant: it already follows from `a < b` being defined as `partial_cmp(a, b) == Some(Less)`, which implies `!(a > b)` (defined as `partial_cmp(a, b) != Some(Greater)`).
- "asymmetry" is the wrong term, an "asymmetric" relation is a relation that satisfies "if `a < b` then `!(b < a)`".

asymmtery (in the correct sense of the word) is a consequence of duality, so we could state it in the corollary section if you wish. antisymmetry is more closely related to what the docs are currently stating, but it is defined for `<=`-style relations: `R` is antisymmetric if `R(a, b) && R(b, a)` implies `a == b`.

body:
> Warn or panic? Let me know of your decision.

I think panic! is probably best.

> [...] cmake env

Looking into our use of cmake a little more, it looks like we only ever actually invoke it through the cmake crate, so if users are supplying configuration to us via env variables, the cmake crate would already be picking that up appropriately. In sanity checking, we do use "cmake" without doing the same env-variable lookup that the cmake crate does. (Target-specific *cmake* binaries do not feel particularly likely to be actually necessary, as it's really a host tool).

I'm not too worried about env-variables overriding bootstrap's configuration in the cmake crate - that seems unlikely to be an issue in practice, given how bootstrap itself isn't using cmake directly (except for sanity checks). Given that CMAKE isn't a "standard" env variable (or at least I've seen no evidence of that), I'm not really worried about supporting setting it as an alternative to editing config.toml, either.

So I think the value of config.cmake probably comes down to:

* config.toml, if set
* cmake, if not

After we load that, we want to put it in our own environment (set_var("CMAKE")) so that the cmake crate picks it up, at least as things stand today. Just before doing that I think it makes sense to check that it's not set to a different value (mostly just as a sanity check, but it doesn't make sense for this to be in sanity.rs).

Pretty much all of that logic should go into config.rs.

body:
No, `is_dir` follows symlinks, so in case of a symlink->symlink->symlink->dir, that's multiple symlinks. (Though I guess technically only one can be broken, since traversal stops there.) `is_symlink` however, will not traverse them, so there's only one symlink.

In addition, any of the other components of the path can be a symlink too. E.g. `/something/symlink1/something/symlink2`. `is_symlink` returns false if the first one is broken (because then the full path doesn't even exist), but true if the second one is broken. Changing the wording to 'a broken symlink' makes it a bit clearer that this is just about the one symlink that the path refers to, and that we're not talking about all the ways broken symlinks can be involved.  Maybe `In case the symlink is broken, ..` is a bit clearer though.

body: Does that really solve the stated problem though? serde could still encounter an EOF in the middle of parsing an input.
author: the8472

body: If serde encounters an EOF in the middle of deserializing an object then it's a syntax error and the input is invalid, at least for that object. If serde finishes parsing the last object in a valid input then all that's left in the reader would be EOF. In that case having EOF checking would prevent serde from attempting to deserialize another object and throwing a syntax error. Having EOF checking between deserialize calls allows the loop to end gracefully when encountering EOF in a valid input.

body:
I don't know any way to write rust code that produces things like `icmp eq i96` and `icmp eq i256`.  I could write rust code that manually expands it out to loading the pieces as `u64` or something, but having a loop generating a bunch of that manually makes it much harder for LLVM's optimizer to understand what's going on -- when it's a single `icmp`, things like `a == [0; N]` collapse beautifully.

I actually tried putting the length check in here first.  That worked great in the optimized code, but it was horrific for the `opt-level=0` codegen of `array_eq_long` -- the `icmp eq i19744` was unreachable, but it didn't know that and proceeded to emit over 300 qword comparisons into the assembly output.

I'd definitely *rather* have the length check in the library -- it seems reasonable that different places might want different thresholds, and I'd prefer to call `memcmp` from there instead of the intrinsic -- so if you have a good solution for that I'd be happy to update things.

body:
I think that'd work, but I really don't feel like it'd be a good idea to spread knowledge of the poorly-justified threshold out between all four of core/codegen_llvm/codegen_cranelift/miri, even if it's documented.  I'd like it to be easy for someone to test things like "it should be `>=`, not `>`", for example.

Having slept on this, I think I actually *like* leaving it up to codegen to decide where the threshold is.  That's basically what was happening with the `memcmp` call -- the target-dependent codegen decided whether to leave in the function call or to emit loads instead.  (Except that that was too late for the optimizer to be able to also remove the `alloca`s, leading to the unfortunate "pass the arguments in registers, then write them to stack, then read them from stack again, then look at them".)

It wouldn't seem unreasonable, for example, to do something like "well, if `sess.opts.optimize == OptLevel::Aggressive`, then allow up to 8×usize".  (Though I'm not sure that that *specific* change would be worth the testing implications of having codegen emit different IR at different optimization levels, but maybe if well-justified it could be worth it like running mir-opts can be.)

And from a semantic cleanliness perspective, I'd much rather the definition be "it compares them", than "it compares them, unless they're bigger than 4×usize, in which case it aborts".  The MIRI implementation is nice and clean right now, for example, and adding something like a threshold into it makes it feel worse to me.

body:
The ultimate goal is to generate a URL to the source code for a given example. For instance, take [gtk-rs](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs). It has examples in `/examples/`. Let's say we're documenting `/gtk/sys/` and there's a call to `gtk_sys::foo` in `/examples/overlay/main.rs`. The goal is to generate a URL to https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs/examples/overlay/main.rs .

I'm not sure how you accomplish this task without knowing the workspace. A crate-relative path to `main.rs` would be `overlay/main.rs`, which doesn't include the `examples` directory. 

Alternatively, we could avoid this task altogether by including source code for examples as a part of Rustdoc's generated files, and then linking to those files.

body:
So the core issue is that examples are scraped from reverse-dependencies. AFAIK, such files aren't guaranteed to be in the source map while documenting the crate that defines a given function. This has a few implications:
* Spans don't translate from the scraped crate to the documented crate. Hence, the need for a separate `SyntaxRange` structure, and why I have to generate the example URL at scrape time instead of document time.
* DefIds don't translate from crate to crate. The DefPathHash of a function while scraping doesn't seem to be the same as while documenting. This one I'm less sure why, but it's been my observation when trying to use `DefPathHash` to identify a function. Hence I have the hacky `def_id_call_key` function instead.

I don't know cargo or rustc well enough to say whether these issues are fixable.

body:
Well, first of all note that I didn’t write the original text, I just clarified it w.r.t. `Clone`, but second: if `__iterator_get_unchecked(self.size() - 1)`, then the requirement will be that
> `self.next_back()` will only be called at most `self.size() - idx - 1` times

so…
> idx == size-1

> size - idx - 1 == size - (size - 1) - 1 == 0

There you go, now you’re officially no longer allowed to call `next_back` _at all_.

body: Can we give any guarantees about non-finite values? E.g. that any nan wil result in a nan result, and/or that if only one of the values is infinite, the result will be that infinite value.
author: m-ou-se

body:
So, I was considering doing the full list of guarantees that [C++ provides](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/lerp), which are:

* If isfinite(a) && isfinite(b):
    * If t == 0, the result is equal to a.
    * If t == 1, the result is equal to b.
    * If t >= 0 && t <= 1, the result is finite.
* If isfinite(t) && a == b, the result is equal to a.
* If isfinite(t) || (!isnan(t) && b-a != 0), the result is not NaN.
* Let CMP(x,y) be 1 if x > y, -1 if x < y, and 0 otherwise. For any t1 and t2, the product of CMP(lerp(a, b, t2), lerp(a, b, t1)), CMP(t2, t1), and CMP(b, a) is non-negative. (That is, lerp is monotonic.)

But I figured that it might potentially limit what kinds of implementations we allow. I'll try adding tests for these (and comment them out if they don't work) and maybe we can hash it out in the tracking issue.

body:
The comment above says:
```rust
// We prepend this bin directory to the user PATH when linking Rust binaries. To
// avoid shadowing the system LLD we rename the LLD we provide to `rust-lld`.
```
Namely, the `lib/rustlib/<host>/bin` directory is added to `PATH` in `fn get_linker`.

This means `ld` (or `ld.exe`) will interfere with gcc's linker search even if `-Zgcc-ld=lld` is not passed.

GCC prefers hardcoded paths like `/mingw64/x86_64-w64-mingw32/bin` (on windows-gnu) to searching `PATH` so the right ld was chosen in my case, but this newly added `ld` can still interfere with search in other cases.

body:
Suggestion: what if we turn this the other way? Say we have a `FxHashMap` (which is a hash map with a faster hashing algorithm that we use throughout the compiler) that represents all the `#[expect]` attributes that need to be fulfilled. It takes a `(LintStackIndex, LintId)` pair as its key and everything that we need to emit the lint (the `#[expect]` attribute's span, the reason, etc) as its value. Every time we emit an `expect`ed lint, we remove that lint's entry from the map, and at the end of compilation, we emit an `unfulfilled_lint_expectation` lint for every remaining entry in the map.

This would require a few changes to how lints are emitted so I don't feel confident to say "it's the way to go", maybe you'll want to wait on someone more qualified to weigh in.

body:
In https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/rfc-emit-check/14711/5?u=jsgf I measured it as ~8% difference on `cargo check` for Cargo itself. I don't know how that relates to anything else.

I experimented with making a distinction between `--emit metadata` and `--emit check` and corresponding `.rmeta` and `.rcheck` files, but the addition of a new file type in the mix made things complex in location resolution in rustc and in Cargo itself. It would be much easier to just make `.rmeta` invariant.

One advantage, in principle, is that if `cargo check`'s emitted metadata is "full fat", then it can be used immediately from cache in `cargo build` which would effectively make the dependency graph flat and allow the rlibs to be generated completely in parallel - though I expect that would only really be interesting for builds which are closer to build from scratch vs incremental rebuild.
author: jsgf

body:
I also wonder what the practical effect of this will be. I presume the risk is that some build system - like `cargo` will intermix invocations of `--emit metadata` (cargo check) and `--emit link,metadata` (cargo build) and get failures if check metadata gets used for builds.

But what's the actual outcome? In the worst case, it could appear to succeed but generate subtly broken output. But I don't think that's the case here, is it? It will fail to find " list of reachable non-generics, the list of exported symbols and dependency_format::calculate_type", and fail as a result. Vs if the hashes are different, it will fail for that reason ("found possibly newer version of crate ...").

(If need be, could we extend the .rmeta format to include a type to explicitly flag "for check use only"?)

I haven't looked into how `cargo` specifically managed check vs build .rmetas, but I think it avoids the problem by always regenerating .rmetas as part of a build. In my own experiments with Buck, I make sure to put them in separate dirs (which is the motivation for this PR, since currently doing that changes the crate hash independent of anything else).

Either way, any failure is a bug in the build system, not something that an end-user would expect to see with a correctly implemented build system.
author: jsgf

body:
> I also wonder what the practical effect of this will be. I presume the risk is that some build system - like cargo will intermix invocations of --emit metadata (cargo check) and --emit link,metadata (cargo build) and get failures if check metadata gets used for builds.

That is exactly what you want to do, right? Using the `--emit metadata` output of dependencies to compile `--emit link` crates.

> But what's the actual outcome? In the worst case, it could appear to succeed but generate subtly broken output. But I don't think that's the case here, is it? It will fail to find " list of reachable non-generics, the list of exported symbols and dependency_format::calculate_type", and fail as a result. Vs if the hashes are different, it will fail for that reason ("found possibly newer version of crate ...").

A wrong result of dependency_format::calculate_type will cause linking to silently fail due to mixing up static and dynamic linking of crates. For example trying to statically link a crate that is already linked into a dynamic library dependency.

A wrong result for the list of reachable non-generics and exported symbols would likely result in the mono item collector creating mono items that are already included in dependencies (or maybe omitting necessary ones), causing duplicate linker errors.

> I haven't looked into how cargo specifically managed check vs build .rmetas, but I think it avoids the problem by always regenerating .rmetas as part of a build.

It currently handles check and regular builds independently, but we want `cargo check` to reuse `cargo build` rmeta files in the future.

body:
I agree that this short-circuiting behavior could probably use a better introduction. There's short-circuiting in terms of side effects (which we could maybe distinguish by calling it "lazy evaluation"), and there's short-circuiting in terms of which truth value to return if there are multiple values considered to be equally "true".

The instances of this sort of boolean short-circuiting that I'm most familiar with are Python and Perl, where boolean operators can return the value of one of their operands, which aren't necessarily boolean (but can be interpreted as having "truthiness").

In a way, Rust short-circuits both the lazy and eager variants of the boolean methods here. The eager operators evaluate the operand, but don't output it unless it's required to determine the output truth value. We could interpret that as a sort of partial short-circuiting (which is only visible because these methods output one of their operands, not necessarily a `bool`).

(I'm not especially familiar with this part of the compiler, these are the results of skimming the source code, so take it with a grain of salt)

`inherent_impls` uses the `impls_map` that is collected by `InherentCollect` in this somewhat lengthy function: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4d3ce2e7dac840d6ac7d658a5506eb31492fb3ef/compiler/rustc_typeck/src/coherence/inherent_impls.rs#L43-L354
Notice this line: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4d3ce2e7dac840d6ac7d658a5506eb31492fb3ef/compiler/rustc_typeck/src/coherence/inherent_impls.rs#L51
This has the effect of converting the `Self` type to a semantic `ty::Ty`, resolving any type alias, so no type alias's `DefId` ever gets registered in there, hence `inherent_impls` returns nothing.

body:
> Looks like the alignment vs minimum mismatch is a thing to fix.

Well, after further experimentation, I agree that `max(4, layout.size.bytes_usize())` is not correct, and I've updated this, although I haven't pushed yet.

Based on what I've observed, it seems that stdcall expects that the space for a given argument is the smallest multiple of 4 bytes into which that argument can fit; this is true even for types like `f64` that might under other circumstances be aligned to the nearest 8-byte boundary.

The alignment information that I get from the `Layout` struct doesn't really help here.  As one example, the `Layout` value for `u8` indicates an alignment of 1 byte (both abi and preferred), which doesn't match stdcall: `fn f(x: u8, y: u8)` has an argument size of 8 bytes, not 2.

Unfortunately, messy code is probably unavoidable -- best I've got so far is `(layout.size.bytes_usize() + 3) & !3`, with a comment explaining what's going on.

Beyond that, is there anything else you want to see here?

Ok, it looks like I'm sort of stuck here.  As far as I can determine, something in the query system requires `NativeLib` to implement `HashStable`.  (I'm sort of guessing here because the error happens somewhere in a big stack of macro invocations, and I'm having trouble figuring out where in this stack this requirement is imposed.)  Therefore, adding `Span` information to `NativeLib` (even indirectly, as I have) doesn't seem to be an option.

The `Span` is only necessary so I could give some sort of source location information in the error message that we signal if we encounter multiple declarations of the same external function with inconsistent calling conventions.  Do we want to settle for issuing a diagnostic without location info?  (I'm not wild about this choice.)  Alternatively, is there a better place in the compiler to detect this case and issue the error?  I would expect that a big difficulty with doing this before we've created the `NativeLib` structs is that we don't have easy access to information about all of the external declarations in one place.

> `import_table` should probably keep only `DllCallingConvention`s instead of full `DllImport`s.

I think this gets into a question about how much future proofing we should be doing here.  The RFC does call for eventual support of linking by ordinal instead of by name, and `DllImport` contains the `ordinal` field to support this in the future.  At the moment, nobody ever reads that field.  Going forward, I have no idea if/when I'm going to get around to implementing that specific bit of functionality; our primary concern is to make interoperability with the Windows API easier, and support for ordinals isn't very important for that.  I'm starting to wonder if I should just drop the field (but otherwise leave `DllImport` intact) rather than including only half-hearted support for ordinals.
