body:
Thanks! I think there needs to be a very clear indication that the example is erroneous, preferably on a line by itself. I know it seems redundant, but somehow the erroneous nature of the example to be clearly communicated when the explanation is displayed in plain text in a terminal. I think it's very easy for someone quickly scanning the `--explain` output in a terminal to assume that the second code block is an example of how to fix their code. (I think I've heard one or two examples in Discord of someone copy and pasting such an example, maybe even this one, and being upset when it didn't work.) Right now the `rustc --explain E0716` begins with 
A temporary value is being dropped while a borrow is still in active use.

Erroneous code example:

```
fn foo() -> i32 { 22 }
fn bar(x: &i32) -> &i32 { x }
let p = bar(&foo());
         // ------ creates a temporary
let q = *p;
```

Here, the expression `&foo()` is borrowing the expression `foo()`. As `foo()` is
a call to a function, and not the name of a variable, this creates a
**temporary** -- that temporary stores the return value from `foo()` so that it
can be borrowed. You could imagine that `let p = bar(&foo());` is equivalent to
this:

```
let p = {
  let tmp = foo(); // the temporary
  bar(&tmp)
}; // <-- tmp is freed as we exit this block
let q = p;
```
Note there is nothing obviously highlighting the second code block as erroneous, not even the minimal highlighting that `compile_fail` examples get in the error index web page. Even the `compile_fail` annotation that's in the `.md` file gets stripped from the code fence. I guess we could repeat the wording before the first code block and say ``` Erroneous code example: ``` on a line by itself? Maybe also change the comment to something like this? ``` }; // <-- ERROR: tmp is freed as we exit this block ```
author: tlyu

body:
Hm, I think "You could imagine that `let p = bar(&foo());` is equivalent to this:" should mean it's also erroneous. If it's unclear, it's better to reword that instead of just saying it's equivalent again otherwise it'll be repeating the same wording with the same meaning. I'd reword something like "You could imagine that `let p = bar(&foo());` is equivalent to this which also fails".
And note that "tmp is freed as we exit this block" is not the error itself, it explains why the error happened.
author: JohnTitor

body:
How do you feel about putting another

```
Erroneous code example:
```

line in front of the second erroneous code block? I think making it any more verbose, or trying to have the explanatory paragraph serve the purpose of highlighting the erroneous nature, will make the code block more likely to be misinterpreted as a fix.

Also, the existing error output (from the playground) is very close to what the existing comment in the example says.

```
error[E0597]: `tmp` does not live long enough
 --> src/main.rs:7:7
  |
5 | let p = {
  |     - borrow later stored here
6 |   let tmp = foo(); // the temporary
7 |   bar(&tmp)
  |       ^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
8 | }; // <-- tmp is freed as we exit this block
  | - `tmp` dropped here while still borrowed
```

[RFC 1567](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/1567-long-error-codes-explanation-normalization.md) says to put a comment on the erroneous line, which I guess is line 7 here? Either way, it seems to recommend explicitly putting `// error:` in a comment.

body:
This seems to change the behavior of `can_emit_warnings`. In particular, if there is a non-lint-based warning, it is now allowed to be emitted (that is, something that creates a warning diagnostic without going through `struct_warn`).  Those are very rare.  This seems to hobble `can_emit_warnings` such that it only impacts non-lints that use `struct_warn`, which is also very rare.

This also doesn't seem to be correct for TRACK_DIAGNOSTICS.  I believe it should only be called if the diagnostic is pushed onto `future_breakage_diagnostics` below. It is not clear to me how important it is that TRACK_DIAGNOSTICS gets called. It appears to have something to do with incremental, but what happens if it is not called?

Also, the old code seems broken to me. I don't see how it is possible for a diagnostic to have a level of Warning and `can_emit_warnings` is false (I believe the level will always be Allow with `--cap-lints=allow`).  It seems like that call to TRACK_DIAGNOSTICS would never happen.

In general, the problem seems that `emit_diagnostic` does not have enough information to know if this was a force-warns diagnostic.  Maybe DiagnosticId::Lint could add a field to indicate it was force-warn (similar to the has_future_breakage field)?

Actually I don't think we should box here. The assertion exists to prevent memory bloat; 48 and 56-sized objects will typically take part in the same arena region (i.e. both are stored in 60-64 byte blocks) so there won't be additional bloat. On the other hand, boxing guarantees that there will be additional allocation.

Or we should measure it. But I would prefer to bump this number over boxing.

Aha, finally found that issue - https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/73047 (and https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/74731).

Sometimes it's preferable for the "other crate" to not exist in its `.rlib` form, proc macro crates and other "macro only" crates clearly "overstay their welcome" when they exist only for the spans to be decodable from them.
I also know that right now we simply drop some spans from proc macro (dependency?) crates so their rlibs are not required, but ideally they would be preserved.

body:
Well, more so, you can now use multiple generic lifetimes in `impl Trait` *where the lifetimes don't explicitly outlive another*.

For example, you can now do
```rust
fn foo<'a, 'b>(...) -> impl Trait<'a, 'b> { .. }
```
whereas before you had to do (for example)
```rust
fn foo<'a, 'b: 'a>(...) -> impl Trait<'a, 'b> { .. }
```

Note that this is has already been conditionally stable in the desugared `impl Trait` of `async fn`, but can now is stabilized for all functions.

body:
I have some good news and less good news here. ~The good news is, this PR uses basically the same piece of code that emits the error above, the "nice region errors"~ (I take that back the error above is not a nice region error 😅 but some of the others in the blessed test expectations are), so it's at least not impossible to reach parity. I believe this was purposeful and one of Matthew's goals (I'm only the slightly-informed messenger here).

The "bad" news is the data: I don't think I have access to the actual same `ObligationCause`s in this case (or couldn't find them when I looked) so if you or @nikomatsakis (I know he won't see this notification, it's more of a message for when/if he also reviews this PR) can point me in the right direction to add them, I'll be glad to work on this more.

To be more specific, the migrate-mode error note above is emitted by [`report_placeholder_failure`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/b5a2ccee81406303324016d03399fac68ceb6718/compiler/rustc_infer/src/infer/error_reporting/note.rs#L327) which specifically looks for a `BindingObligation` cause. 

With this PR, this is an [`UpperBoundUniverseConflict`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/86700/files#diff-29ead0842640658ccc449c0f3457618f666ba141016fe65d45e1a2d71d3cb926R322-R328) but with types value pairs, so [the nice region error is not actually emitted](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/b5a2ccee81406303324016d03399fac68ceb6718/compiler/rustc_infer/src/infer/error_reporting/nice_region_error/placeholder_error.rs#L166) as these placeholder conflicts are only about placeholder and traits mismatches. body:
Thanks for the suggestion, but I don't think that this is what we want here. The `if` block is responsible for adding the following explanatory note to the error message:
```
error[E0572]: return statement outside of function body
 --> test.rs:2:10
  |
1 | / fn foo() {
2 | |     [(); return];
  | |          ^^^^^^ the return is part of this body...
3 | | }
  | |_- ...not the enclosing function body
```
Without it, or if the enclosing item is not a function, the same error is emitted, just without the extra note:
```
error[E0572]: return statement outside of function body
 --> test.rs:1:25
  |
1 | const N: usize = { [(); return]; };
  |                         ^^^^^^
```
The intention is that the note should explain why the `return` is outside of a function body, if it _appears_ to be inside one. But it only makes sense to issue such a note if the enclosing item actually _is_ a function.

You are right in that the check should also cover functions in trait and impl items, which I have fixed now.

The offset in the slower `step` and `step_by` using the primitive slice is made up for by the faster `is_empty` and `check_len` code, and since they're always called in conjunction, this should in practice be identical (or trivially faster). So, deduplication is definitely worth it here.

```asm
;; Version1 uses the raw pointers.
example::Version1::new:
        mov     rax, rdi
        lea     rdx, [rsi + rdi]
        ret

example::Version1::step_by:
        mov     rax, rdi
        add     qword ptr [rdi], rsi
        ret

example::Version1::step:
        mov     rax, rdi
        add     qword ptr [rdi], 1
        ret

example::Version1::is_empty:
        mov     rax, qword ptr [rdi]
        cmp     rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8]
        sete    al
        ret

example::Version1::check_len:
        mov     rax, qword ptr [rdi + 8]
        sub     rax, qword ptr [rdi]
        cmp     rax, rsi
        setae   al
        ret

;; Version2 uses the primitive slice type.
example::Version2::new:
        mov     rdx, rsi
        mov     rax, rdi
        ret

example::Version2::step_by:
        mov     rax, rdi
        add     qword ptr [rdi], rsi
        sub     qword ptr [rdi + 8], rsi
        ret

example::Version2::step:
        mov     rax, rdi
        add     qword ptr [rdi], 1
        add     qword ptr [rdi + 8], -1
        ret

example::Version2::is_empty:
        cmp     qword ptr [rdi + 8], 0
        sete    al
        ret

example::Version2::check_len:
        cmp     qword ptr [rdi + 8], rsi
        setae   al
        ret

example::main:
        ret
```

Actually, this has different logic. We can't do `self.num_digits <= Self::MAX_DIGITS`, because that would cause an indexing error in the cause where `self.num_digits == Self::MAX_DIGITS`, and we can't do `self.num_digits < Self::MAX_DIGITS`, since that would prevent incrementing to `MAX_DIGITS`, which then causes significant issues elsewhere.

A quick test on values with a lot of digits will demonstrate this:

```rust
let value = dec2flt::<f32>(format!("{}e-38", append_zeros(f1, 656))).unwrap();
assert_eq(value.to_bits(), 0x7ffffe);   // Fails, actual value is 0xccccd
```

body:
I'll submit another PR then later, since this PR Is relatively large already. That being said, it might be a bit more complex to do, since the question is "what differs". `let f: f64 = 0.1;` differs from what the user wrote, but it's very close to the nearest possible float. Also, there is no exact representation: do we use `0.10000000000000000555`, the rounding to 20 decimal places? If someone writes `let f: f64 = 0.10000000000000000555`, since by default it formats to `0.1`, do we warn of the difference, even though the representation is quite exact?

It might be doable by limiting the output to the number of input digits, with the same exponent as the input, but that would likely have to be handled elsewhere. 

I'm assuming the best way would be as follows, which is mostly handled by the tokenizer:

1. Get if there's exponent notation.
2. Count the number of significant digits.
3. If there's scientific notation, check if the output is identical to `format!("{:.*e}", digits - 1, f);`, after removing the `+` sign digits, and shifting digits from the exponent to the significant digits or vice versa as necessary.
4. If there isn't, check if the output is identical to `format!("{:.*}", digits, f);`.

Note, that we do need to shift digits, since cases like:

```rust
let f = 12345e10;
```

Will be formatted as:

```rust
"1.2345e14"
```

Which obviously, would require us to shift the decimal place to ensure the same exponent (shift the decimal point 4-places right, and since the decimal point is missing in the input, remove it). Currently, the tokenizer produces:

```rust
/// "12.34f32", "0b100.100"
Float { base: Base, empty_exponent: bool },
```

So we would need likely to have more information when parsing the float from the token. Which is doable, and would likely go in `compiler/rustc_mir_build/src/thir/constant.rs::parse_float`.

Other cases we'd need to handle include floats with `1.` where the values differ from the formatted cases by trimmed leading or trailing zeros. For example:

```rust
println!("{:.*}", 1, 1.);   // 1.0
```

body:
> Then you wouldn't even need the seemingly-unrelated I: FusedIterator constraint here.

In place iteration works roughly like this

1. retrieve source iter to get a write pointer
2. perform loop that gets elements from the iterator and writes to the pointer
3. retrieve source iter again to drop the remainder and then steal the allocation

Which means that once we have started iterating the source must stay retrievable. Which means the iterator cannot be fused through the option because that would drop the source. So it can only work for `FusedIterator` which doesn't switch the option variant.

> I think a decision from T-libs-api on what the policy for const-unstable trait impls should look like would be merited.

I don't think we have any objection to starting to land const impls as long as they are properly gated, i.e. stable code cannot be broken by ongoing churn in the const impl feature, all the way through its stabilization or eventual removal. I can't judge that from the PR but if the compiler team asserts it's properly gated, then it's ready.

As for which impls to make const, I think the bar is going to be the same as for const inherent methods: it has to be reasonably usable in const or have an extremely strong justification otherwise. For example we regularly reject const on an inherent method of a type that is impossible to construct in const, even if that method's implementation is otherwise compatible with const.

body:
This is a good start. I've not checked the logic in too much detail, I will do after some initial changes are made. 

There should only be a single lint name involved here - this currently uses `reachable` and `reachable_patterns` (`reachable_patterns` being the lint itself, and `reachable` being used to indicate a match expression ought to be being checked). I'd recommend changing this so that there's only `reachable_patterns` (perhaps renamed to `non_exhaustive_reachable_patterns`), that is allow-by-default. When you emit a lint, the logic for that will work out if it should be shown to the user based on the lint level, so you shouldn't need to check if the attribute is present or not, if the expression is annotated with a `#[{allow,deny,warn}(reachable_patterns)]` then it'll fire, if not, it won't.

Given that a new lint is a user-facing change, this probably warrants a [major change proposal](https://forge.rust-lang.org/compiler/mcp.html) too.

The `reachable_patterns` lint detects when a match expressions would not be considered exhaustive if the required wildcard arm were not present.

body:
Handles are actually truncated to 32 bits before being used in `OwnedStore`, so this will actually impact both 32-bit and 64-bit hosts similarly:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a8b8558f083d86247ef3260ebb4f97b276cdbf73/library/proc_macro/src/bridge/handle.rs#L29-L30

This was actually already the case before the changes in this patch stack, and this change isn't making anything worse. Previously the code atomic was defined in handle definition macro instead of being written out separately:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/a8b8558f083d86247ef3260ebb4f97b276cdbf73/library/proc_macro/src/bridge/client.rs#L23

Whenever a new `Ident` was created it would be intered in this store, and the counter stored in the client dylib's globals would be atomically incremented by `{Interned,Owning}Store`. To my knowledge, @eddyb did this to make sure that if a proc macro stashed an `Ident` (or `Literal`, `Span` or other handle) in global state it would not be possible to observe identifier re-use on subsequent invocations. Because of that, randomized idents won't actually be necessary to exhaust this number, as `*Store` is destroyed after each macro invocation, but the counters are global (within each loaded dylib) so a set of completely fresh integers will be used for the next invocation's store.

author: nagisa

body:
> I wonder if we might want to force private definition of the personality fn in every CU of every crate?

That is impossible. There are two different possible eh_personality functions that can be used. Either the one in libpanic_unwind or the one in libpanic_abort. This means that codegen isn't possible when using private eh_personality functions until you chose the final panic strategy. In addition both depend on at least libcore, so which crate do you compile first? Libcore has to be compiled before either as they depend on libcore, but libcore also has to be compiled after either as it needs eh_personality due to many functions needing to run cleanup on unwinding to drop locals.

body:
we only get these fairly unhelpful errors if our impl is illegal and fails the coherence check.
imo only emitting the following error is the best fix here:
```
error[E0210]: type parameter `Foo` must be used as the type parameter for some local type (e.g., `MyStruct<Foo>`)
  --> $DIR/issue-28981.rs:5:6
   |
LL | impl<Foo> Deref for Foo { }
   |      ^^^ type parameter `Foo` must be used as the type parameter for some local type
   |
   = note: implementing a foreign trait is only possible if at least one of the types for which it is implemented is local
   = note: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for a type parameter
```
so this overlapping impl errors would only trigger for either an actually relevant extern impl, e.g. `impl<T> Trait for Vec<T>` and `impl Trait for Vec<LocalType>`, or when both impls are in the local crate, at which point "nondeterminism" isn't an issue.

Wait, something seems wrong here. Maybe I was wrong to suggest the `commit_if_ok`. 

In the event that `Ok(None)` is returned, I believe we already guarantee that `opt_normalize_projection_type` doesn't modify the inference state.

In the event that `Err` is returned, we will push things into `self.obligations`. If we're going to use `commit_if_ok`, we'd have to ensure that those things are removed, or else they are leaking through a transaction, and that's a bug.

I don't think it actually matters, though, it things *do* leak out in the case of an error. The only thing we push in there is an obligation to prove that the trait-ref holds, and it's ok for that to go on and be proven with the placeholders. This actually holds for any obligations that get pushed.

The case I was worried  about was something like: we return a type whose value will be informed b solving those obligations, but then we abandon it and use `ty` instead. But that just doesn't happen.

body:
Given `foo: &mut (u32, u32)`, there are a few scenarios to consider:

* If the closure mutates `foo.0` but we wind up capturing `foo`, we only need a "unique" borrow of `foo`.
* If the closure mutates `foo.0` *and we capture `foo.0`*, we need a "mut" borrow.

In short, the need for a "mut" borrow depends on what data we ultimately capture. 

Let's put off fixing this for a follow-up PR.

These panics were intentionally added in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/66059, as a way of catching misuses of uninitialized memory. Even though `std::mem::uninitialized` now 'happens' to zero out these types, users **should not** be relying on this behavior (as your doc comment states). That is, writing `std::mem::uninitialized::<bool>()` is still a bug - any code doing so is broken, and should not be 'un-broken' by removing the legitimate panic.
author: Aaron1011

body:
Note that this is the only user of that function, so if we end up removing it we might also want to remove its support infrastructure.

> I thought the whole point was that mem::uninitialized is broken for any type. Why are types with niches being singled out?

It is "slightly less broken" for types like `i32` in the sense that, as far as we know, it will not actually cause miscompilations when used with such a type.

It is in fact not at all broken for types that are allowed to be uninitialized, such as `MaybeUninit<T>`.

> That is, writing std::mem::uninitialized::<bool>() is still a bug - any code doing so is broken, and should not be 'un-broken' by removing the legitimate panic.

I guess the point is that yes, it is a bug, but if we can guarantee that nothing will actually go horribly wrong then maybe we should also not have the panic -- therefore we increase "de-facto" but not "de-jure" compatibility with old broken code.

This brings me to an idea... can you make this code still return proper uninit memory under `cfg(miri)`? That way Miri can still detect incorrect uses of this function.
author: RalfJung

This was started in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/79296 but then stalled when the rather large crater results had to be analyzed.

body:
> Are there any types that are allowed to be uninitialized other than MaybeUninit (and arrays and tuples of MaybeUninit)?

Yes:
- The type `()` (or really any inhabited zero-sized type... if you only consider the validity invariant, not the safety invariant)
- Any user-defined `union` type... well to be fair this is not ratified yet, that's just what I would propose. But I think there is consensus that any `union` with a field of size zero (essentially, a user defining their own `MaybeUninit`) is okay to be left uninitialized.

Now, I am not saying that this is all that useful, I just want to get our facts straight so we have a solid basis to make decisions on. :)  The only legitimate reason I can think of to call `mem::uninitialized` is to create an array of `MaybeUninit`, and we should probably just offer a better API for that (possibly using const generics, like other stdlib APIs are already doing AFAIK).

Worth noting here too that even with this PR removing the panic and changing the implementation to `zeroed`, rustc still independently produces a scary warning when attempting to use `uninitialized` with any type with invalid values:
```
warning: the type `bool` does not permit being left uninitialized
 --> un.rs:3:22
  |
3 |     let x = unsafe { std::mem::uninitialized::<bool>() };
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |                      |
  |                      this code causes undefined behavior when executed
  |                      help: use `MaybeUninit<T>` instead, and only call `assume_init` after initialization is done
  |
  = note: `#[warn(invalid_value)]` on by default
  = note: booleans must be either `true` or `false`
```
So even though the panic no longer exists (to the benefit of people using libraries that do this), people writing this code themselves (who will therefore be seeing warnings) will still be made aware that this isn't a good idea (even if, for the moment, it may not actually be invoking UB from the compiler's perspective).

While it would be possible, I intentionally wanted to avoid doing that for two reasons:

body:
Should we report an error on every error return path so that callers can't rely on any failure not reporting an error & failing compilation to be even more conservative, or just report the parse error?

With just reporting an error on expansion failure or parse errors, I could see callers relying on e.g. checking if an expression is literal by calling `expand_literal`, and assuming it isn't literal & using it as a runtime expression with a different expansion if `expand_literal` fails. This could theoretically be used to support something like a `regex!` with a potentially dynamic string argument which eagerly compiles if the expression is a literal.

I don't really see much use for recovering on parse errors other than potentially avoiding duplicate errors if the macro both checks if it's a literal and uses it as a normal expression (though a macro should be able to pre-parse the expression with `syn`)

body:
>  see rustc-dev-guide

*subtly* implying that I have to write a section for the rustc-dev-guide for us to merge this :p

> When the substs are loaded, they will be the "identity substs" (is this true?) for the constant

not quite, going to write the `rustc-dev-guide` section soon, but e.g.
```rust
fn foo<const N: usize>() -> [u8; N + 1] { todo!() }

fn bar() {
    foo::<3>();
}
```
here the substs for the `N + 1` constant is `3` inside of `bar` while the default substs is the parameter `N`.

So if `substs_` is `Some`, it may either be the default substs - which are all used generic parameters of the parent and, in the future, the bound vars used by the const, e.g. `for<'a> Trait<[u8; foo::<'a>()]>`-  or an instantiation of these params.

> In other words, why do we need HAS_KNOWN_TY_PARAM vs HAS_TY_PARAM?

In other words, where does it cause problems to always assume something has generic parameters if there are unknown anon const substs? 

In wfcheck this would cause us to incorrectly not emit an error here if the default type if the default of a param contained an anon const with unknown substs:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/effea9a2a0d501db5722d507690a1a66236933bf/compiler/rustc_typeck/src/check/wfcheck.rs#L856

Most of the other uses of `has_param_types_or_consts` would not cause any bugs as we call `var.subst(tcx, subst)` before that which exposes all default substs. Verifying that isn't trivial though and requires some subtle knowledge about how all of this works, so we should avoid relying on it imo.

For `HAS_FREE_REGIONS` the relevant method is `is_global` which uses the negated type flag, so if we always set `HAS_FREE_REGIONS` and use `var.is_global() == false` to influence user visible behavior this would also be a bug.

I guess that e.g. this would be an issue https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/effea9a2a0d501db5722d507690a1a66236933bf/compiler/rustc_typeck/src/impl_wf_check/min_specialization.rs#L366

body:
That's right. I don't know that it matters much, I don't expect that most people would be mixing these, but it made for an easy way to make something well-defined, rather than one command-line argument having precedence over the other.

It would be slightly simpler code to not maintain the ordering, but I considered it a net win to have something more easily explained. In this case `--debug-compilation-dir` acts exactly like an alias for `remap-path-prefix=$(pwd)=`. Anything else seems to require more explanation in the docs, and more risk of an arbitrary change breaking some edge case in the future.
author: danakj

body:
This only matches the precise cwd, not a trailing slash, so you're required to map to a non-empty path. So `/home/me/src/foo.rs` with a cwd of `/home/me` can only be mapped to `./src/foo.rs`. But if you match against `/home/me/` then you can choose to map it to '' giving `src/foo.rs` which is a bit cleaner. But that means you need to take the current path separator into account.

This implementation also has the pitfall that it will remap `/home/meat/src/bar.rs` to `at/src/bar.rs` since `--remap-path-prefix` works strictly on strings without regard to path separators.

I think there's an opportunity to discuss a more pathname-aware prefix-replacement algorithm, but there are a lot of edge cases to take into account (the current algorithm, for all its faults, is very simple to explain).
author: jsgf

body:
It’s cleaner without the path separator but there’s no less functionality with it, right?

If you wanted to specify a different prefix you can with something like “/foo/.” which would translate “/home/me/src/file.rs” into “/foo/./src/file.rs”. It’s not how you’d normally write it by hand, but it functions just fine, and is universally deterministic. Is it worth it to you to add extra code in here to avoid some dots in command lines?

> This implementation also has the pitfall that it will remap /home/meat/src/bar.rs to at/src/bar.rs

Yes, true. However as this path will be rooted at the current working directory, all paths have the same prefix, so this shouldn’t actually come up, right?

Is there something we need to change here with the preexisting flag? Or could that be considered separately? The way this new flag is defined, as an alias for —remap-path-prefix, would allow for the existing flag to evolve and both command line flags could change in tandem.
author: danakj

body:
You wouldn't be able to map a path to `src/foo.rs` with no prefix, and random intermixing of ``, `./` or even `././` gets messy esp if you're trying to be careful because of exact string matching. But no, not the end of the world.

Edit: it's implemented in terms of `Path::strip_prefix`, which ignores spurious `./` `foo//bar`, etc, so its more robust than plain string matching. It also won't be confused by partial components in the prefix.
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/7db08eeb0057de86ea2bdbd4c3a085cb8516b653/compiler/rustc_span/src/source_map.rs#L1026

body:
> I don't think it follows that we need components to preserve that semantic difference.

Well... the thing is that `Components` implements `AsRef<Path>`, so if you have a generic function taking it via `AsRef` then it'll behave differently depending on whether you pass in a `Components` or something else that implements `AsRef<Path>`.

It's consistent with existing documentation, it's clearly spelled out that `path.components()` will strip trailing slashes, but previously that wasn't considered a semantic difference (since `Eq` considered them equal), now it is.

Here I mean `const`. `const` and `pure` are C function attributes (e.g. see [Common Function Attributes](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Common-Function-Attributes.html#Common-Function-Attributes)). Annotating a function with `ffi_const` says that it's C `const`, and annotating with `ffi_pure` says that it's C `pure`. I could use `ffi_const` and `ffi_pure` instead, but I felt it was more readable to lift the covers up to what they mean in GCC or other C compilers. What do you think?

The `cfg_data` could be cached somewhere around this point. Doing so could presumably result in some small performance saving for the case where `target == self.target`, which is likely to come up with the most frequency. I'm not sure whether this is worthwhile, or if so, how to go about it.

body:
I'm not sure if this is the correct behavior; in the implementation I had started, I initially went with `FfiSafe` but then switched to `FfiUnsafe`. The reason is that according to the issue where the new behavior was discussed (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/77841#issuecomment-716575747) \[emphasis mine\],

> That's a good point. So here is a proposed set of rules:
> 
>   * A `repr(transparent)` type `T` must meet the following rules:
>       
>     * It may have any number of 1-ZST fields
>     * In addition, it may have at most one other field of type U
> 
> 
> If that other field is present, then T behaves like type U for ABI purposes. **Otherwise, T consists only of 1-ZST types, and it behaves like `()`, which is the "canonical" 1-ZST.**

and `()` is currently FFI-**unsafe**:

```
warning: `extern` block uses type `()`, which is not FFI-safe
 --> src/lib.rs:2:18
  |
2 |     fn good17(p: ());
  |                  ^^ not FFI-safe
  |
  = note: `#[warn(improper_ctypes)]` on by default
  = help: consider using a struct instead
  = note: tuples have unspecified layout
```

There's also this later comment in that thread (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/77841#issuecomment-716698421):

> Hmm, the lint considers `()` an improper_ctype. But then an empty struct is UB(!?) in C, so I guess there isn't a canonical ABI for this.

body:
I believe the reason the target data layout exist is that rustc needs the information itself for layout calculation and some other things.

But we don't need all the information -- only the parts parsed into TargetDataLayout. So possibly what we could do is reduce the data layout info in targets to just the necessary information, and then only check that this is consistent with the LLVM data layout (but then use the more precise LLVM data layout for code generation).

In these two cases, the newly added information is stack alignment and non-integral address spaces, both of which we don't care about.

Hey I was [refreshing my knowledge](https://www.gnu.org/software/libc/manual/html_node/Duplicating-Descriptors.html) on `dup()`/`dup2()`/`FD_DUPFD` this morning (as I wrote this code 9 months ago!), and I don't think your interpretation "since duped file descriptors normally don't share a seek position, nonblocking status and various other properties" is correct.

According to the above link, it is exactly the opposite: dup-ed file descriptors DO share seek position, nonblocking status and various other properties. Duped file descriptors are nothing else but aliases of each other, and their only (limited) use seems to be lifetime management, where you can close the original file descriptor while the duped one continues to live and vice versa.

I think more or less this is what my implementation also does, doesn't it? (we can forget about the `CLOEXEC` semantics as that's irrelevant when you don't have processes)?

As for the use case with Rocket (remembered that too) - Rocket was `dup`-ing the file descriptor (socket really) so that it spins a separate socket writer from socket reader, and manages their lifetimes separately too.

body:
OK, so I've force-pushed a cleanup of the `os/espidf` module:
* First of all, I decided to leave as stable everything, because, well, filesystems on the ESP-IDF might be a corner case but they are there, the `stat()` function works (even if a bit slow on the SPIFFS FS), so why shall I be seeking for unstable, where it does not make sense
* I've removed all commented out code that should not be there, double-checked that the `raw::stat` module is a faithful representation of what is in there in the ESP-IDF in terms of stat structure
* Some stubbed out code *MUST* stay and return 0. Turns out, the "platform specific" `MetadataExt` trait is not so platform specific, as it is used by `os::unix::fs` which is re-exposing its methods to the outside world. Since the ESP-IDF claims to be in the unix family, it *must* support all methods `os::unix::fs` re-expose, even if a subset of those (the `*_nsec` ones) return 0. I'm not setting a precedent: our sibling bare-metal RTOS `vxworks` port [does the same](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/library/std/src/os/vxworks/fs.rs#L82) with `*_nsec`, for the very same reasons.  
* Finally, I've kept versions at 1.1.0 (for the deprecated stuff) and at 1.8.0 for the `MetadataExt` trait as everybody else does. Again, an example: the vxworks port [was merged](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/61946) ~ 2019, while 1.8.0 is at least 3 years older (2016), let alone version 1.1.0. Yet, it uses these very same versions, instead of the compiler version at the time the port was merged
* Moreover: I would actually argue that re-using these versions as they are is even the correct behavior: imagine a cross-platform crate that uses this stuff, either via `os::unix::fs` or `os::platform` and sets the minimum compiler version requirement to 1.8.0. From the point of view of the crate that's the correct behavior, as everybody else except the ESP-IDF port is having those since 1.8.0. Now, people willing to consume that fictitious crate with ESP-IDF will of course never use a 1.8.0 version of the compiler simply because ESP-IDF support is not there. So putting a higher version on those std items does not seem to help. Quite the opposite.

body:
Support for Xtensa touches multiple crates and does not necessarily land into all of them in an atomic fashion:
- (1) `libc` crate: Here, it landed for the first time [> 1 year ago](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/pull/1748) and was [recently extended](https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/pull/2310) with extra APIs and reworked to not really mean "Xtensa" but ESP-IDF for Risv32 *and* Xtensa and any architecture supported by ESP-IDF in fact.
- (2) `library/std`: Here, it lands now. The only place that needs "Xtensa" explicitly listed (as opposed to branching based on `target_os = "espidf"`) is this one AFAIR.
- (3) `rust/compiler/rustc_target`: Not landed yet, but we have a patchset for that. However, the Xtensa arch needs to be upstreamed in LLVM first.

Now, if you or somebody else feels uncomfortable having this conditional before the actual support for the Xtensa *targets* being upstreamed first, I can remove that line.

But if it does not do harm, why bother? We'll have to add it back anyway once (3) lands. And in the meantime, we'll know that libStd is Xtensa "ready" once the Xtensa targets get upstreamed.

body:
You proceed to give some semi-complete description of implementation details how the specialized `from_iter` implementation in this module operates. The description seems hard (or impossible) to follow without also looking at the actual source code. AFAIK, explaining in words exactly what some source code does is often not a very useful form of documentation.

You intermix some short mentioning of relevant safety requirements, related issues, important points. Thus this is probably more than just the “description of implementation details” that I called it in the previous paragraph. I suppose, the heading “In-place iteration performs the following steps” doesn’t hint at the presence of all this extra information either, though. Some (or all?) of the additional information provided here seems like it might be better placed alongside the implementation itself.

**Overall, I’m wondering who is intended to read this text and for what reason.**

I can think of someone who
* wants to read and understand the specialization infrastructure and concrete implementation(s) of `.collect()`
  * _but_ they’d read the source code, too, so for them there’s probably lots of redundancy, and a lack of linking the explainations to the actual source code in these docs
* wants to get a feeling of which cases of calling `.collect()` results in what kind of runtime behavior regarding optimization of code and number of allocations
  * _but_ they wouldn’t care about the exact implementation and wouldn’t necessarily read some `alloc`-internal (private) module level docs in the first place
* wants to modify the implementations in or around this module
  * _but_ they’d prefer to work with concrete invariants attatched to concrete `unsafe` functions and traits
  * I guess they do appreciate your explicit mention of the fact that the current situation requires lots of “holistic”, “non-local” reasoning because it tells them that they won’t get all the relevant details regarding memory safety of the existing specializations in the form of concrete invariants on concrete functions/traits

<hr>

Let me show in an example how there’s a problem of unclear target audience for these docs as well as some general lack of details (or alternatively references to other places that fill in the details)

Take for example the phrase “For this to be sound the source has to use pointers too to perform its reads, otherwise there would be aliasing conflicts.” in step 1. From reading this sentence, I don’t know the exact location in the source code that this part discusses, I don’t know if there’s sufficient documentation on these soundness requirements on the trait infrastructure for `SourceIter` (and/or other traits) already and if yes where to find those. I’m not told that this isn’t discussing some generic properties of a widely-used trait infrastructure; instead “the source” is referring to just two types, `IntoIter` for `Vec` and for `BinaryHeap`.

And what to take from this “A has to do B” statement!? Does it tell me that it’s important to know that these two types use raw pointers directly? body:
> The issue here is that afaik rustdoc has no mechanism to link to the source and some of the traits are `doc(hidden)` so they can't be linked to either. But I can give the latter a try anyway.

Regarding `doc(hidden)`, the linking may still work when you’re using something like
```
RUSTDOCFLAGS='--document-private-items --document-hidden-items' x.py doc library/std
```
to build the docs. Except if `doc(hidden)` items generate error messages when you intra-doc-link to them (from private items, which are usually not rendered either), I haven’t tested that much yet. Unfortunately I myself seem to have recently broken this command (with the `--document-hidden-items`) by replacing the import of `TrustedRandomAccess` with `TrustedRandomAccessNoCoerce` in a module that had a hidden doc link to `TrustedRandomAccess`… oops… maybe we should fix this and somehow add a test for this?

> Except that "the implementation" is not a single place given all the moving parts that are involved. So to give an overview it has to be placed in one piece so that the reader doesn't have to collect all the individual pieces first to get a picture.

Maybe this can be fixed… I just remembered something I’ve seen in the Haskell standard library. Take a look [here for example](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/containers-0.6.5.1/docs/src/Data.Map.Internal.html). There’s some named “[Note: …]” sections explaining implementation details that are lengthy and/or relevant at multiple places in the source code. Then, comments in the code refer to them by `See note: …`. Assuming that you’re unfamiliar with the lexical syntax of Haskell, note that these notes and the references to them are only part of comments, not any rendered documentation, and I personally don’t know if these “See notes: …” links have any sort of tooling that allows you to follow them when reading the source code or if they are just human convention. Anyways, my takeaway: We could copy this style/approach somewhat. Instead of the rather unstructured approach of just randomly addressing important soundness considerations hidden in the middle of a section describing itself as “In-place iteration performs the following steps”, you could give every notable aspect, a small headline \[e.g. **“Use of pointers for inplace-from_iter”**, etc…] and a self-contained description, and then simply refer to it from multiple relevant parts of the source code that all form “the implementatation”.



> Or do you think it would be better to just drop the information that this module requires the interaction of multiple unsafe traits to work correctly and then just leave the reader to figure out the details by reading the implementation and the documentation on those other traits?

AFAICT, the implementation is not all that long, so realistically reading the implementation is an approach that everyone trying to gaining an understanding of the implementation will attempt. Maybe all we need is to improve the inline docs of the implementation to be easier to understand without too much prior knowledge on all the traits involved, i.e. the approach could be: Make the implementation itself an even better and more readable alternative to the list you created here.

Even if we don’t do this, I think there could be: References in the implementation referring back to the “steps” laid out in the module-level docs (in order to link those more clearly, and also to keep this list of steps up to date); separating the description of what happens from discussion of safety considerations, either by completely separating the step-by-step description of what’s done from the following discussion, or at least by visibly separating the “what happens” part from the rest _within_ each of the steps listed. Also I wouldn’t mind if you added – on every aspect you’re discussing – an explanation whether that aspect is _fully_ covered/explained by documented safety-invariants on unsafe functions/traits, or if – instead – there’s non-local reasoning involved. The latter (i.e. explanations of some instance of non-local reasoning) should probably best be called out explicitly everywhere, so the reader knows to pay attention and maybe even to encourage them to think about future improvements that could make requirements more locally documented.



> We can certainly reduce it, but ultimately you'll at least have to reason about the interaction of multiple unsafe traits, a dozen implementations thereof and the safe things those implementations can do (such as the clones and panics mentioned). I think having a place that explains how those things fit together still helps even if in principle each piece already does its part in isolation.

I think you’re addressing two different things here. There’s definitely merit in explaining interactions of multiple unsafe traits, etc, even when each trait already has its own documentation with a correct complete list of safety requirements, etc. And then there’s explanations of implementation details that are only sound because we applied knowledge of lots of other implementation details of other parts in the standard library, i.e. the “non-local reasoning” we’re talking about. Making clear to the reader which is which seems valuable.

Regarding fixing the non-local stuff in the future, I think some reasonably low-effort approaches for improving the situation could be to (not mutually exclusive):
* Point out important details as you did, but put them in a place that can be referenced from multiple places, then reference them from all relevant places. (See the Haskell comparison above.)
* Make clear indications about which other parts in the standard library depend on implementation details of a function / struct / etc… especially across file boundaries. Similarly indicate when unsafe code relies on implementation details of other functions / structs / etc, especially if those other functions / types might seem unrelated. (And make sure to also add “back-references” in those implementations then.)
* For **private** (and often small) specialization traits or helper traits like `AsIntoIter`, consider documenting the trait with the exhaustive list of implementors and the exhaustive of users. (For `AsIntoIter` that’s 2 implementors and one use-case, I think.) This way we don’t necessarily need to come up with a complete list of safety invariants immediately, it could just say “This trait is implemented by `vec::IntoIter` and `binary_heap::IntoIter` and used exclusively for the `SpecFromIter` implementation in `vec/source_iter_marker.rs` where unsafe code depends on the implementation details of those types.” (Still, also marking the trait and its method `unsafe` would be useful, too.) Someone who wants to add implementations would either need to understand the use-case enough in order to soundly add an implementor (updating the documentation accordingly) or they would need to flesh out some explicit safety invariants first. Arriving at an intermediate state where _some_ invariants are listed (without claiming to be complete) and the use-cases and implementors are still listed is also reasonable.

body:
So, this variadic thing was the last bit I struggled with, and I'm happy to explore better ways to represent it.

The specific example that tripped when building `std` was `libc::fcntl`, which looks like this:

```rust
pub fn fcntl(fd: ::c_int, cmd: ::c_int, ...) -> ::c_int;
```

That turns into LLVM `fn(i32, i32, ...) -> i32`. The call site for `set_cloexec` in `std` passes three args, and the `FnAbi::llvm_type` from there gave me `fn(i32, i32, i32, ...) -> i32` -- having that "extra" arg when its `FnAbi` was constructed, but still represented as variadic. However, that tripped an assertion:

```
rustc: [...]/rust/src/llvm-project/llvm/lib/Bitcode/Writer/ValueEnumerator.h:167: unsigned int llvm::ValueEnumerator::getTypeID(llvm::Type*) const: Assertion `I != TypeMap.end() && "Type not in ValueEnumerator!"' failed.
```

So I used `fixed_count` to try and get the original declaration type, which seems to work -- giving the same signature as `element_type(val_ty(fn_ptr))` would if we didn't care about being opaque.

> Maybe always using `&self.args[..self.fixed_count]` would work too though?

It at least needs to check for `c_variadic`, because I know that the `#[track_caller]` argument for `&Location` is also past the `fixed_count`. I can try it without considering the new `decl` parameter though, or outright removing that.

body:
`ParamEnv::empty()` is almost always the wrong thing.

The reason we are getting the ICE "region constraints already solved" is that the `infercx` has already reported all lifetime errors and thus destroyed its region inference system.

Usually when we want to do isolated checks like this we generate a new inference context, so you could wrap the entire function call in a `self.infcx.tcx.infer_ctxt().enter(|infcx| ..)` which will give you a fresh inference context.

The advantage of using a new context and the full `ParamEnv` over your current change is that it will also work in generic contexts where we only know that `&T: IntoIterator` because of where bounds instead of only working for types for which this is known even without bounds.

You may have to use a new lifetime (not `re_erased`, but `infcx.next_region_var(RegionVariableOrigin::Misc(DUMMY_SP))`)

body:
I have a [somewhat different approach](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/88729) that might be able to make some of this code easier to reason about.

Instead of using `look_ahead` for cases where we kind of need to parse things with non-deterministic lookahead, I do `let snapthot = self.clone()` on the `Parser` and *try to successfully parse* what the "fake" syntax would be. If that succeeds, we know that we can provide an accurate suggestion, if that doesn't, we cancel the error and rollback the parser to the previous state to emit the "normal" error we currently see and let the existing error recovery machinery take its course. With this approach, it should be possible to emit a suggestion on a case like `{0, if 1 < 2 {1} else {1}, 2, 3}`. Because cloning is somewhat expensive (but not terrible, from what I've seen), we want to avoid it on the "happy path" of well-formed code, but you can use limited `look_ahead` to see if *it could be* this case, like doing `self.look_ahead(2, |t| t.kind == &Comma)` or something.

We could even try to keep information on the `Parser` for "we are in a `const` assignment, of array type" that we check here in `maybe_suggest_brackets_instead_of_braces`, and if it is not the case, we exit early, like we do for things coming from a macro.

What do you think? (Sorry for the delay in reviewing)
